**Rival task predictors, frozen before any target was read.** For the movability half to mean anything, beta had to beat simpler explanations of why a task moves. The audit computed eight ban-free predictors for the 15 existing tasks and catalogue size as a covariate, wrote them to a canonical file, and froze them by sha256 in a hash chain before opening any outcome file (frozen at 11:59:44 UTC, first scored at 11:59:50; two later freezes left the values identical). The predictors are the twin's opening margin (the margin in log probability, under teacher forcing, of the opening of the default over that of the runner-up), the forced can rate, association clarity, the off-default excess under the novelty instruction, the diversity of human solutions (Mercury solutions labelled by the frozen rules with a judge on unknowns; audit agreement 0.97, kappa 0.97, 121 programs), the runtime merit gap between the reference programs of the runner-up and of the default (76 references timed on their hidden tests), the twin modal share and the ratio of ban unit to residual norm. Five of them (the opening margin, the novelty excess, the merit gap, the twin modal share and catalogue size) can be computed on new tasks and were frozen for the confirmation panels. Scored against the pooled escape fraction of the screen, none is informative after Holm correction (every adjusted p is 1.0), and 10 of the 15 tasks are tied at an escape fraction of 0 (Tables 179 to 181). These scores are descriptive: the escape fractions generated the hypothesis, so the freeze protects only the confirmation on new tasks.

## 5.3 Transplanting the base model's plan states into the instruct model (Qwen3-8B)

**Why.** If post-training narrowed the choice at the plan site, the narrowing should be undone by giving the instruct model the base model's own task-specification states. No earlier iteration had tried this: iteration 1 subtracted an instruct minus base direction estimated at the read position only, which destroyed the output format (Section 1.9). This experiment [ARTIFACT:art_CcZLW-9NX00l] was the first causal test of the transplant claim, and it also measured the base repertoire that every other Qwen3-8B analysis of the iteration needed.

**Design.** Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-8B-Base (revision 49e3418f, the base revision of iteration 1) ran in bf16 on one RTX 4090 with thinking off, temperature 1.0, top-p 1 and no top-k. The base model sampled 100 programs per task under the instruct chat template on identical token ids (200 on the two path tasks, with top-ups to 200 on connected components, nonoverlapping intervals and cycle detection) and 100 in plain completion. Its labels used the iteration-4 labellers with a blind judge on disagreement, and a 15-program judge audit per task agreed at least 0.86 everywhere. The base repertoire (default, beta with a 95% interval, stratum, base runner-up) was committed by hash before any hooked sample. The transplant set the hooked states to h_instruct + lambda (h_base − h_instruct) at blocks 12 to 23 for lambda in {0.25, 0.5, 1}; the states were set, not added, so nothing compounded, and at lambda 1 the hooked blocks carried the base state exactly. The controls on the same common-random-number slots were a matched-norm random displacement (per block and position), the borrowed shift (another task's mean base minus instruct direction at the same norm), and, where the random control broke the model, a random push matched on pass rate. Site controls transplanted at the read position, at blocks 0 to 11 and at blocks 24 to 35. Lambda was selected on one set of slots and confirmed on fresh slots, both under commits made before the samples.

**The base model is more diverse than the instruct model on most tasks** (Table 182). Under the same prompt the instruct twin wrote its default in 96% to 100% of programs on all 15 tasks, while 5 tasks were diverse in the base (kth smallest, shortest path, connected components, grid and top-k frequent), 7 intermediate and 3 collapsed in the base (merge intervals, nonoverlapping intervals and topological order). The base model under the chat template is a poor programmer: it wrote 14 to 55 correct programs per 100 to 200 samples, and on the grid task only 14 of 200, so the grid beta rests on attempts. On connected components it writes DFS more often than union find (32 against 19 correct programs), so the instruct default is the base model's second choice there.

## 5.4 Panel A: does the base repertoire predict which new tasks move? (Qwen3-8B)

*Three instruct twins of new units are mixed: trapped rain water (default share 0.64), minimum spanning tree weight (default share 0.66) and valid anagram (default share 0.76); on two units the instruct model is more diverse than the base: trapped rain water (twin off-default 0.36 against beta 0.23) and minimum spanning tree weight (twin off-default 0.34 against beta 0.11) (iteration-6 note).*

**Why.** The screen correlation of 0.78 was measured on the tasks that generated the hypothesis. The movability and landing halves could only be confirmed on tasks never seen, with every forecast committed from base samples before the first push. Panel A [ARTIFACT:art_8WbrpoEFslk9] built one half of those tasks.

**Design.** Nine new units derived from LeetCode problems [12] were frozen up front in new wording (a grep audit found no algorithm word or catalogue name), each with hidden tests from the dataset's input and output pairs plus seeded edge, random and stress cases, one reference per algorithm, mutants that must fail, quadratic baselines and runtime and AST labellers. A labeller passed its gate at a kappa of at least 0.8 between runtime and AST labels, an agreement of at least 0.9 between runtime and adjudicated labels and 100% of references, with one revision round on a holdout. Six of the seven planned units passed; number of islands failed after its revision (holdout kappa 0.74), and the two reserves, jump game and median of two sorted lists, ran as a logged extension. Per unit, the instruct twin drew 50 programs and the base model 100 on identical ids plus 50 in plain completion, the rivals were computed, and the forecast (default, beta with its interval, base runner-up, rivals) was committed by hash; a guard in the GPU worker refused push jobs until then. Only then did 8 isotropic directions at alpha 1 and 2 (N = 10, confirmed at N = 30 by an exact binomial test), plan noise at alpha 1 and 2 (N = 50) and temperature 1.3 (N = 50) run. The 15 existing tasks were remeasured in the same engine on the ban-free unit; we call this the remeasurement arm.

**The movability half is not supported in panel A** (Table 191). Over the six preregistered units, Spearman between beta and the escape fraction is -0.03 (exact one-sided p 0.56; Kendall 0). The one unit collapsed in the base, maximum block sum (beta 0), is immovable, as the movability half predicts, but 2 of the 5 units diverse in the base are also immovable, among them the most diverse: count primes (beta 0.81) never escapes. A bootstrap over measurement error gives a median of -0.09 (90% interval -0.37 to 0.21). With the two extension units, both diverse in the base (0.47 and 0.71) and both immovable, Spearman falls to -0.33 (p 0.80). Simple rivals tracked movability better than beta (Tables 192 and 193), and so did beta's own variants: Spearman with the escape fraction is -0.09 for beta from plain completion, -0.03 for beta that also counts correct programs labelled other as off-default (identical to beta on these units) and 0.40 for the base Hill-1 (0.16, -0.33 and 0.22 with the extension units). The three units that moved have an alternative at least twice as fast as the default (minimum runtime merit ratio 0.10 to 0.51), the three that did not have ratios of 0.86 to 4.35, and the runtime merit rival reaches -0.88; the extension unit median of two sorted lists breaks this (ratio 0.11, never escapes), and with it the rival falls to -0.66. The twin's own modal share reaches -0.70, ahead of beta by a task-bootstrap interval that excludes zero (-1.90 to -0.09).

## 5.5 Panel B: seven more new tasks and disguised variants (Qwen3-8B)

*Three instruct twins of new units are mixed: trapped rain water (default share 0.64), minimum spanning tree weight (default share 0.66) and valid anagram (default share 0.76); on two units the instruct model is more diverse than the base: trapped rain water (twin off-default 0.36 against beta 0.23) and minimum spanning tree weight (twin off-default 0.34 against beta 0.11) (iteration-6 note).*

**Why.** Panel B [ARTIFACT:art_9a8LrIv2lHbV] built the other half of the confirmation units under the same protocol, and added what we call *disguised variants*, eight bench tasks rewritten as narratives, each with a paired remeasurement of its parent, to separate a task's wording from its algorithmic affordances.

**Design.** Seven units (missing number, single number, minimum spanning tree weight, integer square root, all subsets, valid anagram and count inversions) were built with wording free of algorithm words, hidden tests checked by two independent oracles, three to six references, mutants and excluded brute force methods, and gated labellers; all seven gated, four after one revision round, and the 15-program blind audits of base labels agreed at 0.93 to 1.0. Because the base model was 46% to 61% off task under the chat template, its repertoire was raised to N = 200 per unit before any commit. Each unit's beta, base runner-up, base composition and rivals were hash-chained before its first push; then came 8 directions at alpha 1 and 2, plan noise and temperature 1.3.

**The movability half is not supported in panel B either** (Table 201). Spearman between beta and the escape fraction is 0.21 (exact one-sided p 0.33, bootstrap interval over units -0.75 to 0.95). Four units moved (single number, count inversions, minimum spanning tree weight and integer square root) and three did not: missing number (beta 0.06), all subsets (0.37) and valid anagram (0.81), the clearest disconfirming case. No unit was collapsed in the base, so the part of the movability half that says collapsed tasks are immovable is untested here. Beta ranks the graded plan noise excess better (0.82, p 0.017), and the runtime and length merit rivals track the escape fraction more closely than beta (0.54 and 0.58; Table 202), all with wide intervals. Under the preregistered sensitivities, beta from attempts gives 0.39 (p 0.18), beta from plain completion -0.45, beta from correct programs 0.04, and excluding the uncertain class or the flagged twins gives -0.03 and 0.06; a placebo with beta shuffled 1,000 times has a mean Spearman of 0.008 and rejects at 0.048.

## 5.7 Plan noise against text-level plan samplers, decoding at matched departure, and the literal cell (Qwen3-8B)

**Why.** The positioning audit of iteration 4 found that the price comparison lacked its strongest competitors: text-level plan samplers, which diversify code by sampling a plan before the program [73, 74], and a decoding baseline matched to plan noise's own departure from the twin, the baseline under which an ICLR 2027 submission (OpenReview oag3wgNLRh) found activation steering no better than ordinary decoding. The review also asked for the literal cell of the request. This experiment [ARTIFACT:art_jR6Pyy3W9xum] ran both.

**The literal cell never changes the algorithm** (Table 206). On the shortest path task with thinking on, top-k 10 and the same 20 token seeds as the iteration-4 thinking arm, moving the temperature over 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 changed the final program's algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds (one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound 0.14), and the first approach named in the thinking changed in 0 of 20. All 100 traces completed, every final program was heap-based Dijkstra, and every trace named Dijkstra first. Temperature changed the tokens: a repeat at temperature 0.7 was byte-identical on only 4 of 20 traces while the labels agreed on 20 of 20 (median common prefix 309.5 tokens), and paired with the top-p 1 traces of iteration 4 at the same seed and temperature the labels agreed on 100 of 100 pairs although the traces shared a median of only 34 tokens. A judge agreed with the first-approach lexicon on 19 of 19 audited traces. With this cell, question 1a-c of the request is answered under every sampler the run used: with thinking off at top-k 10 (Table 76), with thinking off and on at top-p 1 (Section 4.5), and with thinking on at top-k 10 here.

**Design of the knob comparison.** Every knob ran in one HF bf16 engine with exact inverse-CDF common random numbers, so all arms of a slot shared the uniform stream of the code stage, on all 15 existing tasks (N = 50 per cell on the five decisive tasks, 30 on the other ten). Plan noise drew a fresh isotropic direction per sample at the task-specification positions of blocks 12 to 23, prefill only, at alpha 1 and 2 ban-free units, under the twin frame and on the plain prompt. The text-level plan samplers used the twin's frame, with the twin's neutral sentence first: intent factored generation at the direction's (1.3, 0.7) and the paper's tuned (0.73, 0.60) temperatures [73]; a lite plan search (five observations, a random pair of them combined into a plan, then code) [74]; enumerate and pick, in which the model lists up to eight algorithms and an external random number picks one; and base intent, in which Qwen3-8B-Base writes the intent sentence and the instruct model the code. Decoding at matched departure applied a temperature to generated tokens 1 to 32, bisected per task so that its mean per-token KL from the twin equalled plan noise's own at each alpha, measured on prefixes used only for calibration. Prices came from a randomisation hull over the full simplex with 2,000 slot bootstraps that select the best mixture again inside every replicate. The committed rule calls the plan sampler comparison supported if the 5-point Hill-1 of plan noise is at least that of the best text sampler on at least 3 of the 5 decisive tasks.

**The plan sampler comparison is DISCONFIRMED** (Table 207) (ban-free unit and iteration-5 seeds; pending the 2x2 of Step K). In Table 207 the margin is the 5-point Hill-1 of plan noise minus that of the best text sampler. Plan noise matched or beat the best text sampler on 1 of the 5 decisive tasks, kth smallest (1.98 against 1.83 for enumerate and pick, P(plan noise at least best) 0.58, unresolved). On connected components, the shortest path task and two sum, base intent won (2.53, 1.45 and 1.61 against 1.09, 1.18 and 1.17), and on the grid task nothing moved much. The mean margin is -0.40 (95% interval -0.70 to -0.24), and only 1.8% of bootstrap replicates reach three wins. Every sensitivity keeps the verdict except one (Table 209): with the multistage samplers dropped (they were padded on the left), intent factored generation is the only text sampler left and plan noise beats it on 4 of 5 tasks, so the disconfirmation rests on base intent and on enumerate and pick. On the ten other tasks (Table 208) plan noise moved only cycle detection and first and last position, while text samplers moved substring search, find duplicate, Fibonacci, longest increasing subsequence, top-k frequent and first and last position. Two prompt knobs outside the text-sampler set also beat plan noise where it was strongest: the novelty instruction on kth smallest (2.03) and the semantic seed on the shortest path task (2.12). An independent recomputation reproduced the literal cell, every McNemar count and the verdict, with the 5-point Hill-1 of the hull within 0.08 of the committed value and a win count of 2 rather than 1 (a near tie on the grid task), still DISCONFIRMED; relabelling plan noise rows as the twin gave margins of 0 or below on all five tasks, and shuffles of the arm labels centred at 1.6 wins (3 or more wins in 3 of 20 shuffles), so the count rule over five tasks is only weakly selective on its own. The plan's one allowed wording revision was used after the first format pilot failed (the model wrote code at once), the committed drop order fired after stage 100 and the dropped cells were restored when the queue finished early, and cells with fewer than 30 (decisive) or 15 (other) programs were excluded from hulls, a rule decided after a dry run that favours plan noise on kth smallest. Post hoc, with iteration-1 base label names harmonised, landing mass outside the base support is 0.11 for enumerate and pick on the grid task (bidirectional BFS) and 0 for every shortest path landing.

## 5.8 The second family: gemma-3-4b-pt against gemma-3-4b-it

**Why.** The Gemma replication asked whether the account replicates in a second family, with the base repertoire of gemma-3-4b-pt committed before a fresh, never-run push population was applied to gemma-3-4b-it [76]. Gemma's iteration-4 push outcomes were seen, so this experiment [ARTIFACT:art_hG0QPiaIPNhP] is a replication on fresh directions and samples, not a held-out confirmation.

**Design.** Both models ran in bf16 on one 23 GB NVIDIA GPU, one at a time. A fresh it twin (N = 50 per task) fixed each task's default under the iteration-5 rule; the grid twin now gave DFS on 30 of 40 correct programs, so every one of the 15 tasks had a default. The pt model wrote 100 programs under the it chat template on the same token ids and 50 in plain completion of a `def solve(...)` stub. Under the chat template 91% of its programs had no usable code and only 10 of 1,500 passed, so the preregistered chat validity gate failed, both formats were pooled, and every unit fell under the low-correct rule: beta, the runner-up and the landing forecast come from valid attempts, not correct programs. These were committed by hash before 16 never-run isotropic directions (seeds 52001 to 52016) were applied at alpha 1 and 2 to the task-specification positions of blocks 11 to 22 on the outlier-excluded ban-free unit. A transplant from pt into it at lambda 1 then ran on the seven tasks diverse in the base with a matched random control, a borrowed shift and a transplant at the read position on the same slots, and on three controls collapsed in the base.

**In Gemma the movability half is inconclusive and the landing half passes** (Table 214). Spearman between beta and the escape fraction is 0.42 (one-sided permutation p 0.060, n = 15), against a bar of 0.5 at p below 0.01; 2 of 3 tasks collapsed in the base are immovable against a bar of 80%; and beta is ahead of no rival, with the twin modal share (0.67) and the novelty instruction (0.64) tracking movability better (Table 215). The direction is the predicted one: 6 of 7 tasks diverse in the base are movable against 2 of 8 others (one-sided Fisher p 0.032, not registered). The partial Spearman given catalogue size and the forced can count is 0.41 (0.45 given catalogue size alone), and the fresh population agrees with iteration 4's movability on 13 of 15 tasks (8 movable now, 6 then). No sensitivity meets the preregistered bar (Table 216); beta from the chat template alone reaches 0.62 (p 0.0095), but that arm is 91% unusable output, and beta from correct programs only reaches 0.27. The pt runner-up equals the modal landing of confirmed escapes in 5 of 7 events (hit rate 0.71 against a mean chance of 0.30; exact Poisson-binomial p 0.025), and the pt composition beats iteration 4's association forecast by 1.50 nats per event (exact Wilcoxon p 0.023) and AST proximity by 0.51 (Table 217). The two misses are kth smallest (landing size-k heap, runner-up quickselect) and connected components (landing union find, pooled runner-up BFS; union find is the runner-up under the chat template alone).

**The transplant moves two of seven tasks diverse in the base** (Table 218). Every transplanted program stayed valid (pass ratio 0.98 to 1.00). Substring search moved from the naive scan to the built-in find in 40 of 50 programs (twin 6 of 50), and first and last position from the linear scan to binary search in 39 of 50 (twin 4 of 50); both land on the pt runner-up. The other five tasks diverse in the base stayed at their default. The two that moved are exactly the tasks diverse in the base whose it twin already writes the pt runner-up 8% to 12% of the time, so the transplant amplified an existing minority mode and did not install an absent one. The pt-minus-it difference at the task-specification positions is large (median 5.2 ban-free units, 4.7 to 5.8 across blocks), above the dose at which random noise broke programs in iteration 4, and five massive channels carry 86% of its squared norm at block 11, falling to 31% to 36% by blocks 21 and 22. Random controls and borrowed shifts that copy the massive-channel move and match the remaining norm broke most programs (pass ratio 0.16 to 0.50 and 0 to 0.22), so the random comparison is confounded by norm and the borrowed shift is itself broken: what the controls show is that the coherent pt content is benign where an equally large random displacement or borrowed shift is destructive. The transplant at the read position and the three controls collapsed in the base stayed within 0.05 of the twin (Table 219); on nonoverlapping intervals the transplant halved the pass rate without moving the algorithm.

**Movability depends on the engine and the unit.** Table 222 sets the existing tasks' movability side by side across the measurements of iterations 4 and 5. Under iteration 4's 8-bit engine and the ban unit, six tasks were movable; under this iteration's bf16 engine and the ban-free unit, only kth smallest and connected components escape with 8 fixed directions, and per-sample plan noise moves more than 10% of programs off the default only on kth smallest (0.28 at alpha 2). On the shortest path task, per-sample plan noise moved 26% of all samples at alpha 1 in iteration 4 (13 of 50 valid attempts off the default; 9 of 43 correct programs) and 0 of 50 correct programs at alpha 1 here (2 of 47 at alpha 2, 1.67 8-bit ban units by the ratio of mean norms and 1.78 by the mean ratio). A dose-bracketed comparison (iteration 6) sets the bf16 alpha-2 cell, which delivers more than the 1.00 ban unit of the 8-bit alpha-1 cell under either dose definition, against the 8-bit alpha-1 cell: a lower bf16 share there cannot be a dose shortfall. By the rule fixed before computing, connected components and shortest path did not replicate in bf16 at the population level (correct-only bracket one-sided Fisher p kth smallest 0.588, connected components 0.056, shortest path 0.017, two sum 1.000, grid 0.732); kth smallest: not established; two sum: not established (no 8-bit effect of at least 10% at alpha of 2 or less to replicate); grid: not established; find duplicate: not established (no 8-bit effect of at least 10% at alpha of 2 or less to replicate). The engine control of Section 6.3 then tested the numerics directly: at iteration 4's own absolute displacement, direction seeds and slots, the bf16 engine reproduces the 8-bit rows (per-sample plan noise at alpha 2: connected components 25 of 50 valid attempts off the default under bf16 against 30 of 50 under the 8-bit engine; shortest path 22 of 50 under both), so the non-replication tagged here belongs to iteration 5's ban-free unit and direction seeds, not to the bf16 numerics. The engine checks pushed two fixed escaping directions at the ban unit in both engines and agreed within or near the resampling null (shortest path: Dijkstra 31 and Bellman-Ford/SPFA 19 in bf16 against 26 and 24 in the 8-bit engine). Those two directions therefore do not explain the difference, and its cause is not established here. *(Correction, iteration 6: the engine control of Section 6.3 establishes that the cause is not the bf16 numerics. At the absolute unit, direction seeds and slots of iteration 4 itself, bf16 escapes on almost the same directions as the 8-bit engine (connected components 26 of 40 against 29 of 40; shortest path 6 of 40 against 8 of 40). The shrinkage belongs to the ban-free unit of iteration 5 or its direction seeds, and the heading should read that movability depends on the unit and the direction draw.)* Movability is therefore a property of a task under a given engine, unit and direction population, and the confirmation panels measured it under bf16 and the ban-free unit only.

## 5.11 What iteration 5 established, what it ruled out, and what it abandoned

Everything below is one or two model families at 4B to 8B parameters, memorised tasks in the style of LeetCode, and labels from gated labellers, except the base-model labels of Gemma, which agree with an adjudication at only 0.64. Every Qwen3-8B number of this iteration comes from a bf16 engine.

**Established.**

1. *Temperature does not change the algorithm, under every sampler the run used.* With thinking on, top-k 10 and the same seed, the algorithm changed in 0 of 20 seeds across four temperatures on the shortest path task, and the first approach named in the thinking never changed.
2. *(Moved to the descriptive results, iteration 6.)* *Where a random nudge moves the instruct model, it often lands on the base model's runner-up.* Per set the base runner-up named the push landing 5 of 5 on the 8-bit screen, 1 of 2 on the bf16 remeasurement of existing tasks, 3 of 3 in panel A, 3 of 4 in panel B and 5 of 7 in Gemma (17 of 21, Poisson-binomial p 5.8e-07); on new tasks 6 of 7 events (Poisson-binomial p 0.003). 6 of the 11 held-out hits are also the instruct twin's own minority: on the 8 held-out events where the instruct twin wrote no correct program off the default the base runner-up named 5 (p 0.053; Qwen3-8B 3 of 4, p 0.052; Gemma 2 of 4, p 0.422), and the twin's own most frequent alternative, defined on 7 of 21 events, named 6 of them against 6 for the base runner-up (exact McNemar p 1.000). Where the twin writes an alternative at all, the landing half is therefore the twin's own minority, and the base model adds a forecast only on the events where the twin writes none (iteration-6 correction; record audit, Table 230), with the base composition ahead of association by 0.75 nats (exact Wilcoxon p 0.055 with the corrected association) and of proximity by 0.50. ## 5.12 What the next iteration takes from this one

The narrowed repertoire account split in two. Its landing half held descriptively in both families and on unseen tasks (5 of 5 on the 8-bit screen, 1 of 2 on the bf16 remeasurement of existing tasks, 3 of 3 in panel A, 3 of 4 in panel B and 5 of 7 in Gemma (17 of 21, Poisson-binomial p 5.8e-07)), but it is not yet separated from the instruct twin's own minority (on the 8 held-out events where the instruct twin wrote no correct program off the default the base runner-up named 5 (p 0.053; Qwen3-8B 3 of 4, p 0.052; Gemma 2 of 4, p 0.422); iteration-6 correction): when a nudge moves the instruct model, it moves it to the algorithm the base model writes next, and a forecast built from base samples, before any push, names that landing better than the model's stated alternative. Its movability half failed on unseen tasks: a base model that writes many algorithms does not mark a task the instruct model can be nudged off, and its states, written into the instruct prefill, reopen the choice on one task in five. The base repertoire marks where a nudge can lead, not whether it can lead anywhere.

The open question is therefore what makes a task diverse in the base immovable. Count primes and valid anagram (beta 0.81 each) never moved, while trapped rain water (0.23) did. Two leads came out of this iteration's data. In panel A the three units that moved had an alternative at least twice as fast as the default and the three that did not had none, although median of two sorted lists broke the pattern. And in the transplant experiment early blocks 0 to 11 moved kth smallest and connected components more than the main band, which suggests the narrowing sits at least partly upstream of blocks 12 to 23. The positioning audit names the baselines a further test needs: weight interpolation between the base and instruct models, layer restoration at the transplant's block ranges, and token-level base and aligned collaboration [92, 93, 94, 102]. Base intent, which beat plan noise on three of five tasks, is the strongest practical knob the run has priced, and it is itself a form of that collaboration at the level of sentences. Finally, movability has to be measured under the engine and unit at which it will be used: the six screen-movable tasks of iteration 4 shrank to two under bf16 and the ban-free unit, for reasons this iteration did not establish. *(Iteration-6 correction: a dose-bracketed contrast rules out a scalar dose shortfall on connected components and shortest path, and the engine control rules out the bf16 numerics, since at iteration 4's absolute unit and seeds bf16 reproduces the 8-bit escapes (Section 6.3). What remains is the per-position and per-block profile of the ban-free unit, or the direction seeds; every verdict that rests on bf16 plan noise or escape fractions at the ban-free unit is conditional on that design.)*

**The hypothesis update.** The update turned from the outside of the model to its inside. Five iterations had mapped what moves the algorithm from outside: a ban, a meaningful hint, a plan sentence written by the base model, a list-then-pick step. None had located where the model holds its choice. The update proposed one concrete answer, which it called the plan-variable account. While the model reads the task, it computes a small hidden variable that says which algorithm to write. We call this variable the *plan*. On tasks where a ban acts through the prompt states (shortest path, kth smallest, connected components) the plan sits in the residual stream at the task-specification positions; on tasks where generated tokens read the ban directly (two sum, find duplicate) it sits at the first generated tokens. Exchanging a few of its dimensions between two prompts should switch the algorithm the model writes, with correct code. Random noise should change the algorithm only through the part of it that falls inside the plan, which would explain why most random directions do nothing; temperature should never touch it.

The update tested the account with the instruments the request names and the run had not yet used. An *interchange intervention* replaces a component's activations under one input with those under another and measures the change in output. *Distributed alignment search* (DAS) fits an orthonormal low-rank subspace in which such an exchange reproduces a counterfactual behaviour [110, 111]. A *natural language autoencoder* (NLA) pairs an activation verbalizer, which writes a text explanation of a residual-stream state, with an activation reconstructor, which maps text back to a state; released checkpoints exist for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [124] at layer 20, not for Qwen3-8B. Gemma Scope 2, released in December 2025, provides JumpReLU sparse autoencoders [114] and transcoders trained on gemma-3-4b-it itself, the successor of the Gemma Scope release for Gemma 2 [113], so no transfer test from a base model is needed.

Eleven claims were preregistered, each with a rule committed by sha256 before its first decisive sample. We call them by their content rather than by their codes: the engine claim, the localization claim, the mediation claim, the discreteness claim, the token claim, the resampling claim, the verbal readout claim, the feature claim, the site rerun, the landing contest and the novelty count.

- *The engine claim* (primary): on connected components and shortest path, the same 40 directions and common-random-number slots at the same absolute displacement under four numerics. Activation rounding is the cause if the escape fraction under bf16 weights with 8-bit floating-point activations (W16A8) exceeds bf16 by at least 0.2, the full 8-bit engine (W8A8) matches W16A8 within 0.1 and 8-bit floating-point weights with bf16 activations (W8A16) match bf16 within 0.1, on both tasks. The result is called not reproduced if W8A8 minus bf16 is below 0.1.
- *The localization claim* (primary). Stage A, with no training: exchanging the full residual states of the ban prompt into the neutral twin transfers the ban's substitute at a transfer share of at least 0.5 on at least two of shortest path, kth smallest and connected components, at a pass rate of at least 0.8 times the twin's, and at most 0.2 on two sum and find duplicate. Stage B: DAS at one layer recovers at least 0.8 of the full-state transfer at a rank of 16 or less on held-out templates.
- *The mediation claim* (primary): the energy that a random direction puts into the fitted plan subspace predicts which directions switch the algorithm (Spearman at least 0.5).
- *The discreteness claim*, *the token claim* (temperature leaves the plan coordinate flat while state noise at generated tokens beats temperature at matched per-token KL) and *the resampling claim* (resampling the plan as a diversity knob) (secondary).
- *The verbal readout claim* (secondary): the NLA names the substitute of a ban before any code is written at a rate at least 0.3 above a judge reading the visible text; editing the explanation's algorithm phrase and reconstructing transfers the algorithm by at least 0.2.
- *The feature claim* (secondary): in Gemma's natural BFS against DFS split on the grid task, Gemma Scope 2 features decode the upcoming algorithm at least 0.10 balanced accuracy above a classifier on the visible text, and steer at least as well as a difference-in-means direction at matched pass.
- *The site rerun* (secondary): the iteration-4 noise-site comparison in bf16; the prefill-site claim survives if the task-specification site beats the read position and the condition sentence at matched downstream displacement on at least one task, and is withdrawn otherwise.
- *The landing contest* (secondary): the base runner-up against the instruct twin's own teacher-forced ranking of algorithm openings, on every recorded push-landing event.
- *The novelty count* (secondary).

**The strategy.** Seven artifacts were planned (Table 225). One evaluation on CPU, which we call the record audit, repaired the record from rows on disk and ran the second novelty adjudication. An experiment we call the engine control ran the four numerics on a 16 GB RTX 2000 Ada, an Ada-generation card with the 8-bit floating-point tensor cores that the 8-bit engine needs. A bf16 experiment, which we call the exchange and site experiment, ran the Stage A exchanges, the site rerun, state noise against matched temperature, the top-five push and the landing contest. Gemma and the NLA each received their own experiment, which we call the Gemma feature experiment and the NLA experiment, and a research artifact, which we call the positioning audit, searched the literature for each claim. The seventh artifact, which was to fit the DAS subspaces of Stage B and run the mediation, discreteness, resampling and temperature-coordinate tests together with a manifold of plan coordinates, was lost before it existed: the planning agent returned no plan. Section 6.8 records it as planned and not run. Every Qwen3-8B number of this iteration except those of the engine control comes from a bf16 engine.

## 6.3 The engine control: are the random-push escapes a property of the model or of 8-bit rounding?

**Why.** The engine claim was the primary test of the iteration, because its answer decides which internal results of iteration 4 belong to Qwen3-8B. The review had pointed at a plausible mechanism without establishing it: a displacement changes the per-token absmax of each linear input, so under dynamic per-token 8-bit floating-point scaling it changes the rounding of every downstream activation, and the engine adds its own perturbation to the push. The 8-bit floating-point format in question is e4m3, with a maximum of 448 [115]. The engine control [ARTIFACT:art_lpQalcAXMGr1] separated weight rounding from activation rounding by running iteration 4's own design under four numerics, all built from one bf16 snapshot of Qwen3-8B (Table 235).

**Design.** Everything except the numerics was held fixed: the 40 direction files of iteration 4 (seeds 9101 to 9140, checked bitwise), the absolute displacement per block and position at blocks 12 to 23 and the task-specification positions (the bench unit of iteration 4), the twin prompts, the common-random-number slots and uniforms, the stop rule, a 1,024-token cap, one labeller version (that of iteration 4 plus the iteration-5 re-gate that reads array-based Dijkstra correctly) applied to every row, and the two-stage escape rule of iteration 4, with each engine scored against its own twin. **Mechanism diagnostics.** Per-token e4m3 rounding perturbs every linear input by about 2.5% RMS. Under an alpha-2 push, the push-induced difference in rounding error is 6% to 12% of the push-induced change in activation (median over blocks 13 to 35 per site, peaking at 34% at the block-14 attention input), and 70% to 100% of the rows the push moves receive a new per-token scale. Linear inputs at blocks 0 to 12 are bitwise identical in the pushed and the twin pass in every engine, as the edit site requires. The extra rounding barely changes how the push propagates: relative to bf16, the non-nominal part of the perturbation is 1.01 at the task-specification positions, 1.04 to 1.05 at the read position and 1.03 to 1.12 at generated tokens 1 to 32 under W16A8, and 0.995 to 1.006 under W8A16. Teacher-forced on 40 iteration-4 twin programs, every engine is very close to bf16 (Table 241). One preregistered fidelity check failed uninformatively: teacher forcing runs one long prefill instead of 20-row decode steps, which itself changes the numerics, so log probabilities of iteration 4's programs could not be matched closely enough to resolve engines at that level; the engine was validated instead by byte identity.

## 6.4 Where a ban and an instruction are carried, and where noise acts, in bf16 (Qwen3-8B)

**Why.** The localization claim predicted, from the route classes of iterations 2 and 3, where the substitute of a ban is carried: in the task-specification states on the prompt-route tasks, at the condition span on the direct-route tasks. Stage A tests that prediction without any training, by moving the states themselves. The same experiment [ARTIFACT:art_rMlbrjVB1c__] reran the iteration-4 noise-site comparison in bf16, set state noise at generated tokens against a temperature matched on per-token KL, applied the top-five plan push, and ran the landing contest. Everything ran in one bf16 engine with exact common random numbers on a 16 GB card, with the input embedding table kept in CPU memory; per-slot twin labels agreed with iteration 5's bf16 engine on 0.975 of slots for kth smallest and shortest path and 1.00 for the other tasks. Seven commitments formed an unbroken sha256 chain, and a standard-library script re-derived every headline from raw rows (295 checks, 0 mismatches) while a placebo version of each test failed.

### 6.4.1 Stage A: full-state exchange of the ban

We call a *full-state exchange* the replacement, in the forward pass of the neutral twin, of the residual states at a set of positions and blocks by the states the full ban prompt produces at the same positions; because the twin and the ban have identical token ids from the task text on, every task-specification position aligns. The exchanges covered four block bands at the task-specification positions (0 to 11, 12 to 23, 24 to 35, 0 to 35), a splice of the key-value cache of the condition span (the direct route), and the read position at all 36 blocks. The controls were the twin, a matched-norm random exchange (the state of the twin plus a fresh random direction scaled to the displacement that the ban itself causes per slot, block and position), a placebo that takes a second neutral twin as the source, and an identity exchange. The outcome, as committed before sampling (the first commitment: "share(label == Y | cell) - share(label == Y | TWIN), all samples (invalid rows count as not-Y)"), is the *Y share*: the share of all attempted programs labelled Y, invalid rows counting as not-Y; the *transfer* of a cell is that share minus the share under the twin; a cell counts only if its pass rate is at least 0.8 times that of the twin (the validity gate of the first commitment); and its *recovery* is the transfer divided by that of the full ban. The *correct Y* column added to Tables 244 to 250 counts programs labelled Y that pass every hidden test, because an attempted share counts broken programs as Y: on the grid task the exchange at blocks 0-35 has 14 attempts labelled DFS but 3 correct DFS programs. Each cell has N = 30 on paired slots. Tables 244 to 249 give every cell on the six tasks. (iteration-7 correction)

The prediction held where the route data said it should, and failed at one task where they said it should not. On shortest path, exchanging the full ban's task-specification states at all blocks into the twin turns 24 of 30 slots from Dijkstra to Bellman-Ford/SPFA (24 of 30 attempts, 21 of 30 correct programs; transfer 0.80, McNemar 24:0, Holm p 7e-7, pass ratio 0.90), while the condition-span splice and the read-position exchange transfer nothing. Blocks 12 to 23 alone carry 0.60 (18 of 30 attempts, 11 of 30 correct programs, at a pass ratio of 0.73, below the 0.8 gate) and blocks 24 to 35 alone 0.37 (11 of 30 attempts, 11 of 30 correct programs); blocks 0 to 11 carry none. On kth smallest the same exchange transfers 0.57 to quickselect (17 of 30 attempts, 16 of 30 correct programs) with every slot leaving the full sort, blocks 0 to 11 alone already transfer 0.40 (12 of 30 attempts, 12 of 30 correct programs), and here the condition span also carries the ban (0.93; 28 of 30 attempts, 25 of 30 correct programs). On connected components every slot leaves union find under the exchange at blocks 12 to 23 or 0 to 35 (off-default transfer 1.00), but only 0.37 to 0.47 land on the ban's BFS (11 and 14 of 30 attempts, 11 and 14 of 30 correct programs) and the rest on DFS. On the grid task, whose route was carried by the prompt states in likelihood and mixed in behaviour, the exchange at all blocks transfers 0.47 toward DFS (14 of 30 attempts, 3 of 30 correct programs, pass ratio 0.59, below the 0.8 gate) and the condition-span splice 0.33 (10 of 30 attempts, 7 of 30 correct programs, pass ratio 0.89), so each carries part of the ban in attempts and only the splice passes the committed validity gate. On the direct-route tasks the condition-span splice alone reproduces the ban (two sum 1.00, 30 of 30 attempts, 30 of 30 correct programs; find duplicate 0.90, 27 of 30 attempts, 26 of 30 correct programs), as predicted, but on two sum the task-specification states also transfer brute force at 0.43 (13 of 30 attempts, 13 of 30 correct programs), above the predicted ceiling of 0.2. The committed verdict is therefore not supported. The secondary predictions hold: the condition span carries at least 0.5 on the direct-route tasks and at most 0.2 on shortest path, the read position carries at most 0.2 everywhere (it carries 0.00 on all six tasks), the placebo moves at most 0.03, and the exchange beats the matched-norm random exchange where it transfers (shortest path 23:0, kth smallest 16:2, connected components 11:0, on attempted Y as preregistered); counted on correct Y instead, a post-hoc contrast added in iteration 7, the same pairs give 21:0 (exact p 9.5e-07), 15:2 (p 2.3e-03) and 11:0 (p 9.8e-04). The ban's information, not the size of the perturbation, is what moves the algorithm. (iteration-7 correction)

### 6.4.2 Where noise acts, in bf16

The site rerun repeated iteration 4's grid on kth smallest and connected components in bf16, at the ban-free unit, with a fresh direction per sample, N = 30 per cell and alpha 1, 2, 4 and 8 (Tables 251 and 252). Noise at the task-specification positions moves the algorithm in bf16: on kth smallest blocks 12 to 23 reach a correct off-default share of 0.37 at alpha 2, and on connected components blocks 0 to 11 reach 0.33 at alpha 4. The read position, the condition span and the late blocks barely move it below alpha 8. On kth smallest the plan site (the task-specification states at blocks 12 to 23, as in iteration 4) beats the read position in paired slots 24:5 (exact p 5.5e-4) and the condition span 22:0, and a Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio [129] within quintiles of the downstream displacement is 4.6 [1.9, 11.3]. Connected components shows a weaker picture: its plan site moves only 0.07 at alpha 2 and 0.17 at alpha 4, the early blocks beat it (4:18, p 0.004), and the read position starts moving at alpha 8 (0.30).

The committed rule fitted a Firth logistic regression [125] of a correct off-default program on site indicators and the log displacements, so that sites are compared at matched downstream displacement (Tables 253 and 254). It returned the verdict withdrawn, for two reasons. The raw condition-span arm never reaches the plan site's downstream displacement, so it has no common support and its energy-matched arm stood in; and at alpha 8 every plan-site program failed (pass 0.00) while the read position began to move, which erases the read-position contrast in the preregistered model. A post-hoc sensitivity restricted to alpha of 4 or less (before breakage) puts the read position clearly below the plan site on both tasks: beta -3.76 (profile interval [-7.29, -0.47], cluster bootstrap [-8.18, -1.40]) on kth smallest and -4.98 ([-9.77, -0.89]; [-11.48, -1.53]) on connected components. The prefill-site claim is therefore withdrawn as preregistered. Post hoc (alpha of at most 4) the read position is below the task-specification site on both tasks; the condition-span clause fails post hoc as well (beta -1.70 [-3.96, 0.42] on kth smallest; -0.56 [-4.93, 2.91] on connected components, cluster bootstrap; profile intervals [-6.82, 1.16] and [-6.15, 3.41]), so the site of the choice remains open, as the artifact concludes; its rule label withdraws the site claim as specific to 8-bit floating point and states that the site of the choice is open. The half of that label about 8-bit floating point cannot apply: Section 6.3 shows that bf16 reproduces the escapes direction by direction (Spearman 0.96 and 0.87) and that activation rounding adds nothing, so the withdrawal comes from the missing common support and the breakage at alpha 8 in bf16, not from the engine. Noise sites and Stage A agree on the band on kth smallest and disagree on connected components (Table 254b): there noise moves the algorithm most at blocks 0 to 11 (mean 0.19 over alpha 1 to 4 against 0.08 at blocks 12 to 23; 0.33 correct off-default at alpha 4; coefficient +2.51 [1.39, 3.80] against the plan site; paired flips 4:18, p 0.004, between the plan site and blocks 0-11), while the exchange transfers BFS at blocks 12 to 23. The removal of the default there is depth-redundant: the exchange at blocks 0-11 alone takes 0.87 of attempts off union find and at blocks 24-35 alone 0.63. (iteration-7 correction)

### 6.4.4 The top-five push in bf16

On the grid task, iteration 4's top-five direction (from the mean of the five banned centroids toward the mean of the survivors) was applied at the plan site at alpha 1, 2, 4 and 8 (Table 256). At doses of 1 to 8 ban units, which overshoot the forced-prompt manifold, the push breaks programs before it moves the algorithm; an in-manifold dose was not tried: the pass rate falls from 0.67 at alpha 1 to 0.30, 0.03 and 0.00, with at most one correct program other than BFS per cell, so the landing test could not be computed. Projected onto the plane of the first two principal components of the ten forced-prompt centroids (36% and 25% of their variance), the push leaves the forced-prompt manifold: already at alpha 1 it moves farther along the first component than the whole spread of the ten centroids (the four alpha-1 points move from a twin mean of +0.09 to -0.44 on that component, against centroids spread from -0.098 to +0.144). The prompt version of the top-five ban moves the task-specification states from below the centroid cloud into it, between the banned DFS and greedy best-first centroids and the three surviving centroids (bidirectional BFS and two variants of A*), and its behaviour stays inside the banned set (BFS 25, DFS 23 of 50; avoidance 0.00). ### 6.4.5 Who forecasts the landing

The landing contest scored, on the 21 recorded push-landing events, three forecasts: the base runner-up, the most frequent algorithm other than the default in the instruct twin itself (defined on 7 events), and a teacher-forced ranking of the openings of the catalogue algorithms by the instruct twin, the log-mean-exp likelihood of the first 48 tokens of each algorithm over its reference and forced programs, which we call the opening ranking (Table 257). The base runner-up named 17 of 21 landings and the opening ranking 10. On the 9 events where they disagree the base runner-up wins 8:1 (exact one-sided sign test p 0.020), and its mean log score is higher by 1.62 nats (Wilcoxon p 0.032). Where the twin wrote an alternative, its own minority does as well as the base runner-up (6 of 7; log-score difference 0.02, p 0.69). The comparison is retrospective, because the landings were known when the rule was frozen, and the opening ranking rests on 1 to 6 programs per algorithm. The base model adds information beyond the ranking of openings by the instruct model itself; it does not add information beyond the minority algorithm of the twin where one exists.

## 6.5 Gemma: a one-token fork, and Gemma Scope 2 features against difference in means

**Why Gemma.** Asked one and the same grid-path prompt, gemma-3-4b-it [76] writes DFS about 70% of the time and BFS about 30%, so it offers what Qwen3-8B never does: the request's BFS-against-DFS contrast inside one prompt, with no ban or instruction to confound it. Gemma Scope 2 provides sparse autoencoders on the residual stream after each block, trained on this instruct model, so the feature claim needs no transfer test. Qwen-3 transcoders for circuit tracing exist as well [123], but they would have to study a choice Qwen3-8B does not make naturally. The experiment [ARTIFACT:art_zNyBP6zieI5u] asked where the choice forks, whether it can be read from the internals beyond what the visible text already says, and whether the SAE features steer it better than plain baselines: a difference-in-means direction, the raw residual, random features, isotropic directions, DAS and prompting. It used the residual-stream SAEs at layers 9, 17, 22 and 29 (16k latents, at the release's medium sparsity), one 16 GB card and exact common random numbers, under two hash-chained commitments.

**Natural splits.** Over 200 samples per task, the grid prompt gave DFS 139 and BFS 61 (Wilson interval for DFS 0.63 to 0.75), with DFS on 134 of 172 correct programs (Table 258). The choice depends on the template: BFS takes 6 to 18 of 40 attempts per template. Substring search (naive 173, built-in find 27) and first and last position (linear scan 170, binary search 29) split as well. Labels agreed with iteration 5's Gemma rows on 0.94 of the grid slots and 1.00 of the substring slots.

**The plan is a single-token fork.** Prefix resampling with change-point detection, the method of forking-path analyses [30, 31], located the fork: 24 base paths, 16 prefix lengths, 8 continuations each and a refinement, 3,712 continuations in all, scored by a partial-code labeller that agreed with the full labeller on 200 of 200 programs. Every one of 12 BFS base paths had a significant change point with a rise of at least 0.4, at prefix lengths 16 to 36. In 177 of 200 programs the first 32 tokens are identical (the code fence, `def solve(grid, start, goal):`, `rows = len(grid)`, `cols = len(grid[0])` and an indent), and the next token decides (Table 260): ` visited` leads to DFS (BFS probability 0.011 over 1,409 continuations), while a blank line, `if`, `queue` or `q` lead to BFS (0.95 to 1.00). The first token that identifies the algorithm in code comes a median of 138 tokens after the fork (10th to 90th percentile 80 to 181). The fork index was chosen by the token class with the most mutual information with the outcome (0.62 bits at index 32), after the first median rule landed on a deterministic indentation token; the change was made before the second commitment.

*Executed but not reported until iteration 7.* The empty-prefix unit test of the fork failed mildly: continuations from the empty prefix give BFS 0.38 (73 of 192) against the natural 0.305 [0.245, 0.372] (outside the interval; exact binomial p 0.028 against 0.305), so the resampled continuations are slightly richer in BFS than the natural samples. The deviation log records what did not run: the clamp read-back and matched-norm realisation tests as separate unit tests (the matched norm is imposed by construction in the clamp code, and the realised norm of each edit is logged per row); the clamp-cell overlay on the generated-position panel; the fork and the cross-prompt readouts of two further bench tasks (dropped in order); and per-sample displacement at generated tokens 1-32 (prefill displacement at blocks 11-33 is logged). **Readable beyond the text, at the fork, but not specifically through the SAE.** Within one prompt, decodability before the first identifying token is at ceiling for every method, the visible-text control included (balanced accuracy 1.00 at all four layers), so the SAE has no advantage there; at the fork itself the test is undefined, because 185 of 200 samples share their prefix with a sample of the other class. A Lasso on layer-29 SAE codes at the fork position predicts held-out y with R-squared 0.66, against 0.18 for a text-only model (difference 0.49, 95% interval 0.26 to 0.65, permutation p 0.003), above the difference-in-means readout (0.34) and a 16-component PCA of the raw residual (0.56) (Table 261). Beside the Lasso, the standardised ridge on the same layer-29 SAE codes reaches R-squared 0.15 against 0.086 for a template-plus-noun-norm control (delta 0.064, below the preregistered 0.10 bar); the unstandardised SAE ridge ranges from -0.76 to 0.06 across penalties while the raw ridge stays at 0.70 to 0.72, which is why the SAE advantage depends on the estimator. Moreover, a linear readout of the fork log-odds from the residual at the fork position is close to a next-token readout, so the raw-residual 0.72 shows that the next-token distribution is linearly encoded there, not that a plan is; no logit-lens control of matched capacity was run. At the task-specification positions, before any response token, the SAE codes do no better than the text (0.18). (iteration-7 correction)

**Steering: the features move the fork, difference in means moves it more, and edits toward BFS cost correctness.** We call an *SAE clamp* setting the k latents that best separate forced-BFS from forced-DFS prompts (input-selected) to their BFS-class mean at the fork position; output-scored latents are chosen instead by their attribution to the fork's logit difference, and the two sets of 20 share 2 latents. At the fork position of layer 22, edits at matched norm moved y by +4.04 nats for the difference-in-means direction, +1.78 for the SAE clamp of the top 20 input-selected latents, +0.51 for 20 random latents and +0.12 for an isotropic direction. Table 261b gives the whole dose-response sweep over the 120 prompt variants (11,280 measurements), at the fork and at the task-specification positions. In generation (N = 50 paired slots), the twin wrote BFS in 13 programs; the SAE clamp raised this to 30 (top 20 latents) and 36 (top 50), the difference-in-means edit at the same norm to 46 and 49, and random latents to 21 (Table 262). Edits toward BFS at the fork lowered the pass rate from 0.84 for the twin to 0.58 and 0.48 for the top-20 and top-50 SAE clamps and 0.32 and 0.16 for difference in means (0.60 to 0.78 for the other BFS-ward fork edits, 0.00 for the DAS interchange), except the SAE top-5 clamp (18 BFS of 50, pass 0.84), so the preregistered outcome, correct BFS programs, shows no significant effect anywhere after Holm correction, and no feature claim is made. The preregistered feature rule (SAE target-correct count at least the difference-in-means count, at a pass rate of at least 0.8 times the twin's) is also met by random latents at k = 50 (9 against 7, pass 0.76), so it cannot discriminate here. The informative comparisons are on attempted BFS, and they are descriptive: the SAE clamp beats the twin (17:0 and 23:0 discordant slots, p 1.5e-5 and 2.4e-7) and random latents (15:0, p 6.1e-5), and difference in means beats the SAE clamp at matched norm (16:0, p 3.1e-5). At matched effect on y rather than matched norm, difference in means and the SAE clamp shift the plan equally (32 against 30 BFS, p 0.50; 34 against 36, p 0.63) and difference in means keeps slightly more programs correct (13 against 9, 14 against 10). Edits at the task-specification positions do nothing (12 to 19 BFS against 13). Steering toward DFS works cleanly for both (SAE 47 of 50, difference in means 50 of 50, against 37 for the twin; pass 0.98 to 1.00). Difference-in-means steering of a code model's choice of language and library has shown the same trade-off, with overly strong interventions reducing output quality [130]. **DAS moves the fork log-odds within the controls it had, and forcing it breaks the program.** DAS at the fork position of layer 22, with forced-BFS prompts as sources, moved held-out y by +8.8, +9.5 and +9.8 nats at ranks 1, 2 and 4, against -0.08 to +0.05 for random subspaces of the same rank (Table 263). Stated within its controls, a rank-1 DAS subspace fitted on forced-BFS sources moves the held-out fork log-odds by 8.8 nats (random subspaces of the same rank -0.08 to +0.05); because every source was forced-BFS, the shuffled-source control is uninformative by construction (10.1 nats); no random-initialisation or target-shuffled control was run; and the rank-4 interchange gives BFS in 50 of 50 attempts with 0 of 50 programs passing, so this does not show that the choice is one-dimensional. With unrestricted alignment maps interchange accuracy reaches 100% even on randomly initialised language models (Sutter et al., Table 277 row 14), so the fit stays uninterpretable until those controls run; pushing hard costs correctness, as subspace interventions can when they leave the model's natural range [122]. ## 6.6 The plan in words: a natural language autoencoder on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

**Why.** The request names NLA as an instrument, and the release of NLA checkpoints for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [124] made it possible to ask, in words, whether the residual stream states before the first code token say which algorithm will be written. The experiment [ARTIFACT:art_dbUtqBjT0tPf] read layer-20 states with the released verbalizer and reconstructor pair, judged the explanations blind, and tested an edit of the explanation as a steering vector. Published verbalizers of the same kind include LatentQA [117] and SelfIE [118], and a 2026 analysis of a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer found that only a small share of an explanation's specific claims are ones the reconstruction depends on [119]. Pre-registration was a sha256 chain of four commitments, each preceding its samples; the parts added after the committed nulls are marked exploratory.

**Behaviour.** Over eight tasks, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct defaults to BFS, Dijkstra (0.88), a hash map (0.98), a hash set (0.71), DFS for connected components (0.62, where Qwen3-8B writes union find), the naive scan and binary search; kth smallest has no default (quickselect 0.40, size-k heap 0.34) and failed the style re-gate. The model mostly ignores bans (Table 267). Only two sum gave a substitute (brute force in 32 of 46 correct programs). On connected components a ban of DFS raised DFS from 29 to 43 correct programs, with 15 paired slots flipping from union find to DFS, the rebound that naming a forbidden concept can cause [7, 53]. Every one of the 70 programs written under the fourth template attempted the banned default. The shortest path semantic seed barely moved the model (Dijkstra 28, Bellman-Ford 6, against 38 and 5 for the twin). The labellers recognised 51 of 51 references, and the style re-gate passed on 7 of 8 tasks against two blind code judges.

**The NLA never names the planned algorithm before the code.** Two blind judges from different families (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite and Mistral Small 3.2, both scoring 1.00 on calibration; a third model resolved 1,064 disagreements) mapped each of 6,180 explanations to a catalogue algorithm or to none named (Table 269). Every preregistered readout at the end-of-prompt positions is exactly zero (Table 270). On ban prompts, explanations named the substitute in 0 of 16 states (only two sum had a substitute, so this test is underpowered); on twin prompts they named the default in 0 of 112, as did the text-only reader; on ban failures they named the default the model still writes in 0 of 96. The positive control failed too: on forced `Implement Y` prompts the explanations called Y planned in 0 of 7 tasks, while the text-only reader did so on all of them, and they mentioned the algorithm named in the prompt in 0.7% of cases. The explanations describe the local format line, such as a request for no explanation or a Python code block to follow, and confabulate the task (Fibonacci, medians, prime numbers); 4,733 of 5,700 judged explanations name no algorithm at all. At generated tokens the NLA sometimes names the realised algorithm before the visible text identifies it (up to 0.28 at token 8 under the ban), but an outside reader who sees only the prompt and prefix predicts the realised algorithm better, per sample (0.25 against 0.07; exact McNemar 20:88, p 2e-11 when the 364 units are treated as independent). The units are nested in 104 samples and 5 task clusters: the task-cluster bootstrap interval of the difference is [-0.35, 0.02], with one unit per sample (the first in position order, 104 samples) the contrast is 0:25 (exact p 6.0e-08), a median over 2,000 draws of one random unit per sample of 4:29 (p 1.9e-05; 1.00 of draws below 0.05), a sign test on the per-sample differences 12:38 (p 3.1e-04) and a Durkalski-adjusted McNemar with samples as clusters p 6.5e-05. The samples share 5 task clusters, and with 5 clusters no cluster-level test can reach a two-sided p below 0.0625, so the evidence at the task level is inconclusive whatever the sample-level p. On find duplicate the edit at dose 8 (about 0.3 of the state norm at each position) raised Floyd cycle detection from 0.28 to 0.76 (25:1 over 50 paired slots), replicated on fresh slots (15 of 20, 13:0, p 2e-4), and beat a matched random push (28:1), an unrelated-word edit built the same way (12:1, p 0.003) and a norm-matched round trip (13:1, p 0.002); at dose 16 the programs broke (pass 0.37). On two sum brute force rose from 0 to 10 of 50 at dose 8 and to 23 of 30 at dose 16 with a pass rate of 0.90, while the random push never moved it. On connected components only the forced-state difference in means steered (union find 0.80 at dose 16, 15:1); on substring search nothing steered short of breaking the program. The prefill site stayed inert even at dose 16 or at the natural norm of the difference in means. Asking for the algorithm in the prompt remained the ceiling (forced adherence 0.90 to 1.00 on all four tasks), as the AxBench comparison of prompting and steering predicts [34]. The NLA paper itself reports that editing a plan explanation and steering at one token succeeds roughly half the time; this run's success on two of four tasks is of the same kind and is not a reliable control knob.

## 6.8 Planned but not run

The seventh artifact of the strategy never existed. It was to fit DAS subspaces of rank 1 to 16 at one layer of the task-specification positions in bf16 Qwen3-8B on three training templates and confirm them on two held-out templates (Stage B of the localization claim), test whether a fresh random direction's energy in that subspace predicts its effect (the mediation claim), interpolate and extrapolate the plan coordinate between algorithms (the discreteness claim), measure the plan coordinate's variance across temperatures (the first half of the token claim), resample the plan per generation as a diversity knob (the resampling claim), and draw the request's manifold of algorithms in the fitted plan subspace, with the top-five prohibition placed on it. It was lost at the planning stage: the planning agent returned no plan, so no experiment ran. These claims are untested and open; nothing in this report is a result for them, null or otherwise. The only DAS result of the iteration is Gemma's, at the fork position (Section 6.5). The deviation log of the Gemma experiment adds what it did not run: the clamp read-back and matched-norm realisation tests as separate unit tests (the matched norm is imposed by construction in the clamp code, and the realised norm of each edit is logged per row); the clamp-cell overlay on the generated-position panel; the fork and the cross-prompt readouts of two further bench tasks (dropped in order); and per-sample displacement at generated tokens 1-32 (prefill displacement at blocks 11-33 is logged). ## 6.10 What iteration 6 established, what it ruled out, and what it abandoned

Everything below is one model per claim except where a second family is named, at 4B to 8B parameters, on memorised tasks in the style of LeetCode.

**Established.**

1. *Iteration 4's random-push escapes are a property of Qwen3-8B, not of 8-bit floating-point rounding.* At the same absolute displacement, the same 40 directions and the same slots, bf16 escapes on connected components at 0.65 against 0.725 under W8A8 and on shortest path at 0.15 against 0.20, with per-direction shares ranked alike (Spearman 0.96 and 0.87), and per-sample plan noise reproduces (25 and 22 of 50 against 30 and 22). Activation rounding alone adds nothing; a 5-point per-slot boost on connected components comes from the 8-bit floating-point weights or the native kernel. Iteration 5's bf16 null belongs to its ban-free unit or its direction seeds.
2. *In Qwen3-8B the substitute of a ban and the algorithm of an instruction are carried by the residual states at the task-specification positions on the prompt-route tasks.* Exchanging those states alone transfers the ban on shortest path (24 of 30 attempts, 21 of 30 correct programs) and kth smallest (17 of 30 attempts, 16 of 30 correct), and a forced instruction on shortest path (30 of 30 attempts, 30 of 30 correct) and connected components (28 of 30 attempts, 24 of 30 correct); matched-norm random exchanges and a placebo twin transfer at most 0.13. The condition span carries the ban on the direct-route tasks (two sum 1.00, find duplicate 0.90). The read position carries nothing. (iteration-7 correction)
3. *Gemma's BFS-or-DFS choice is made at one generated token,* ` visited` against a blank line, `if` or `queue` at response index 32, about 138 tokens before any algorithm-identifying code, and its fork log-odds is linearly decodable from the residual stream at that position across prompts (Lasso on SAE codes R-squared 0.66 against 0.18 for text, preregistered; ridge on the raw state 0.72, post hoc); at the fork position that is close to a next-token readout, so it shows that the next-token distribution is linearly encoded there, not that a plan is, and the standardised ridge on the same layer-29 SAE codes reaches R-squared 0.15 against 0.086 for a template-plus-noun-norm control (delta 0.064, below the preregistered 0.10 bar). (iteration-7 correction)
4. *Steering the fork works and costs correctness.* Difference in means moves the fork 2.3 times as far as the SAE clamp at matched norm, both move the plan equally at matched effect, and edits toward the minority algorithm lowered the pass rate from 0.84 to 0.16-0.58, except the SAE top-5 clamp (18 BFS, pass 0.84); edits toward the default are clean. (iteration-7 correction)
5. *The NLA does not verbalise the planned algorithm at pre-code positions in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct,* although it names an algorithm at the token where the prompt names it; an outside reader of the text predicts the realised algorithm better than the NLA per sample (0:25 at one unit per sample, p 6.0e-08), and at the task level the evidence is inconclusive (5 task clusters; bootstrap interval [-0.35, 0.02]). (iteration-7 correction)
6. *Record repairs.* The landing half is descriptive (17 of 21 per set, 5 of 8 where the twin wrote no alternative, p 0.053); the movability half is not a strong predictor with a moderate relation not excluded (0.15, interval -0.44 to 0.65); the 14 disputed programs are not novel.

## 6.11 What the next iteration takes from this one

The plan-variable account was tested in part, and its two halves came out differently. Three different quantities were measured, one per model (Table 279): where a ban or instruction is carried in Qwen3-8B (the task-specification states on the prompt-route tasks), where the natural choice of Gemma is made (one generated token), and whether the plan of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is verbalisable before the code (not to this NLA); the natural choice of Qwen3-8B and the read position of Gemma were never measured. Whether the choice is a low-rank variable in Qwen3-8B, and whether random pushes act through it, is untested, because the DAS experiment was lost at planning. The engine control has removed the obstacle that made such a test look premature: random pushes at iteration 4's absolute unit move the algorithm in bf16 as they did in 8-bit floating point, so the escapes are a stable target that a fitted plan subspace can be asked to explain. The next measurements are DAS at the task-specification positions of shortest path and kth smallest, with the Stage A exchanges as the full-state ceiling, and the projection of iteration 4's 40 directions onto the fitted subspace. (iteration-7 correction)

Three leads come with it. The ban-free unit moves fewer programs than the ban unit at a larger scalar dose, so its per-position and per-block profile, or the direction seeds, decide movability; a controlled comparison of the two units on the same seeds would say which. Gemma's one-token fork offers a clean site where a rank-1 DAS subspace moves the fork log-odds by 8.8 nats, a fit that needs the Sutter controls (random initialisation, shuffled targets, forced-DFS sources) before it says anything about dimensionality; whether a smaller push there switches the algorithm without breaking the program is the question for a usable knob. And two sum's task-specification states carry part of a ban that iteration 3 had classed as direct, so the route classes are not all-or-none. (iteration-7 correction)

**The hypothesis update.** The update kept the plan and added a fork. We call it the *plan-and-fork account*. While the model reads the task, the residual states at the task specification positions carry a variable of low rank that sets which algorithm the model will write; during generation, the program opens with tokens that every algorithm shares, and the variable is realised at the first token where continuations of different algorithms part. We call that token the *fork*, a forking token in the sense of Bigelow et al. [30]. The *fork margin* is the teacher-forced log odds, at the fork, of the default class of tokens against the class off the default. If the account holds, three things follow. A subspace of low rank fitted by DAS [110, 111] should carry the transfer of a ban or a forced instruction, under the controls that would expose a spurious fit. A random push should change the algorithm in proportion to how far it moves the fork margin. And temperature should act on the algorithm only through the fork: at temperature T, the share off the default at the fork is the softmax of the fork logits divided by T, so the account predicts each temperature's share from the logits alone, before sampling.

Ten claims were preregistered, each with a rule committed by sha256 before its first decisive sample. We call them by their content.

- *The fork claim* (primary): the teacher-forced fork margin under each of 40 equal-dose random pushes predicts which pushes change the algorithm, on connected components and shortest path.
- *The DAS claim* (primary): a DAS map of rank 16 or less at the site of Stage A recovers at least 0.8 of the full state transfer (the transfer when every residual state at that site is exchanged, which we call the *full state exchange*) in held-out generation, beats random subspaces of the same rank, and survives a fit on permuted labels and a fit on a randomly initialised network [132].
- *The routing claim*: whether an edit in the fitted subspace lands where the forced source points (categorical) or follows a margin toward the ban's usual substitute.
- *The axis claim*: the projection of a random push on an axis from the default to the second choice predicts and mediates its effect; we call *second choice* the algorithm a model ranks second on a task, the runner-up of earlier sections.
- *The temperature claim*: at mixed units, the algorithm given the fork token's class is nearly certain, the share off the default at each temperature follows the fork logits divided by T, and on the collapsed tasks the fork margin is large enough that no temperature in range reaches the alternative.
- *The manifold claim*: in the fitted subspace, bans sit outside a paraphrase null and seeds and instructions sit inside it.
- *The discreteness claim*: scaling the fitted edit from 0 to 1.5 changes the algorithm as a step, not a ramp.
- *The dose unit claim*: the 2x2 of dose unit (the absolute unit of iteration 4 against the ban-free unit of iteration 5; we call the latter the *relative unit*, because it scales the noise to a fixed fraction of the twin's residual norm) by direction seeds (those of iteration 4 against those of iteration 5) says which explains iteration 5's weak plan noise, and plan noise is then repriced at the unit that moves.
- *The Gemma claims*: temperature through the fork in a second family, DAS at Gemma's fork with the full set of controls, and a validated circuit for the fork margin.
- *The search claim*: an evolutionary program search with an executable evaluator writes correct programs outside the catalogue at least 10 times as often per call as the best knob applied to single samples, on at least two tasks.

**The strategy.** Seven artifacts ran (Table 281). The record audit repaired the record from rows on disk and ran the checks the review asked for. A DAS experiment fitted the plan subspace on Qwen3-8B [5] and tested it in generation. A fork experiment located forks by prefix resampling and tested the fork and axis claims. A temperature experiment tested the temperature claim on the three units where the instruct twin is already mixed. A dose unit experiment ran the 2x2 and repriced plan noise. A search experiment ran evolution in the style of FunSearch [81] over a MAP-Elites archive [133]. A Gemma experiment ran temperature, DAS and a circuit at the fork of Gemma.

## 7.3 A fitted plan subspace in Qwen3-8B

### 7.3.1 Design

The DAS experiment [ARTIFACT:art_veI9l_Rb9wDY] asked whether the choice Stage A transfers is carried by a linear subspace of the task specification states that has low rank. DAS fits one orthonormal map R (4096 by 16, with nested ranks 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16) such that exchanging only the coordinates of R between a source prompt and the neutral twin reproduces the source's behaviour [110, 111]. The map is fitted on teacher-forced pairs: a source prompt (a ban of the default or an instruction forcing an algorithm Y) and the twin, scored on the log likelihood of programs of Y. It is tested in held-out generation scored by hidden tests, on held-out templates, against the full state exchange at the same site, which is the ceiling. Three tasks were used: shortest path (default Dijkstra, ban substitute Bellman-Ford/SPFA), connected components (default union find, substitute BFS or DFS) and kth smallest (default full sort, substitute quickselect or a size k heap).

The controls follow the published objections to DAS. Random subspaces of the same rank test whether any subspace would do. A *fit on permuted labels* trains the same map with the source labels permuted; if it transfers as well, the fitted subspace does not encode the label. We call *random-initialisation control* a fit of the same map on a randomly initialised copy of the network; if the untrained network admits an equally good teacher-forced fit, fit quality says nothing about a learned variable [132]. Two dormancy checks follow Makelov et al. [122]: the share of the twin's natural variance across prompts that lies in the subspace, and a *projected map*, the fitted map restricted to the top 64 principal components of natural variation, whose retention of the teacher-forced effect should be high if the subspace acts through directions the model uses. A *reverse interchange* writes the twin's coordinates into the ban prompt; a variable should restore the default.

A full state exchange at a single block peaks at block 18 on shortest path and at block 16 on connected components and kth smallest (Table 290). The two kinds of source behave differently in generation. A forced instruction is carried by one block: exchanging the forced prompt's states at that block alone transfers Bellman-Ford/SPFA in 30 of 30 slots on shortest path and BFS in 28 of 30 on connected components. A ban on the two core tasks is not: the same exchange at a single block moves 0 of 30 slots on both, and only the band of blocks 12 to 23 transfers it (11 of 30 on shortest path, against 1 at base; 17 of 30 on connected components, against 0).
