### 7.3.5 The controls that make it a handle, not a variable

The DAS claim is not supported on any task. Three controls fail. The fits on permuted labels transfer 0.47 on shortest path, 0.70 on connected components and 0.60 on kth smallest of the full state effect, against a committed limit of 0.1: on connected components a permuted fit at rank 16 still gives 21 correct BFS programs of 30. The permuted fit can also write its own label: at rank 16 it turns the shortest path ban into Floyd-Warshall in 15 of 30 slots, because one training ban had been relabelled Floyd-Warshall by the permutation. With only two kept algorithms per task the permutation changed 44% of the training labels (56% on kth smallest), so the signal to leave the default survives any such shuffle, which weakens this control as a test of label content. The untrained network admits a teacher-forced fit almost as good as the trained one (13.31 nats against 14.45 on shortest path, a ratio of 0.92 against a limit of 0.5). And the dormancy checks flag two of three tasks: the reverse interchange on shortest path restores the default in 0 of 30 slots, against 21 of 30 for the full state reverse, and on kth smallest the projected map keeps only 0.20 to 0.26 of the teacher-forced effect. The connected components reverse was not testable. The subspace is not dormant by variance: it holds 0.7% to 18% of the twin's natural variance across prompts against 0.03% to 0.4% for random subspaces of the same rank, at the 100th percentile of 1,000 random draws on every task and rank (Table 307).

The reading is that the fitted subspace is a strong steering handle of low rank on the choice, and that this experiment cannot say it is the variable the model computes. A subspace that permuted labels also find, and that an untrained network also admits, is a direction along which the downstream computation is sensitive, which is what a steering vector needs and less than what a causal variable needs. The control arms behave as before: DAS and the full state exchange at the read position, and a rank-1 difference-in-means direction and a PCA-16 subspace at the task specification states, each transfer at most 2 of 30 (Tables 298 and 299). Under the fourth template, whose ban the model mostly ignores, the full state exchange still transfers 4 of 10 on shortest path and 9 of 10 on connected components.

### 7.3.8 The manifold in the fitted coordinates

The manifold claim placed prompts of shortest path in the rank-16 coordinates of the fitted map. The *paraphrase null* is the distribution of the distance D from the default centroid over neutral paraphrases of the twin (median 0.52, 95th percentile 1.13). All five ban templates lie outside it (D 1.73 to 2.62, at the 100th percentile), each displaced toward the second choice along the axis from the default centroid to the Bellman-Ford/SPFA centroid (+1.10 to +1.76). The two random seeds, the short instruction to make a new algorithm and the 2,000-word novelty instruction lie inside it (76th to 88th percentile), as predicted. The semantic seed was predicted outside and lies inside, at the 94th percentile (Table 309). Behaviour agrees with the placement: the neutral prompt, both random seeds and the short instruction write Dijkstra in every correct program, the semantic seed adds one program labelled other, and the long novelty instruction is the only prompt that reaches a named alternative (6 Bellman-Ford/SPFA programs of 28 correct; Table 308), a shift that happens while the model writes its rationale, not in the prompt states. Multidimensional scaling of the centroids has stress 0.079; centroids and implemented counts are in Table 310, and geodesic distances on neighbour graphs in Table 311. Bans that name all but one of the five algorithms (bans that leave one survivor) are not placed near their survivor: the survivor's centroid ranks 3.10 of 5 on average by geodesic distance (random relabelling p 0.63), and every such ban sits nearest the forced Bellman-Ford/SPFA prompts. The geometry does not predict where a ban lands.

### 7.3.9 Seeds, discreteness and the full cell list

A second initialisation seed fits a different subspace (principal angles of 38 to 90 degrees to the first) with similar behaviour: no discordance between seeds reaches significance (Table 312). The subspace is therefore not unique, as in Gemma (Section 7.8). The discreteness claim fails. Scaling the rank-2 edit of the ban by lambda from 0 to 1.5 raises correct Bellman-Ford/SPFA programs from 1 of 20 (lambda 0 to 0.2) through 4 of 20 (0.4 to 0.5) to a plateau of 6 to 9 of 20 from lambda 0.6 to 1.5; the committed logistic width is 3.25 in lambda (midpoint 1.47), against 0.3 or less for a step, and the one candidate hybrid among 114 correct programs was judged a single algorithm (Table 313). Of the 38 correct programs labelled other across the experiment, 36 are catalogue variants and 2 are labeller misses; none is novel. The engine reproduced the iteration-6 twin labels in 20 of 20, 19 of 20 and 20 of 20 slots; two GPU unit tests missed their tolerance because of bf16 noise from kernel shapes (packed against separate forward passes differ by up to 0.273 nats per program, cached against full forward passes by 0.160), so every compared quantity is measured within one batch shape. ## 7.4 Where the algorithm is decided in generation (Qwen3-8B)

### 7.4.1 Design

The fork experiment [ARTIFACT:art_pHL7LWNhpcCS] asked whether one early generated token decides the algorithm, and whether the decision at that token explains which random pushes of iteration 4 change the algorithm. Forks were located by *prefix resampling*: from each base program (one written under the neutral twin, under a push of plan noise or under a ban), the model was restarted at positions along the program's first 128 tokens, and eight continuations were sampled and labelled at each. A *change point* is a position where the share of continuations off the default changes significantly; a fork is a change point on the *shared opening*, the token sequence that most twin programs share before they part. Where no fork exists the committed fallback is the *opening log likelihood ratio* (opening LLR): the teacher-forced log likelihood ratio of the opening of the second choice to the opening of the default over the first L tokens (48 on shortest path, 20 on kth smallest, whose programs are about 20 tokens long). The 40 random directions of iteration 4 were then scored for their fork margin under the push and compared with the correct share off the default (y) that each direction produced in bf16, the share of its programs that pass the hidden tests and implement a named algorithm other than the default; the fork margin under a push is written m.

### 7.4.2 Forks

Connected components has two forks, at generated tokens 10 and 11 of the opening `def solve(n, edges):`, which 94% of twin programs share (Tables 315 and 316). At token 10, a comment token leads to BFS or DFS in all 159 continuations, ` parent` leads to union find in all 130, ` def` leads off the default in 0.69 of 72, and ` from` leads off in all 11. At token 11, after ` def`, the routine's name settles it: ` dfs` leads to DFS in all 45 continuations and ` find` to union find in all 32. The entropy of the label given the token falls from 0.97 bits to 0.00 at token 11. Shortest path has no single fork: pushed programs stay undecided through token 60, and its only change point (token 92) lies off the shared opening. On kth smallest a ban fixes the algorithm before the first generated token: at the first position only 0 to 2 of 8 continuations differ from the base program's class, and no change occurs in 128 tokens.

### 7.4.3 The fork claim

On connected components the fork margin under each push predicts which of the 40 directions change the algorithm, at Spearman 0.80 (95% interval 0.62 to 0.91; Table 317). It separates iteration 4's 26 confirmed escapers from the rest with AUC 0.81; its Spearman with the attempted share is 0.82, and the 48-token opening LLR in place of the fork margin reaches 0.87. On shortest path the committed fallback fails: the 48-token opening LLR reaches 0.15 (p 0.18). The fork claim therefore fails as a two-task claim (Holm p 0.357) and is recorded as not supported, inconclusive. A binomial model calibrated on all 104 cells of both tasks predicts held-out shares with mean absolute error 0.25, against a committed 0.10. The record of each cell is in Tables 318 and 319. Two checks qualify the connected components result. A placebo that shuffles the map from fork tokens to outcomes still reaches the observed 0.80 in 18% of 200 permutations (median 0.22): with four or five mapped tokens per fork, the margin's power comes from the probability of staying on the default fork tokens, not from the exact outcome rates of the other tokens. And the resampling screen is sparse: in simulation, a jump of 0.4 in the share off the default with only three screen positions before it was detected in 54% of runs, so weak or very early forks can be missed.

On kth smallest a prospective test was committed before generation. The 20-token opening LLR of 24 fresh directions predicts their correct share off the default at Spearman 0.60 (one sided p 0.0014), and 18 of the 24 directions move at least one program (Table 320). The failure on shortest path is a matter of where the decision falls: the Spearman of the opening LLR with the share rises from 0.15 at 48 tokens to 0.42 at 160 (p 0.0032; Table 325), as it should if shortest path decides late.

### 7.4.5 Necessity and sufficiency of the axis

Clamping the axis component of each escaping push at blocks from the axis layer to 35 removes nothing: 105 escapes with the clamp against 104 without it and 106 with a clamp along a random direction (Table 323). Pushing along the axis itself is a different matter (Table 324). Doses s are counted in units of the distance between the centroids of the prompts forcing the default and the second choice along the axis. At the committed doses (s up to 1) nothing escapes on any task. At four times that distance, beyond the committed range, connected components switches to DFS in 29 of 30 slots and BFS in the 30th, with all 30 programs passing, while the matched random direction moves none (30:0, p 1.9e-9). The axis edit at that dose has 0.55 of the norm of the median escaping random direction. On shortest path the axis does nothing even at eight times the distance (1 of 30), and on kth smallest the axis at eight times the distance moves 5 of 30, exactly as many as the random direction. On connected components the axis is a sufficient control direction without being the path random pushes take.

### 7.4.7 The top five prohibition inside the manifold

The review asked for the top five push at a dose that stays on the forced prompt manifold of the grid task. The fork experiment pushed the twin's states toward the centroid of the survivor region, toward a random survivor, away from the banned centroid and toward IDA*, at a quarter, a half and one times the distance between centroids (Table 327). All 300 programs implement BFS, at pass rates between 0.73 and 0.93; none implements an algorithm outside the banned five. The prompt top five ban of iteration 6 had at least moved the model between BFS and DFS (25 and 23 of 50). ## 7.5 Temperature acts through the fork (Qwen3-8B)

### 7.5.1 Design

The temperature experiment [ARTIFACT:art_MZAfDPVhM6Ui] tested the temperature claim where it can be tested: on the three units where the instruct twin already writes two algorithms. Minimum spanning tree weight mixes Kruskal and Prim, trapped rain water mixes prefix and suffix maxima with two pointers, and valid anagram mixes sorting with counting. Iteration 5 had recorded minority shares of 0.34, 0.36 and 0.24; this experiment's twins give 0.19, 0.31 and 0.13 on prompts identical byte for byte (Table 330). The claim has three committed tests. Test 1: the entropy of the algorithm given the class of the token at the fork is at most 0.3 bits on at least two units. Test 2: predictions made from the teacher-forced fork logits divided by T, committed before any temperature sample, match the observed minority share (drop from T 1.0 to 0.3 of at least 0.15, mean absolute error at most 0.10, and the change from 1.0 to 1.3 within 0.10 of prediction) on at least two units. Test 3: on the four collapsed tasks the fork margin is at least 4 nats, large enough that no temperature in range reaches the alternative. Every temperature cell shares its random numbers across temperatures (same seed), at temperatures 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3, under top-p 1 and top-k 10.

### 7.5.3 The fork logits predict the temperature response

Test 2 passes on minimum spanning tree weight and fails on the other two units, so the temperature claim is recorded as PARTIAL (Tables 333 and 334). On minimum spanning tree weight, lowering T from 1.0 to 0.3 removes Prim from 17 slots and adds it to none (one sided p below 1e-4); the observed drop of 0.34 is twice the predicted 0.17, and the mean absolute error across temperatures is 0.083. On trapped rain water the mean absolute error is 0.105 and the drop 0.08 (7:3), and on valid anagram the minority share does not drop (2:5), with an error of 0.043. Pooled over the first two units the drop is 24:3 (p 2.5e-5), which survives a Bonferroni correction over the seven committed tests. Three post hoc readings qualify the misses. The replay per slot, which walks the opening with each slot's own random numbers and reads the class of the fork token it picks, names the algorithm of an individual program in 0.90 to 0.98 of slots on the opening in every cell (Table 333, last column). On trapped rain water the shares implied by the replay of the actual 50 streams (0.08, 0.18, 0.18 and 0.16) reproduce the observed sweep (0.10, 0.18, 0.18 and 0.20), so the miss there is the gap between a cell of 50 streams and its expectation, not a failure of the mechanism. On minimum spanning tree weight the sweep's 50 streams lean toward Prim at T 1.0 (0.40, against 0.20 for the twin's own slots, Fisher p 0.011), which is why the observed drop is twice the predicted one. On valid anagram the prediction itself had said the drop would be small: one template prefers ` count` even greedily, and about 19% of samples leave the opening at every temperature. Above T 1.0 nothing is added on any unit: the observed change from 1.0 to 1.3 is between -0.02 and +0.06, and the predicted change is at most 0.013, because what the minority gains at the fork is offset by samples that leave the shared opening as T rises (on minimum spanning tree weight the predicted share on the opening falls from 0.72 at T 1.0 to 0.55 at 1.3). Across all temperatures the ideas stay the two or three known algorithms of each unit; only phrasings multiply (Table 340). Top-k 10 gave the same program as top-p 1 in all 600 paired slots, because every token at the fork lies in the top 10.

### 7.5.6 Question 1a-c of the request

The request's question 1a-c asks whether, with the seed fixed and top-k 10, a tight temperature gives one idea in many phrasings or many ideas, and whether loosening it multiplies ideas or phrasings. The only correct programs off the catalogue are 40 continuations from one fork token of low probability on valid anagram; they form 2 distinct programs, both the catalogue's extra counting mode, and are catalogue variants.

## 7.6 The dose unit, not the seeds, made iteration 5's plan noise weak (Qwen3-8B)

### 7.6.1 Design

Iteration 4 found plan noise strong under its *absolute unit*, in which each cell (block and position) receives a random direction scaled to the displacement a ban itself causes at that cell. Iteration 5 found it nearly inert under its *relative unit*, which scales the direction to a fixed fraction of the twin's own residual norm at each cell, and with different direction seeds. Section 6.3 showed that the 8-bit engine was not the cause. The dose unit experiment [ARTIFACT:art_8O5eaNc5gxJs] crossed the two units with the two seed sets in bf16, on the same 50 slots per design, and committed a decision rule before the first row: the answer is the unit if the main effect of the unit is positive with its interval above zero and the effect of the seeds lies within plus or minus 0.10. Two anchors reproduce the earlier artifacts on the same slots: the absolute unit with iteration-4 seeds gives 26 of 50 attempts against 25 in the engine control (agreement per slot 0.98), and the relative unit with iteration-5 seeds gives 1 of 50 against 1. Iteration 5's null is thus reproduced without its left padding, so the decoding path is not the cause either.

### 7.6.2 The 2x2

The answer is the unit (Table 341). On connected components at alpha 2, the absolute unit gives a correct share off the default of 0.50 and 0.52 under the two seed sets, and the relative unit 0.10 and 0.02: a unit effect of +0.45 [0.35, 0.55], a seed effect of +0.03 [-0.07, 0.14] and an interaction of -0.10 [-0.28, 0.08]. A conditional logistic regression with slot strata agrees (unit coefficient 4.34, p 1e-4; seeds 1.68, p 0.13). On shortest path, at 100 slots, the unit effect is smaller (+0.115 [0.06, 0.17]) and most attempts under the absolute unit fail the hidden tests (13 correct of 41 attempted at pass 0.66; Table 342). On 50 fresh connected components slots the unit effect replicates (+0.42 [0.32, 0.52]), and on kth smallest it is +0.27 [0.18, 0.37] with a seed effect of +0.03 (Tables 346 and 347). On kth smallest, unlike connected components, the relative unit does move the algorithm, at half the absolute unit's rate.

### 7.6.3 Why the units differ

The two units differ in where the energy sits. The absolute unit is peaky: on connected components its top quartile of cells holds 81% of its energy, on bands of a few task tokens, and its largest cell receives about 2.1 times that cell's residual norm. The relative unit is flat by construction: its top quartile holds 42%, and its largest cell receives 0.25 times the residual norm. A fifth design applies the per-position profile of the relative unit at the energy per block of the absolute unit; it moves 0.28 on connected components, between the two, so the profile (+0.22 [0.08, 0.36], McNemar 13:2) and the energy (+0.18 [0.06, 0.30], 10:1) each carry part of the effect.

A split of the absolute unit by cell confirms that the peaky cells matter (Tables 343 and 344). At the same total energy, the cells of the top quartile alone move connected components in 29 of 50 slots, the other three quartiles in 15 (18:4, Holm p 0.01), and the same energy at shuffled positions in 4 (21:0 against the full unit). On shortest path the other three quartiles include the cell with a massive activation at position 87 (the token `0`, norm about 10,290, 82% of the unit's energy there); noise on them breaks every program (pass 0.00), and the top quartile alone moves 5 of 50. Sweeping the dose of the relative unit shows that it comes close to the effect of the absolute unit on connected components only near alpha 4 (20 of 50 at pass 0.98, against 25 for the absolute unit at alpha 2), and that at alpha 6 the programs break (pass 0.46; Table 345). At alpha 4 it pays 1.8 times the downstream displacement of the absolute unit at the read position (423 against 240), and at a matched dose at block 12 (alpha 3, 13.6 against 13.8) it moves only 9 of 50 (McNemar 1:17 against the absolute unit). On shortest path it never moves more than 5 of 50 before the programs break.

The size of the downstream displacement does not explain the difference. At alpha 2 the realised displacement at block 35 is about the same under the two units, at the read position and at the first generated token, yet the absolute unit escapes 5 to 25 times as often. Adding the log block-35 norms to the per-sample logit leaves the unit coefficients unchanged on connected components (-2.35 to -2.54 for the relative unit with iteration-4 seeds, -3.31 to -3.49 with iteration-5 seeds). And the arm of the top quartile has the smallest downstream displacement of all pushed arms while moving the most. An exploratory analysis of individual samples found that which samples escape is close to a coin flip for a given direction and token stream: two directions on the same common random numbers agree weakly (phi coefficient 0.16 to 0.20 on connected components, about 0 on shortest path), the same direction is not monotone in dose (escape at alpha 2 given escape at alpha 1 in 2 of 6 samples, against a marginal 0.52), and neither the size nor the direction of the block-35 displacement predicts escape within the absolute unit (AUC under cross-validation 0.40 to 0.53). The unit sets the rate of escape; single outcomes behave like per-sample random variables.

### 7.6.4 Plan noise repriced at the unit that moves

At the absolute unit with iteration-4 seeds, plan noise was priced against the five knobs of iteration 5 that act on the text on five tasks (Tables 348 to 351). We call the price measure the 5-point Hill-1: the Hill-1 number of distinct correct algorithms reachable within a pass cost of 5 points along the dose range of each knob. Beside it we report the pass cost of reaching Hill-1 of 1.5 and 2. Plan noise beats an intent sentence written by the base model (base intent) on kth smallest (3.22 against 1.73) and the grid (1.39 against 1.05), and loses on connected components (2.13 against 2.53), shortest path (1.21 against 1.45) and two sum (1.10 against 1.61). The committed prediction was 3 of 5 and the result is 2 of 5. Iteration 5's comparison, which plan noise had lost at the relative unit, is reversed in its mean (the margin of plan noise over the best text sampler moves from -0.40 to +0.12 [-0.18, 0.27]) but not in its rule: the iteration-5 rule replayed at the absolute unit is still disconfirmed, 2 of 5. Temperature 1.3 and top-k 10 reach Hill-1 of at most 1.09 on every task. The six verdicts that the record audit tagged as resting on the relative unit are now retagged: at the design that moves (the absolute unit with iteration-4 seeds at alpha 2), kth smallest (+0.58) and connected components (+0.50) are movable, and shortest path (+0.16, at pass 0.62 against the twin's 0.98), two sum (+0.02) and the grid (+0.08) are not. Five correct kth smallest programs labelled other count frequencies in a hash map and walk the sorted distinct keys by cumulative count; they are counting sort with key compression, a catalogue variant. Of the 25 pairs of task and text knob, 17 reproduced the iteration-5 labels in 10 of 10 check slots and reuse its rows, and 8 were regenerated in this engine; the 250 base-model intents were identical in text and token ids to iteration 5's. Against the exchange experiment's engine, labels and pass agreed in 15 of 16 slots on shortest path and kth smallest, 40 of 40 on connected components and two sum, and 34 of 40 on the grid (all BFS, with 6 pass flips), which the artifact logs as kernel sensitivity across GPUs.

## 7.7 Evolutionary search with an evaluator (Qwen3-8B)

### 7.7.1 Design

Six iterations of generation one sample at a time had produced no correct novel algorithm. The search experiment [ARTIFACT:art_VhaHGe7SxV95] tested the documented alternative [81, 82]: an evolutionary program search in which the model mutates parent programs and an executable evaluator keeps the correct ones. The search uses four islands, each with a MAP-Elites archive [133] whose cells are the runtime label and a signature of the program's data structures; each round draws two parents per prompt by a Boltzmann choice over cells, asks for four children per prompt, and resets the worst island every 500 calls. The *evaluator* runs each program in an isolated subprocess with memory and time limits through 8 quick cases, the full hidden suite and 10 stress inputs of maximum size; a program that embeds hidden answers as constants fails the stress stage. A *novelty critic* compares each program, as hashed 4-gram shingles of its tokens after normalisation of identifiers, with 18,237 known solutions from 10 datasets, and a program passes the *catalogue screen* if it is correct and either labelled other or less similar to every known solution than the 5th percentile of the forced catalogue programs (Table 353). Two levels are counted: level a, distinct programs passing the screen, and level b, programs that adjudication places outside the catalogue (a known technique outside it, or novel).

The comparison arms use the same evaluator, labeller and critic: no evolution (the same prompt with frozen seed parents, the AlphaEvolve ablation [82]), the novelty instruction with no parents, enumerate and pick, base intent, the neutral twin, and a larger mutator (qwen3-235b through OpenRouter, 500 calls). The committed prediction was that search reaches at least 10 times the level a rate of the better of enumerate and pick and base intent, on at least two of shortest path, kth smallest and trapped rain water.

### 7.7.2 Results

The search claim is not met at either level (Tables 354 to 356). At level a, search beats enumerate and pick by 3.83 times on shortest path, 6.65 times on kth smallest (lower bound 4.86) and 0.91 times on trapped rain water. At level b only kth smallest produces any program: 78 distinct programs from search against 0 from enumerate and pick (lower bound 12.8), 0 from no evolution and 2 from the instruction alone. The level b gain on kth smallest comes from evolution: against no evolution with the same prompt it is 78 to 0 (lower bound 5.1), and 66 of the 93 level b rows sit at depth 2 or more with parents other than the seeds (Table 362). At level a on kth smallest most of the gain is the instruction's: the instruction alone beats enumerate and pick by 4.6 times, and search beats the instruction alone by 1.45 times.

The programs outside the catalogue are known techniques (Tables 357 and 358). On kth smallest, 103 distinct programs implement order statistics on a Fenwick tree, binary search on the value range, bucket select, partial selection sort and a treap with order statistics; 540 are catalogue variants. On shortest path the 15-fold lead of search over no evolution at level a is restyled SPFA: every adjudicated program is a catalogue variant or degenerate, and two of them pass every test while being wrong in general, because they deduplicate on distance modulo a constant. On trapped rain water search loses to both no evolution and the instruction alone. No program is novel: the rule-of-three bound [67] is 7.5% over the 40 merged adjudicated clusters and 0.16% per correct search program on kth smallest.

### 7.7.3 Adjudication, the larger mutator and robustness

The judge gate failed: no judge family reached 9 of 10 on the controls of known class (Table 359). Every judge called the D'Esopo–Pape control a variant of SPFA, and three of five called novel a control that processes heights in decreasing order. Under the committed fallback the final class of every candidate is the executor's manual read (121 full reads and 123 structured reads). The reads were not blind to arm, so a rule-based reclassification blind to arm was run; it agrees with the manual classes on 94.4% of 816 distinct programs and reproduces the level b contrast on kth smallest (87 of 2,500 against 2 of 1,250, lower bound 6.7). The pair of judges fixed in advance was still run as advisory votes, with kappa 0.42; all 11 of their novel calls were overturned on reading (dead-code tournaments, partial selection sort and SPFA on a lifted graph).

The larger mutator, over its 500 calls, reaches level a at 0.84 times the rate of the first 500 calls of search and level b at 2.6 times (23 against 9, lower bound 1.28; Table 360). It writes mostly quickselect (402 of 441 correct programs), while search writes counting sort, quickselect and programs labelled other in nearly equal numbers. The search rate on kth smallest is stable across islands (bootstrap 0.173 to 0.227), and at matched effort no other arm approaches search's 63 idea clusters (Table 361). A placebo that shuffles the arms is significant in 1% to 6% of shuffles with median rate ratio near 1.

## 7.8 Gemma: temperature, a controlled DAS and a validated circuit at the fork

### 7.8.1 Engine and calibration

The Gemma experiment [ARTIFACT:art_HY7uYZz-OjRW] returned to the fork of gemma-3-4b-it on the grid task, where a shared 32-token opening ends at a token that decides between DFS and BFS (Section 6.5). The engine check on 50 twin slots gave 19 BFS programs (0.38), just outside iteration 6's interval for 61 of 200 (0.245 to 0.372), so the check fails as preregistered; iteration 6's own share on the same 50 slots is 0.36, so the slots, not the engine, lean toward BFS. The discrepancy from the empty prefix of iteration 6 did not reproduce: 200 continuations from the empty prefix give 65 BFS on the path over several prompts and 72 on the path for a single prompt, both consistent with the natural 61 (Fisher p 0.75 and 0.29). The two paths disagree on 9 of 200 slots (1 against 8, p 0.039), so the batch shape changes a few coupled programs; by the rule committed beforehand, the probability of BFS given each fork token comes from a calibration run on the main engine (Table 363). The fork token fixes both the algorithm and its implementation: ` visited` leads to DFS (BFS 1 of 125), and ` queue` leads to a BFS that carries whole paths and pops from the front of a list, which is BFS but too slow for the 30 by 30 hidden tests (0 of 125 pass).

### 7.8.2 Temperature through the fork in a second family

The temperature claim holds in Gemma (Table 364). The predicted attempted BFS share, computed from the teacher-forced fork logits divided by T and committed before any temperature sample, matches the observed share in every top-p 1 cell: 0.015 against 0.02 at T 0.3, 0.166 against 0.24 at 0.7, 0.323 against 0.34 at 1.0 and 0.450 against 0.46 at 1.3 (mean absolute error 0.026; every prediction inside its Wilson interval). The entropy of the algorithm given the fork class is 0.153 bits. Lowering T from 1.0 to 0.3 switches 16 slots from BFS to DFS and none back (p 1.5e-5), and half of all slots change their algorithm somewhere across temperature. Top-k 10 cells are identical to top-p 1 program for program. A placebo that shuffles the temperatures of the sweep gives an error of 0.123 and fails the 0.10 bar.

### 7.8.3 DAS at the fork with the controls iteration 6 lacked

DAS at the fork was fitted on held-out templates and held-out forced sources (768 pairs). The layer was chosen by the committed rule, the argmax of rank-1 recovery under cross-validation, at block 17. Swapping the whole fork state moves the held-out margin by 3.6 nats at block 17, rising to 8.2 to 9.1 nats at blocks 25 to 29; DAS at block 17 recovers 1.98, 2.36, 2.58 and 2.81 of that at ranks 1, 2, 4 and 8 (Tables 364b and 364c), because a trained direction moves the margin further than the weak full state swap at an early block. This time the controls hold. Fifty random subspaces recover nothing (0.000). Permuting the source labels gives recovery between -0.27 and -0.30 against the true targets (one permutation of three reaches 0.17 at rank 1). A randomly initialised Gemma moves its margin at most 0.25 times as far (interchange intervention accuracy 0.50 to 0.72 against 1.00). The DAS claim's Gemma version is therefore supported at every rank, and the controls that failed for Qwen3-8B in Section 7.3 pass here.

Two limits remain. The committed wording rule does not license calling the subspace one dimensional: rank-1 recovery passes, but the subspace coordinate tracks the natural fork log odds of 120 twin variants at Spearman -0.50, just short of the 0.5 the rule required, and the subspace holds 0.0009 of the twin's natural variance across prompts, at the random 95th percentile. And the subspace is not unique: across three seeds only one direction is shared (cosine 0.50 to 0.52), and a difference-in-means direction sits at cosine 0.39 to it.

### 7.8.4 A dose dial that keeps the programs

In generation the DAS edit at block 17, applied once at the fork position with the opening prefilled, acts as a dose dial (Table 365). From the twin's 11 correct BFS programs of 50, the edit raises correct BFS to 20, 27, 31, 37, 38 and 42 as lambda rises from 0.1 to 1, at pass rates of 0.68 to 0.88; at lambda 1 it gives more correct BFS programs (42) than the explicit instruction to use BFS (35). A difference-in-means direction scaled to the same teacher-forced effect flips the algorithm just as well (up to 50 of 50 attempts) and destroys the programs (pass 0.70 down to 0.00, never significantly more correct BFS than the twin). A version of the DAS edit restricted to the logits, which changes the fork token's distribution but not the state that persists in the cache, gives 35 correct programs: the edited fork state helps the later code. The teacher-forced prediction of the attempted share (the fork distribution times the probability of BFS given each token) matches the observed share within 0.10 in all 26 cells (mean gap 0.029). Toward DFS, the edit gives 41 to 50 correct DFS programs of 50 against the twin's 32 (Table 365b). The strong difference-in-means edit toward DFS, left unmatched by a bisection bug, keeps most programs (45 correct of 49 attempted, pass 0.90), so the difference-in-means edit breaks the programs when it pushes toward BFS, not toward DFS. In iteration 6, a rank-4 interchange at block 22 had produced 50 BFS attempts and 0 valid programs; a dosed edit to the coordinate of the class mean at block 17 keeps them.

### 7.8.5 A circuit for the fork margin

*Path patching* replaces a component's contribution along one path with its value under a contrasting input and measures the effect on the output [134, 135]; *attribution patching* (AtP) approximates the same effect for every node with one gradient pass [136]. The experiment screened 1,224 nodes (272 attention heads and 34 MLPs at four position classes: the fork position, the shared opening, the task specification and the condition sentence) by AtP on 15 contrasting pairs, patched the top 60 exactly by *noising*, which writes a node's value from the run of a pair that leans toward BFS into the run that leans toward DFS (AtP against exact noising: Pearson 0.65, Spearman 0.73; the reverse, denoising, has the opposite sign for every node), and edges measured by path patching among the top 15. Half of the exact noising effect enters at the fork position (53%) and a third at the condition sentence (36%). The top ten nodes are MLPs at the condition sentence (layers 0, 2, 6 and 14) and a stack at the fork position (MLPs at layers 17, 21, 22, 25 and 26, and head 5 of layer 22; Table 366). Kept edges, those whose effect under path patching is at least 5% of the total effect, form a chain at the fork position (MLP 17 to MLP 19, MLP 21 to MLP 22, MLP 25 to MLP 26, and head 5 of layer 22 to MLP 25), with direct paths to the margin from head 2 of layer 33 and MLPs 22, 25 and 26.

Each top node was validated in the real model against 50 random components of its position class matched on write norm (Table 367). Seven of ten nodes pass when ablated to the opposite class's mean, and eight pass when steered; the joint sets of the top five and the top ten beat all 50 matched random sets. In generation, steering the top five toward BFS doubles correct BFS programs (16 of 30 against 8 for the twin, p 0.019) at pass 0.83, while a matched random five does nothing (Table 368). Ablating the same nodes to the natural BFS mean does not move generation, because the natural classes differ by only about 2 nats at the fork. The reading is a circuit hypothesis for this one fork: MLPs at the condition sentence carry the prompt's lexical cue, and the stack at the fork position turns it into the token at index 32. An *attribution graph*, the graph of direct linear effects between transcoder features from the prompt to the fork margin, built on the Gemma Scope 2 transcoders [113], would test the circuit on features; it was attempted three times and dropped: the container lacked a C compiler for Triton, and with one installed, attribution exceeded the 16 GB GPU at batch 64 and again at batch 16 (16.4 GB). No correct program among 2,325 was outside the catalogue (rule-of-three bound 0.0013).

The deviation log of the Gemma experiment records five departures that bear on these results. One unit test missed its tolerance: the cache path for a single position differs from a full recompute by up to 0.27 nats on the fork margin, an effect of bf16 kernels and batch shapes, so every DAS effect is measured against the base's own margin on the same path and in the same batch shape. The DAS optimiser ran at a learning rate of 2e-2 instead of the planned 2e-3, because a toy check showed that 400 steps at 2e-3 leave the subspace near random. A bisection bug left the six difference-in-means cells toward DFS unmatched, so they are reported as one strong reference edit (45 of 50 correct DFS). The mediation test of the fork subspace on random pushes was not run (dropped in order), so the DAS claim covers forced prompt transfer only. And the transcoder graph was dropped after the three attempts described above.

## 7.9 Comparisons across this iteration's experiments

**Temperature through the fork, in two families.** The temperature claim was tested on four mixed units in two models. The fork logits predicted the temperature response within the committed error on two of them (the grid in Gemma, mean absolute error 0.026, and minimum spanning tree weight in Qwen3-8B, 0.083, where the observed drop was twice the predicted one), just outside it on trapped rain water (0.105), and not in direction on valid anagram, where the minority share did not fall at low temperature. Table 369 sets them side by side. On every unit the algorithm given the fork class was nearly certain (0.05 to 0.19 bits) and top-k 10 changed nothing. Temperature above 1 raised the minority only where the fork logits said it would: in Gemma the BFS share rose from 0.34 at T 1.0 to 0.46 at T 1.3 against a predicted rise from 0.323 to 0.450, while on the three Qwen3-8B units the predicted rise was at most 0.013 and the observed change lay between -0.02 and +0.06. On the collapsed tasks the fork margins of 4.85 to 17.04 nats explain why no temperature in iterations 1 to 4 changed the algorithm. Temperature is a dial on the fork's existing odds; it cannot create an alternative that the fork does not already weigh.

**Where the choice is decided.** Three different answers came out of three tasks in one model. On connected components the decision falls at generated tokens 10 and 11, where the routine is named; forcing the name decides the algorithm in every slot. On kth smallest a ban decides it before the first generated token. On shortest path no single token decides it within 60 tokens, and the opening's likelihood predicts the outcome better the longer the opening measured. The three mixed units of the temperature experiment and Gemma's grid task each have a fork of a single token right after a shared opening of 18 to 61 tokens. The fork is thus a common place for the decision to surface, not a universal one, and where it exists its margin predicts the effect of random pushes (connected components) and of temperature (within the committed error on two of the four mixed units).

**What moves the algorithm, and at what cost.** Table 370 collects the edits of this iteration that move the algorithm in generation, with their correct target programs and pass rates. In Qwen3-8B a rank-1 or rank-2 DAS edit matches the full state exchange at the same site, plan noise at the absolute unit moves half of connected components programs at no pass cost, and the axis from the default to the second choice moves connected components only at a dose beyond the committed range. In Gemma the DAS edit at the fork beats the explicit instruction in correct BFS programs, and steering five validated circuit nodes doubles them. In Gemma the difference-in-means edit toward BFS moves the algorithm and breaks the programs (toward the default DFS a strong edit kept them), and in Qwen3-8B a rank-1 difference-in-means interchange at the DAS site transfers nothing (0 of 30 on both core tasks). In this iteration the edits fitted or validated on the model's own contrasts kept the programs; the difference-in-means edit toward the minority algorithm did not.

**Established.** In Qwen3-8B a rank-1 or rank-2 subspace of the task specification states at blocks 12 to 23 is a steering handle on the algorithm that matches the full state exchange, and on two tasks it routes more cleanly than the full state. The handle is not a certified variable, because permuted labels and an untrained network admit it. In Gemma the analogous subspace at the fork passes all three controls and acts as a dose dial that keeps the programs. Where a fork of a single token exists, temperature acts on the algorithm through the fork logits divided by T, as predicted before sampling on one Qwen3-8B unit and on Gemma; on the collapsed tasks the fork margins put the alternative out of temperature's reach. On connected components the decision falls at the token that names the routine, and the fork margin under a random push predicts the effect of the push (Spearman 0.80), through the probability that stays on the default fork tokens rather than through which algorithm each other token leads to (a placebo that shuffles the token map reaches 0.80 in 18% of permutations). The weak plan noise of iteration 5 came from its dose unit; the absolute unit's peaky profile on a few task tokens carries the effect. Evolutionary search with an evaluator reaches known techniques outside the catalogue on kth smallest at a rate no arm that draws single samples approaches (78 distinct programs against at most 2).

**Ruled out.** The axis from the default to the second choice as the channel of random pushes (disconfirmed and not mediating). Discreteness of the effect of the fitted edit. The seeds as the cause of the null of iteration 5. Temperature above 1 as a source of a new idea: on every unit it only reweighted the algorithms the fork already weighs. Search at ten times the best text knob's level a rate on two tasks.

**Dead ends.** The committed contrastive DAS objective, which diverged and broke programs, was replaced by the likelihood objective. The transcoder attribution graph in Gemma was dropped after three attempts on a 16 GB GPU. The judge gate for novelty failed for every judge family in the search experiment, so its classes rest on manual and rule-based reads. A top five push inside the forced prompt manifold of the grid task produced no algorithm outside the five in 300 programs, which closes the push route for that question at the doses tried.

## 7.11 What the next iteration takes from this one

The next iteration takes four leads. First, the DAS handle in Qwen3-8B needs the control it failed: a fit whose versions with permuted labels and with an untrained network do not transfer, which may require fitting at the fork in generation, where Gemma's controls passed, rather than at the task specification states. Second, shortest path decides late, so the fork claim needs a measure that follows the decision to where it happens (the opening LLR improved from 48 to 160 tokens). Third, the temperature claim held on two of four mixed units; the misses on trapped rain water, which has a second opening with its own split, and valid anagram, where a second decision (fixed array against hash map) follows a few tokens after the fork, call for a prediction that composes more than one fork. Fourth, evolutionary search found known techniques outside the catalogue on kth smallest at a rate no knob applied to single samples approaches, so a search on a task whose catalogue already covers the known techniques, where a correct program outside it would be new, is the remaining route to a novel algorithm.

# What we have learned so far

After seven iterations the run has a firm picture of the collapse, a mechanism for why temperature does not undo it, a measured place where the choice surfaces in generation, internal handles that move the algorithm while keeping the programs, and no correct novel algorithm. Qwen3-8B [5] writes BFS and Dijkstra almost without exception on the two path search tasks and one algorithm on each of 13 further coding tasks (modal share 1.00 on 12, 0.98 on one). The collapse is not universal: three of 15 new tasks are already mixed in the instruct twin (trapped rain water, minimum spanning tree weight and valid anagram, whose minority shares in the twin's baseline samples range from 0.13 to 0.36), and on two of them the instruct model is more diverse than its base model. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [22] attempts more algorithms but its correct grid programs are BFS 20 of 20; gemma-3-4b-it [76] writes DFS in about 70% and BFS in about 30% of programs for one grid prompt; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [124] shares most of Qwen3-8B's defaults.

The algorithm surfaces at a fork where it can be found. On the mixed units of Qwen3-8B and on Gemma's grid task, programs share an opening of 18 to 61 tokens and the algorithm is settled by the next token: ` Kr` or ` Prim` on minimum spanning tree weight, ` visited` or a blank line in Gemma; the entropy of the algorithm given the fork token's class is 0.05 to 0.19 bits. On connected components the fork is the token that names the routine (` def dfs` against ` def find`), and forcing it decides the algorithm in every slot. On kth smallest a ban decides before the first generated token, and on shortest path no single token decides within 60 tokens. The margin at the decision predicts what moves the algorithm. Under 40 random pushes, the fork margin on connected components ranks which pushes change the algorithm (Spearman 0.80), although a placebo that shuffles which fork tokens lead to which algorithm reaches the same value in 18% of permutations, so the ranking rests on how much probability stays on the default fork tokens. On kth smallest, where no fork exists, the log likelihood ratio of a 20-token opening predicted the effect of 24 fresh pushes in a test committed before generation (Spearman 0.60).

Temperature acts on the algorithm only through the fork. Dividing the fork logits by T predicted the minority share at each temperature before sampling within the committed error on Gemma's grid task (mean absolute error 0.026) and on minimum spanning tree weight (0.083, with the observed drop twice the predicted one), just outside it on trapped rain water (0.105), and not in direction on valid anagram, where a second decision follows the fork. Lowering T from 1.0 to 0.3 collapses the output onto the default on minimum spanning tree weight and in Gemma (17:0 and 16:0 discordant slots), but not on trapped rain water (7:3) or valid anagram (2:5). Temperature above 1 raises the minority only as far as the fork logits allow: in Gemma from 0.34 to 0.46 at T 1.3, as predicted, and on the Qwen3-8B units by at most 0.06, where the predicted change is near zero. Top-k 10 gives the same program as top-p 1 because every fork token lies in the top 10. On the collapsed tasks the fork margins are 4.85 to 17.04 nats, so no temperature in range reaches the alternative: this is why the sweeps of iterations 1 to 4 under a shared seed changed the algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds on three tasks with thinking off and on the shortest path task with thinking on, while phrasings multiplied. The answer to question 1a-c of the request is that a model has few ideas at tight temperature and the same few at loose temperature, in proportions its fork logits fix. On other problems, temperature above 1 has been reported to raise algorithmic diversity at a correctness cost [72]; the fork margin says where that can happen.

A random displacement of the task specification states at early to middle blocks changes the algorithm in Qwen3-8B, and its size has to be counted in the right unit. At the absolute unit of iteration 4, which scales the noise of each cell to the displacement a ban causes there, bf16 escapes on 26 of 40 directions on connected components and 6 of 40 on shortest path, close to the 29 and 8 of the 8-bit engine on which the effect was found, with the same directions escaping. Iteration 5's weak plan noise came from its relative unit, which scales the noise to a fixed fraction of the residual norm, not from its seeds (unit effect +0.45 [0.35, 0.55], seed effect +0.03, on connected components; replicated on fresh slots and on kth smallest): the absolute unit concentrates 81% of its energy on a few task tokens, and the same energy at shuffled positions moves almost nothing. An axis from the default to the second choice, the second choice being the algorithm a model ranks second, is not the channel these pushes use (Spearman 0.17 and 0.01; clamping it removes nothing), although pushing along it at four times the distance between the forced prompt centroids, beyond the committed doses, moves all 30 connected components slots off the default (29 to DFS, 1 to BFS) with every program passing. Priced as a knob at the absolute unit, plan noise beats an intent sentence written by the base model on kth smallest and the grid and loses on connected components, shortest path and two sum; enumerate and pick and generate then select [43] reach more raw diversity at large pass costs.

Where the noise must enter is not settled. In bf16 at the relative unit, noise at the task specification positions moves the algorithm while the read position and the condition span barely do. The preregistered site rule was nonetheless withdrawn, for lack of common support and for breakage at alpha 8. A post hoc model at alpha 4 or less puts the read position below the task specification site on both tasks but not the condition span, so the site of the choice remains open; on connected components noise acts most at blocks 0 to 11 while the exchange transfers at blocks 12 to 23. Noise in generated tokens 1 to 32 also redirects the choice, and against a temperature matched on per-token KL it was not established (12:6 and 7:3 discordant flips). Under bf16 these internal results hold: the route of a ban (iterations 2 and 3), the band patching on kth smallest and connected components, the Stage A exchange, the escape fractions and per-sample rates of plan noise of iteration 4 at their absolute unit, the transplant results of iteration 5 and the transplant at the read position that breaks the output without moving the algorithm. Every experiment of iteration 7 ran in bf16. The 8-bit site odds ratio (5.72), the contrast of plan noise under the same seed (17.25 of 20 seeds) and the forced prompt subspace tests are 8-bit results that were not rerun.

Internal handles now exist in two families, each with its own model, site and controls (Table 279 and Section 7.9). In Qwen3-8B, exchanging the task specification states of a ban or a forced instruction into a neutral twin transfers the algorithm (shortest path 21 of 30 correct programs, kth smallest 16 of 30; forced instructions 24 to 30 of 30), and a DAS subspace of rank 1 or 2 at blocks 12 to 23 matches that exchange in generation while random subspaces of the same rank do nothing. That subspace is a steering handle and not a certified variable: permuted labels transfer 0.47 to 0.70 of its effect, an untrained network admits a fit 0.92 as good [132], and the reverse interchange does not restore the default [122]. The effect of scaling it is a ramp, not a step. In Gemma, DAS at the fork passes the controls with random subspaces, permuted labels and an untrained network, but the subspace is not unique across seeds and the committed rule does not license calling it one dimensional; as a dose dial it raises correct BFS programs from 11 to 42 of 50, above the 35 of an explicit BFS instruction, while a difference-in-means edit toward BFS at matched teacher-forced effect destroys the programs. A path-patching circuit for Gemma's fork margin, validated against matched random components in the real model, runs from MLPs at the condition sentence to a stack of MLPs and one head at the fork position; steering its top five nodes doubles correct BFS programs. A natural language autoencoder on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct names the algorithm at the token where the prompt names it and not later, and an outside reader of the visible text predicts the algorithm better, also with one unit per sample (0:25). The read position is inert as a carrier in Qwen3-8B and in the NLA's reading.

A single prompt ban, where the model obeys it, removes the default and the output collapses on one replacement: Bellman-Ford/SPFA on the shortest path task, DFS on the grid task, and quickselect and size k heap, brute force, index marking and BFS on the bench tasks where Qwen3-8B obeys. Shown a correct program of another algorithm and told not to use it, the model goes home to its default. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct mostly ignores bans. How often a ban is obeyed depends on its wording more than on anything else measured, and the fourth template, which states only that the algorithm is not allowed here, is the weakest in every artifact and model tested. Bans of five names fail by reimplementation in both families tested, and a push of the grid task's states toward the survivors of a top five ban, inside the forced prompt manifold, produced BFS in all 300 programs. In the fitted coordinates of shortest path, bans sit outside a paraphrase null, displaced toward the second choice, while random seeds and long novelty instructions sit inside it and leave the algorithm where it was; the geometry does not predict where a ban lands.

Where a ban acts depends on the task. On the path tasks it is carried mostly by the prompt states (likelihood readout 0.85; behaviour 0.98 on the shortest path task, mixed on the grid task); on the bench, pooled over five gated tasks, the direct route carries 0.744 [0.38, 1.11] of the behavioural effect and the prompt states 0.611 [0.06, 1.17], with overlapping intervals, and two sum, classed as direct, also carries 0.43 of its ban in the task specification states. The ban is enforced at the opening of the program body, to a single token on kth smallest, the same place where forks surface. The read position predicts how strongly a wording will be obeyed (-0.41 across 110 wordings) but carries none of the effect when exchanged or spliced, and push movability as a forecast of which bans a model obeys is closed. What decides the replacement has measured leads and no confirmed rule. The base model's second choice names the push landing in 17 of 21 recorded events and beats the instruct twin's own ranking of algorithm openings 8:1 where the two disagree (p 0.020, retrospective), but where the twin already writes an alternative that alternative names the landing as often (6 of 7), and on the 8 held-out events where it writes none the base model's second choice named 5 (p 0.053). The base model's variety does not say whether a task can be moved (Spearman 0.15 over 13 new units, measured at the relative unit; at the absolute unit kth smallest and connected components are movable and shortest path, two sum and the grid are not), and writing its task specification states into the instruct prefill reopened its second choice on 1 of 5 Qwen3-8B tasks and 2 of 7 Gemma tasks.

No instruction, knob, push, transplant, feature clamp, verbal edit or fitted edit produced a correct novel algorithm, and neither did evolutionary search. Iterations 1 to 3 produced 116 correct programs outside the catalogue and iteration 5 another 130, and none was new; iteration 4 found none among 14,206 correct programs, and the second blind adjudication of iteration 6, with controls of known class, overturned the only novel call on a full read. In iteration 7 the run tried the documented route to new programs [81, 82], an evolutionary search over a MAP-Elites archive [133] with an executable evaluator and a novelty critic, on three tasks. On kth smallest it found 78 distinct correct programs that implement known techniques outside the catalogue (order statistics on a Fenwick tree, binary search on the value range, bucket select, partial selection sort, a treap with order statistics), against 0 for enumerate and pick, 0 for the same prompt without evolution and 2 for the instruction alone. Counting every arm, including a larger mutator, 103 distinct correct programs implement these techniques, and none is novel. On shortest path and trapped rain water the search found only catalogue variants. The judge gate for novelty failed for every judge family tried, so these classes rest on manual and rule-based reads.

What remains open follows from this. First, whether Qwen3-8B's handle can be certified as a variable: a DAS fit at the fork in generation, where Gemma's controls passed, rather than at the task specification states. Second, where shortest path decides, since its opening likelihood predicts pushes better the later it is measured. Third, a temperature prediction that composes more than one fork, for the two mixed units where one fork did not suffice. Fourth, the transcoder attribution graph at Gemma's fork, which failed on a 16 GB GPU. Fifth, evolutionary search on a task whose catalogue already covers the known techniques, so that a correct program outside it would be new, the remaining route to a novel algorithm. Of the items of the request, these have been run. Geometry plots in activation coordinates exist at a position that depends on the label (iteration 2), at the plan site (iteration 4), for the top five prohibition and the fork (iteration 6) and in the fitted DAS coordinates (iteration 7). The top five prohibition was applied by prompt, token veto, plan push and push inside the manifold. Natural BFS against DFS internals were read within a ban in Qwen3-8B and within one prompt in Gemma, where a circuit for the fork was validated. Thought anchors and forks, the logit and tuned lenses, the test under the same seed with thinking on and off and with top-k 10 (now explained by fork margins), natural language autoencoders on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, sparse autoencoders (Qwen-Scope on Qwen3-8B, Gemma Scope 2 on Gemma), DAS with the full set of published controls and evolutionary search with an evaluator were all run.

# Where a Prompt Ban Sends a Code Model, and What Else Moves Its Algorithm Choice

This report is the internal record of a study of algorithmic diversity in an open-weight instruction-tuned model. The question that started the run is how "creativity" shows up inside a language model and whether it can be influenced: if a model is asked to implement a path search algorithm, does it always write the same one, and which knobs (sampling temperature, random context seeds, instructions, prohibitions, or edits to the activations) change the algorithm rather than only its wording. The behavioural puzzle comes from the inspiration repository by Drejc Pesjak that the request names, in which a closed model wrote Dijkstra's algorithm for a weighted shortest path task in 125 of 125 programs across five prompting strategies, and cumulative bans moved it to SPFA and Bellman-Ford rather than to a spread of alternatives. The same collapse appears in controlled measurements across 15 model configurations, where a no cue prompt gives Dijkstra 94.1% of the time [1], and in broader benchmarks of algorithmic diversity among correct programs [2, 3].

The hypothesis entering the run is mechanistic. When an instruction-tuned model is told not to use its default solution, the prohibition is expected to do two things: suppress the banned algorithm and promote the alternative the model associates with it, so the output collapses again on one predictable substitute instead of spreading over the repertoire. This mirrors the suppression plus promotion account of negation on factual questions [4]. Competing accounts say the substitute is chosen by baseline typicality, by proximity on an activation space solution manifold, by a few early forking tokens during generation, by a single list versus implement commitment direction, or that the whole collapse was installed by post-training. The report records, iteration by iteration, which of these the evidence supported and which it did not. All work so far uses Qwen3-8B [5] with thinking mode off unless stated, on the request's two path search tasks. *(Note added in iteration 2: iteration 2 adds Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [22] and a bench of 13 further coding tasks; Sections 2.7 and 2.8.)* *(Note added in iteration 6: iteration 6 adds Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, read with natural language autoencoders, and gemma-3-4b-it, read with Gemma Scope 2 sparse autoencoders; Sections 6.5 and 6.6.)* The hypothesis reached its tested form after seven rounds of drafting and review before any experiment ran; the reviewer's overall score across the rounds was 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7 and 7, and the final round scored soundness 3, presentation 3, contribution 3 and fidelity 4.

# Iteration 1: a wide screen of six accounts on the two path search tasks

## 1.1 Why this iteration ran what it ran

The first iteration was planned as a screen rather than a test. The hypothesis carried four alternates that disagree with it about what decides the algorithm written after a ban, and none of them had been measured. The strategy therefore ran every account cheaply and in parallel on the same events, with one shared protocol, one per-sample output schema and a selection rule fixed before any artifact ran, and it left inference to a later confirmation on reserved tasks. The selection rule had two columns. The PREDICT column scores each account's forecast of the distribution after a ban, committed by sha256 hash before sampling, by its log score on the realised compliant samples; an account survives if its mean log score beats the next best account by at least 0.10 nats on at least 3 events where the accounts' top-1 nominations disagree. The BUY column scores each knob by the correctness conditioned Hill number it reaches while keeping at least 80% of the baseline pass rate; a knob survives if it beats the next best knob by at least 0.5 effective algorithms. *(Correction, iteration 2: as written in the strategy, the PREDICT rule scores only informative events, those with the banned mode present at 10% or more of the latent baseline, compliance of at least 50% and at least two survivors, and the BUY rule names a winner only if it leads on the pooled tasks and in direction on each task. This paragraph omitted both conditions, and Section 1.11 applied the rules without them. Sections 2.3.6 and 2.3.7 recompute both.)* A third check, the locus diagnostic, asks where the algorithm decision is made: it would move every geometric analysis from the read position (the last prompt token, Section 1.2) to generated-token states if a decoder at a forking token beat the read position decoder by 20 points over a shuffled label control. The strategy also stated in advance that nothing in this iteration would be inferential.

Seven artifacts ran: one dataset and six experiments, each owning one account (Table 1). We call each experiment by the account it screens: the association, geometry, forking token, decommitment and instruction tuning experiments, and the decoding experiment, which covers sampling temperature, random seeds and creativity instructions. The strategy asked the dataset artifact to build a reserved bench of 12 further tasks with hidden tests, labellers and forecasts frozen before any ban, so that the account that survived the screen could be confirmed out of sample in the next iteration.

## 1.2 Shared setup and the conventions used in this report

**Tasks.** Both tasks come from the request. The grid task asks for `solve(grid, start, goal)` returning any valid 4-neighbour path on a grid of free and blocked cells, or an empty list when the goal is unreachable. Its catalogue has six algorithms, that is, breadth-first search (BFS), depth-first search (DFS), bidirectional BFS, iterative-deepening DFS (IDDFS), A* or greedy best-first search with a Manhattan heuristic (A* in tables), and unit weight Dijkstra. The shortest path task asks for the shortest distance from s to t in a directed graph with nonnegative integer weights and cycles, or -1. Its catalogue has five algorithms: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford or SPFA (counted as one algorithm), bidirectional Dijkstra, Floyd-Warshall and Dial's bucket queue. Every experiment wrote its own hidden tests (between 39 and 48 cases per task) with a time limit of ten times the slowest reference implementation and a 1 s minimum, and every catalogue reference had to pass before any model sample was scored.

**Model and decoding.** Qwen3-8B in bf16 with the chat template and thinking off, sampled at temperature 1.0 with top-p 1.0 and no top-k unless a table says otherwise. Engines differed between artifacts because the containers had no C compiler: vLLM 0.11.0 [6] in eager mode in five experiments (association [ARTIFACT:art__skdlFp_o3e9], forking token [ARTIFACT:art_1yV2vQ0EH4OY], decommitment [ARTIFACT:art_U5UKkFrOgSsE], instruction tuning [ARTIFACT:art_HF8nK8B_Lqyy] and decoding [ARTIFACT:art_UoCVh2Qe5RZ0]), and HF transformers `generate` in the geometry experiment [ARTIFACT:art_D6Z0Snf09sFL] and in the hooked steering arms. GPUs were an RTX 5090 (association and decoding experiments), an NVIDIA GPU with 23 GB of memory (geometry and instruction tuning experiments) or an RTX A4500 (forking token and decommitment experiments).

**Prompts.** Every prompt is a condition segment, then a fixed task specification of at least 50 tokens, then the assistant header. The read position is the last prompt token, so no token specific to a condition sits at or near it. The conditions shared by all experiments are the baseline (no condition segment or a neutral one), a ban (`Do not use X.`), the mention twin and the listing control. The mention twin (`X is one well-known approach to this task; implement any correct algorithm.`) puts the same name at the same place without forbidding it, because naming a forbidden item can itself prime it [7]. We call the condition that names every catalogue algorithm the listing control. Each condition segment has 10 paraphrases, and N=100 means 10 paraphrases with 10 samples each. Each experiment wrote its own paraphrases.

**Labels and correctness.** Each program is labelled with one catalogue algorithm or "other" by a runtime signature tracer (the program runs on crafted inputs with instrumented heaps, queues, stacks and grid reads) and by AST rules; disagreements go to a blind LLM judge on OpenRouter. Recursion versus iteration never counts as a separate algorithm. A program is correct when it passes the hidden tests within the limit. Intervals on proportions are Wilson score intervals [8] unless stated.

**Quantities.** We use the following names throughout. The *banned mode share* is the fraction of all coded samples labelled as the banned algorithm. A *compliant sample* is a correct program not labelled as a banned algorithm. The *realised mode* of a ban is the most common label among compliant samples if it leads the next most common label by at least 15 points; otherwise we call the event one with no clear mode. The *correctness conditioned Hill number* (Hill_cc) is the exponential of the Shannon entropy of the label distribution over correct programs, the effective number of algorithms [9]; a value of 1 means one algorithm and 2 means two equally common ones. The *log score* of a predictor on a ban event is the mean natural logarithm of the probability it assigned to the labels of the realised compliant samples, after mixing in 5% uniform mass over the surviving algorithms and a 2% floor for "other". It is a strictly proper scoring rule [10]; higher is better, and a uniform predictor over four survivors scores -1.406. Artifacts reported a quantity they called compliance in two different ways (one minus the banned mode share, or the fraction of compliant samples), so this report states the banned mode share and the number of compliant samples instead, recomputed from each artifact's per-sample rows.

**Labeller validation.** Each experiment validated its own labeller against a gold set adjudicated by two or three LLM judges, with Cohen's kappa [11] between the runtime and AST labels as the main agreement statistic. Table 2 collects the results. Four labellers passed their gates and two did not. Both failures were driven by runtime versus AST disagreement on small gold sets. The combined label (runtime, AST and judge) still agreed with the adjudicated label on 97% of gold programs in the association experiment, and on 93% (grid) and 70% (shortest path) in the decoding experiment, 92% on its correct gold programs.

## 1.5 Association experiment: does the alternative the model names predict where a ban lands?

**Why.** This experiment screened the main hypothesis against its behavioural rival. The main hypothesis predicts the algorithm written after a ban from the model's association between algorithms; the typicality ladder predicts it from baseline frequencies restricted to the survivors. Both predictors were elicited and frozen before any ban prompt was generated, and every prediction file was chained by sha256 hash before the samples it predicts [ARTIFACT:art__skdlFp_o3e9]. The commitment audit found the chain intact and every event committed in advance (commit at 15:18:30 UTC, first ban generation at 15:20:05 UTC).

**Design.** The latent baseline was N=300 per task at temperature 1.0, plus 200 samples at temperature 1.3 and 50 without the neutral condition segment. The association map was elicited on separate queries with thinking off: for each of the 11 catalogue algorithms X, the model returned 20 sampled complete rankings of the other algorithms by the criterion `how standard an alternative to X for this task`, aggregated by Borda count (each ranking gives an alternative points according to its rank) with one extra point per algorithm. We call the normalised result the *association map* A(X); its winner is the association nomination. The *clarity* of X is the share of the 20 rankings whose alternative ranked first is the Borda winner, and Kendall's W [21] measures agreement across the 20 rankings. The model also gave 20 free-form answers to the question `what is the standard alternative to X?`, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [22] repeated the whole elicitation as an external map. The ban arms were all 11 single bans at N=100, the mention twin of each at N=50, the listing control at N=100 and a greedy succession that bans the realised mode of each step cumulatively, in the manner of denial prompting [23]. Generation used vLLM on one RTX 5090 (about 6 GPU minutes); OpenRouter spend was USD 0.27 for the judge, gold set adjudication and the external elicitation.

Yet 19 of its 20 free-form answers named DFS. For Dijkstra, all 20 rankings put Bellman-Ford/SPFA first (clarity 1.0). The map from Llama agreed with the Borda winner of Qwen for 5 of 6 grid algorithms and 4 of 5 shortest path algorithms, and its map for BFS tied DFS and IDDFS on top.

The family test, which the hypothesis treats as its direct test of substitution against subtraction, was degenerate here. It fits a substitution family (a point mass on the association winner with a uniform leak) and a subtraction family (the baseline restricted to the survivors) on half of an event's compliant samples and scores both on the other half. Because the baseline gave zero mass to every survivor, the subtraction family was uniform: the grid event was a tie at -1.63 and the shortest path event went to substitution (-0.058 against -1.406). Mentioning an absent algorithm moved 100 points of mass to DFS and to Bellman-Ford/SPFA, 86 points to Floyd-Warshall, 72 to IDDFS and 56 to A*, and 10 to bidirectional BFS; it moved nothing for unit weight Dijkstra on grids, Dial and bidirectional Dijkstra. ## 1.6 Geometry experiment: the read position manifold, the ban shift, and activation removal

**Why.** The hypothesis places the algorithm decision at the read position and predicts that the ban shift there, the change in the read position state that the ban causes, has a larger component toward the associated alternative than away from the banned algorithm. This experiment built the solution manifold at the read position, tested whether the read position encodes the algorithm at all, nominated the geodesically nearest survivor as a third predictor (the geodesic kernel, a forecast that weights each survivor by the exponential of minus its geodesic distance from the banned algorithm's centroid, scaled by the median distance between centroids), decomposed the ban shift, and tried to remove the modal algorithm with an activation edit instead of a prompt [ARTIFACT:art_D6Z0Snf09sFL]. It ran HF `generate` on one NVIDIA GPU with 23 GB of memory, since vLLM could not start, for about 2.2 GPU hours; OpenRouter spend was about USD 0.09.

**Design.** Forced implementation prompts (`Implement X for this task`) with 30 paraphrases per catalogue algorithm, plus a name masked set that describes X without naming it, gave a point cloud of residual stream activations at the read position for each algorithm for layers 8 to 28 of 36. A logistic linear probe from the read position state to the algorithm label was trained with one paraphrase held out at a time and compared with 20 shuffled label refits, the control-task logic of probe selectivity [24]. Two gate statistics were computed per layer: transfer accuracy from named to name masked prompts, and the Jensen-Shannon divergence, that is, a symmetric and bounded divergence, between the probe's decoded distribution on the baseline prompts and the realised label distribution of the baseline. The manifold used principal component analysis down to 95% of the variance, a k-nearest-neighbour graph with k=10, geodesic distances along the graph as in Isomap [25], two dimensional multidimensional scaling and the TwoNN intrinsic-dimension estimator [26], following the manifold-steering instrument [27].

**Manipulation check.** The model can write most catalogue algorithms when told to, but not all of them correctly (Table 11). Forced IDDFS was implemented as IDDFS every time on the grid task and never passed the tests; forced bidirectional Dijkstra and forced Dial were implemented as asked in only 33% and 37% of samples. These two shortest path algorithms were flagged, and their centroids rest on fewer valid points.

## 1.7 Forking token experiment: is the algorithm decided during generation?

**Why.** If the read position does not fix the algorithm, the decision may be made at a few high entropy tokens during generation, as forking token analyses find for other outcomes [30, 31]. The knob this account implies is a sampler that raises temperature only around those tokens, in the spirit of adaptive temperature sampling for code [32]. This experiment screened that account on its own pool of about 10,000 labelled generations [ARTIFACT:art_1yV2vQ0EH4OY], with vLLM 0.11.0 in eager mode, its own tests (40 per task, 17 reference solutions) and a judge used only on 6 disputed programs (USD 0.024).

**Design.** A resampling screen took 10 base paths per task for the baseline and for the modal ban and drew 8 continuations at every fourth generated token over the first 92 tokens. Baseline paths were screened only at tokens 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64, a fallback declared in advance because the baseline was already fixed at the read position. Change points in the series of continuation outcome distributions were detected against a permutation threshold (a PELT detector [33] run alongside found none on any path), localised to single tokens, and confirmed with 30 continuations at each candidate and at two control positions without a change point. A prompt swap cut a baseline path just before or just after its commitment token (the first token of evidence that identifies the algorithm, such as the `deque` import) and continued it under the ban prompt. The knob arm compared global temperature 0.3-1.3 with temperature 1.3 applied only in a window around detected forking tokens, which we call the forking window knob, against a random window of the same size and an anchored window at the start of the code block. A planted change sensitivity test found that the detector caught a total variation change of 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5 in 82.5%, 95% and 99% of trials, with a 6% false-positive rate at no change.
