## 3.7 Locus experiment: a shared prohibition direction, a locus at generated tokens 1 to 8, the ban-attending heads, and SAE transfer (Qwen3-8B)

**Why.** Four questions about where a prohibition lives inside the model were open after iteration 2. Is there a task-general direction that carries the instruction to abandon the default, and does writing it into a neutral prompt work like a named ban (the causal test of the read position correlation, moved to the positions where the route test located the effect)? Is the within-ban choice of algorithm decodable at generated tokens 1 to 8 beyond the written text? Do the three heads that attend to the banned name matter? Do the Qwen-Scope base model SAEs [50] transfer to the instruct model under a criterion that does not penalise its lower clean cross-entropy? This experiment [ARTIFACT:art_pVlCZ272hDV7] ran all four beside their controls under common random numbers, on the two path tasks and four bench tasks (kth smallest, substring search, find duplicate, two sum).

**Design.** The machine had a 16 GB RTX 2000 Ada, too small for bf16 weights, so every decoder linear layer was quantised at load time to 8-bit floating point with per-channel weight and per-token activation scales (embeddings, norms and the output head stayed bf16). A validation reproduced the iteration-2 shortest path arms (ban 2 of 20 Dijkstra, twin 20 of 20). The sampler coupled every arm exactly (identical uniforms in different rows give identical tokens at 20 rows per batch), and teacher forcing at batch 1 was bit exact. The shared prohibition direction v is the leave-one-task-out mean, over the 13 other tasks and all five templates, of the ban minus twin displacement at the task specification positions in blocks 12 to 23. The ADD arm wrote v into the neutral twin's prefill with the displacement targeted to alpha times the ban's own per-layer norm (alpha in {1, 2}, plus 0.5 on some tasks); the SUBTRACT arm projected v out of the ban prompt's prefill. Controls were three random directions with the same blocks, positions and norms, the twin, and the named ban (N = 100). In all, 5,500 samples followed the frozen design and 1,800 were exploratory. Decision rules were hash committed before sampling.

**The direction exists, but adding it is no better than a random push.** The leave-one-task-out v was reliable (split half cosine 0.95 to 0.99 across blocks 12 to 23). It was aligned with every held-out task's mean ban displacement (cosine 0.29 to 0.86 at block 18, against a 95th percentile of 0.03 for random directions), yet it carried only 2% to 6% of each position's own ban displacement. The preregistered test failed on every gated task (Table 110): ADD beat every random control on 0 of 5 gated tasks, and its avoidance was not above the maximum of the three random directions on 5 of 6 tasks. Where ADD moved behaviour it did not reproduce the ban. On kth smallest it landed on a size-k heap while the ban landed on quickselect (Jensen-Shannon divergence 0.52 against a permutation 95th percentile of 0.03; the committed forecast missed); on the shortest path task ADD and the ban both landed on Bellman-Ford/SPFA, but so did the random directions that moved it. The dose response was not monotone (shortest path avoidance 0.02, 0.35 and 0.12 at alpha 0.5, 1 and 2 over all slots), and the random edits grew more than v downstream (block 35: about 283 against 219 on the shortest path task), so a weak control does not explain the result. SUBTRACT never restored the default: pooled over the gated tasks the banned share changed by -0.026 [-0.07, 0.03] against a required +0.3, and on substring search, find duplicate and two sum removing v made the ban slightly stronger. On the path tasks neither plain nor affine subtraction exceeded a random edit of the same norm by the required 0.15, and that random edit was destructive (pass rate 0.00).

## 3.8 Reach experiment: how far bans and token vetoes push, and what the long-form novelty instruction produces (Qwen3-8B)

**Why.** The update's third claim was that prompts move the model exactly one rung. This experiment [ARTIFACT:art_ccAbfJVcv0LO] asked three things. First, do cumulative token vetoes, an operation the model cannot ignore, reach algorithms that prompt bans cannot? We call this the *token walk*: veto the default's distinctive n-gram, then the next landing's, and so on, up to five algorithms. Second, does a ban that leaves exactly one survivor get that survivor written whenever the model can write it on request? We call the share of programs implementing the survivor *will*, and the share of forced programs labelled as the requested algorithm and correct *can*. Third, does the request's own long-form novelty instruction produce a correct novel algorithm? Rungs are numbered by the walk: rung 1 is the default, rung 2 is the walk's first landing (or, where the walk stalled, a flagged fallback committed in advance), and every other catalogue algorithm is at rung 3 or more. Six tasks ran: the two path tasks in bf16, and kth smallest, substring search, find duplicate and connected components on the official 8-bit checkpoint at which their iteration-2 references were made. Every mask, forecast and protocol was hash committed before the samples it governs.

**The token walk stalls at the default (Table 114).** The persistent veto, implemented as a vLLM logits processor, was exact: no banned token sequence occurred in any of 1,450 vetoed generations. The algorithm came back anyway. On the grid task `current_row` and `current_col` replaced `r, c` in 63% of re-emerged BFS programs (7% in references), and on the shortest path task `current_distinct` and `d` replaced `current_dist`. Vetoed strings also leaked through non-canonical spellings, in up to 0.86 of samples on connected components and 0.80 on find duplicate at step 2. The grid code degenerated into near-miss syntax (`queue popleft()`, 66% to 86% invalid). Imports and calls barely changed: the rerouting is lexical, not algorithmic. Only find duplicate moved one rung, to sort and adjacent check, the same single-rung move that prompt bans produce. A sham veto of an algorithm-generic n-gram of matched length and presence kept the default: grid 50 of 50 (`␣start␣==␣goal:\n`), shortest path 50 of 50 (`␣u,␣v,␣w`), substring search 49 of 50 (`␣len`) and connected components 44 of 44 valid (`␣range`). The distinctive veto cut correctness where the sham did not (shortest path pass rate 0.41 against 1.00, Newcombe difference 0.59 [0.43, 0.72]; grid 0.76 against 0.96). A fixed veto of the distinctive n-grams of BFS, DFS, IDDFS and A* at once, the request's top-five prohibition asked as an operation, left BFS 13, DFS 2 and 35 invalid programs on the grid task after two extra rounds; the prompt version gave avoidance 0.00 (Section 2.6). Neither knob reaches the rest of the catalogue.

**The long-form novelty instruction produces claims of novelty, not new algorithms (Table 118).** The request contains two long-form novelty instructions, which we call the first long-form instruction (asking the model to make a new algorithm) and the second long-form instruction (asking for a fully novel algorithm never seen before); each asks for a design rationale of about 2,000 words before the code. Of those, 189 (39%) contained no code at all, only a rationale of 1,300 to 1,700 words, and 220 of the 295 with code (75%) were catalogue algorithms by the mechanism labeller, under names that modify a catalogue algorithm, such as a modified Bellman-Ford, a BFS with dynamic programming, or an optimised Dijkstra with early termination. **No novel algorithm in any cell.** Every correct program outside the catalogue from every arm of this experiment went through an audit: 38 correct programs (23 from the long-form cells, 10 from the walk, 5 from the lists) plus 15 seeded failing ones. Two blind judges (gemini-2.5-flash-lite and gpt-4.1-mini; each passed a 6-program control gate at 5 of 6 after a prompt fix) compared each program with its three nearest known solutions from the declared dataset's 472 human and textbook programs and its three nearest catalogue references, and the executor read each one and ran it on three extra random inputs. The 38 correct programs were 30 labeller misses (mostly counting sort on kth smallest written with a dictionary or Counter), 7 catalogue variants (counting plus binary search on cumulative counts; a last-in-first-out label correcting search on the shortest path task) and 1 degenerate quadratic brute force. Judge A called 10 programs novel and judge B none (kappa 0.27); the manual pass found 5 of those 10 degenerate (XOR or sum tricks, broken loops), 3 labeller misses and 2 catalogue variants. The exact one-sided 95% upper bound on the novel rate is 0.058 per cell of 50, 0.113 per cell of 25 and 0.26 per thinking-on cell of 10. Together with the record audit (0 of 78), the run's direct answer to the novelty question is that no instruction or knob produced a correct algorithm outside the catalogue and its known variants.

**Deviations and checks.** Distinctive n-grams had to be lexical (a veto of an indentation-tailed n-gram was bypassed by re-indenting in 20 of 20 unit tests), and shams could not be constructed for kth smallest and find duplicate. The analysis code was edited after its hash was committed (corrected compositions, a post hoc sensitivity, a claim mechanism check); an unchanged rederivation script reproduced every preregistered number from raw rows with no mismatch. Dropped: placement of the walk landings on the manifold, the thinking-on temperature sweep, and extending the path task thinking cells to N = 25. Judge spend was USD 0.49.

**One wording, everywhere.** The fourth template of Table 40, which states only that X is not allowed here, is the weakest wording in every artifact that measured it. In the bench forecast experiment it accounted for 197 of 240 banned programs, against 85 to 135 for the other templates. In the bench route experiment its pooled avoidance was 0.19, against 0.42 to 0.62, and it produced 29% of all ban failures. In the exposure template arm its mean avoidance was 0.81, against 0.93 to 0.96. In the locus experiment it kept the default in 20 of 20 bench samples and carried all 61 grid BFS programs under the ban, which is why every within-ban decoder there reduced to a template decoder. In Llama, dropping the fourth template alone flips the frozen branch from no family advancing to substitution. Wording is the largest measured source of variance in compliance, and any analysis that pools templates without modelling them pools different experiments.

**Signature vetoes, five times.** Every artifact that vetoed a default's distinctive n-gram found the default carried by more than its surface tokens. The default survived every round on 9 of 12 bench tasks in the bench forecast experiment, and Y re-emerged after three rounds for 25 of 33 shown algorithms in the exposure experiment. Only one Llama default (the heap of top-k frequent) was removed, the one-shot veto's avoidance was at most 0.41 in the bench route experiment, and the token walk stalled on all six tasks of the reach experiment although the veto was exact. On both path tasks no veto variant moved the default at all, in Qwen3-8B or in Llama, while a single prompt ban moves them by about 85 points. The subtraction forecast was therefore undefined on most events, and the test of whether a ban-free veto reproduces a ban's landing was undetermined everywhere it was planned.

On the Qwen3-8B modal bans no family's forecast beats uniform by a decisive margin, and in neither model does a family advance once undefined forecasts are not counted as wins. On the exposure bans, where the default is still available, the ladder (that is, the default) wins: snap-back. ## 3.10 What iteration 3 established, what it ruled out, and what it abandoned

Everything below is still one model per contest, at most 31 gated events per contest, and labels from labellers that passed their gates; the bench is memorised LeetCode material, and the path tasks are a screen that is never pooled.

**Established.**

1. *The likelihood substitution test of iteration 2 cannot decide the title claim.* Its gain and residual argmax hit the realised landing in 0 of 17 Qwen3-8B single bans, against 14 of 17 for the implied mass. No row keeps three estimable survivors, the bootstrap variance of the mean gain is 2.7 times the noise term it subtracted, and a decision on mass would need about 50 programs per algorithm at the lower bound and 129 Qwen3-8B or 43 Llama events. Whether the gains are pure subtraction, whether their specific part is aimed, and whether the generic profiles form a ladder are all undetectable with that instrument.
2. *Shown a correct program of a non-default algorithm and told not to use it, Qwen3-8B snaps back to its default.* The default's share of attempts rises from 0.05 under the copy twin to 0.72 under the named ban and 0.82 under the unnamed one. The modal replacement is the default in 24 of 31 gated events, and the ladder forecast wins the frozen contest (7 wins; top-1 0.77). Naming the banned algorithm adds little beyond asking for something else (same modal replacement for 0.88 of Y). *(Correction, iteration 4: the frozen counting rule advances some family in 85% of no-information simulations and in 100% of label-permutation placebo draws (the ladder in 43%), and no paired test survives Holm on the named events, so the 7 wins of the ladder are weak evidence. Wording also changes the landing: under templates one to four the default is modal for 13 of 19 priority algorithms, against 15 of 19 under the fifth, and the replacement flips to the associate for the size-k heap and the Z algorithm. Snap-back rests on one wording. It replicates in the present minor bans of Llama, which return to the default in 0.72 to 0.93 of attempts not banned; Section 4.2.3.)*
3. *Where the default is not available, the landing is specific to the task and mostly unforeseen.* On the five gated Qwen3-8B modal bench bans, no ban-free or association forecast beats uniform on average, and three of five landings (index marking, BFS, a failing merge without sorting) were named by no family. In Llama the landing is predictable above chance (ladder and association 7 of 13 each), but the families do not separate. *(Correction, iteration 4: the merge intervals landing is residue, failing programs labelled other (29 coverage arrays, 12 unsorted sweeps, 3 others), and that event passes the gate only through them (catalogue-only avoidance 0.14). In Llama, with other excluded, association hits 7 of 13 (p = 0.032) and the ladder 6 of 13 (p = 0.100), so only association is above chance.)*
4. *A ban's route is task dependent.* On the bench, pooled over five gated tasks, generated tokens reading the ban carry 0.74 of the effect and the prompt states 0.61. The mechanism is redundant on kth smallest and connected components, direct on two sum and find duplicate, and superadditive on merge intervals, and a second draw reproduces every task. The prompt route story of the path tasks does not generalise. *(Correction, iteration 4: the claim that generated tokens carry more of the effect rested on a comparison of point estimates. With their jackknife intervals the fractions are F_direct 0.744 [0.38, 1.11] and F_prompt 0.611 [0.06, 1.17], which overlap, with interaction -0.355. The superadditive class rests on merge intervals, which is gated only through residue; without it F_prompt is 0.648 [-0.08, 1.38] and F_direct 0.865 [0.68, 1.05].)*

6. *Wording dominates compliance.* The fourth template is the weakest in every artifact (template SD about 2.0 logits; likelihood ratio 374), and dropping it flips the Llama branch.
7. *The default is not carried by any small set of surface tokens.* Exact signature vetoes, one-shot, persistent, iterated or cumulative, almost never remove it; the model renames, respells or breaks the code. A single prompt ban moves the model further than any veto.
8. *Prompts reach past one rung where the alternatives are interchangeable.* Bans that leave one survivor got BFS 50 of 50 on connected components and quickselect 50 of 50 on kth smallest; on kth smallest quickselect is the answer to every ban list, including lists that ban it and the list that leaves only the default. Elsewhere (Floyd-Warshall, size-k heap, heapify and pop, binary search on values) the model will not write a survivor it can write on request. *(Correction, iteration 4: the kth smallest disconfirmation depends on the rung definition. 9. *No instruction or knob produced a correct novel algorithm.* Zero of 78 correct out-of-catalogue programs in the iteration-1 and iteration-2 data and 0 of 38 in iteration 3 are novel; the request's long-form instruction makes 84% of outputs claim novelty, 39% of those contain no code, and 75% of the rest are catalogue algorithms.

**Ruled out, or not supported.**

- *Substitution by association in Qwen3-8B.* In none of the three contests did association win; it was worse than uniform on all five gated modal bans and lost to the ladder by about 1.3 nats on exposure bans (Holm 0.081 named, 0.0056 unnamed).
- *A shared prohibition direction as the carrier of the ban.* Adding the leave-one-task-out ban displacement to a neutral prompt passed on 0 of 5 gated tasks against matched random directions, and removing it from a ban never restored the default (pooled -0.026 [-0.07, 0.03]).
- *A ban-free signature veto as the forecast of the next rung.* It was undefined on 10 of 12 Qwen3-8B modal events and 29 of 33 exposure events, and where defined on the path tasks or the bench it landed elsewhere than the ban.
- *The prompt route as the general mechanism of a ban.* Disconfirmed on the bench (pooled direct share 0.74, jackknife [0.38, 1.11]).
- *Prompts move the model exactly one rung.* Disconfirmed on connected components (BFS will 1.00 at can 1.00) and, through the fallback rung, on kth smallest.
- *The three ban-attending heads as a causal site.* Ablating them moved the grid ban by +0.06 over random heads in the same layers, inside the range of any perturbation of the fragile fourth-template ban.
- *A locus at generated tokens 1 to 16.* No decoder beat the template-only or written text controls on any testable task; on the shortest path task the choice diverges at a median of about 29 tokens.

**Dead ends, with the evidence that closed them.**

- *The forced ratio latent probability as the decision instrument for where a ban sends the mass.* Closed by Table 82 (argmax 0 of 17 against the realised landing) and Table 84 (programs and events needed far beyond the budget).
- *Signature vetoes and the token walk as a way past the default.* Closed by the bench forecast, exposure, Llama, route and reach experiments: the default survives exact vetoes by renaming and respelling, and the walk stalled at rung 1 or 2 on all six tasks.
- *The shared prohibition direction.* Closed by Table 110.
- *Head ablation as a test of the attention heads.* Closed by the random-head control.
- *Qwen-Scope base SAEs for readouts of the ban.* They now pass a fairer transfer criterion (fraction of cross-entropy recovered 0.989 to 0.994), but their reconstructions keep only a cosine of about 0.3 of the ban displacement, and their latents never beat difference-in-means.
- *Long-form novelty instructions as a source of novel algorithms.* Closed by Table 118 and the audit (0 novel of 38 correct programs outside the catalogue).

## 3.11 What the next iteration takes from this one

The title claim of the update, that a ban removes the default and the model falls to a next rung that ban-free counterfactuals can read in advance, did not survive in that form. The part that survived is snap-back: with the default available, a ban on a shown algorithm returns the model to its default, which is subtraction in its simplest form. Where the default itself is banned, the counterfactuals meant to expose the next rung either fail to move the model (signature vetoes) or move it somewhere else (random pushes, the shared prohibition direction), and the landing is specific to the task in a way no frozen family foresaw in Qwen3-8B. Substitution by association is not supported in Qwen3-8B and is tied with the ladder in Llama. What decides the replacement under a modal ban remains open, and the run now has two concrete leads for it: the opening of the body, where the prefill sweep localises the ban to the first body token, and the template, which carries more of the variance in compliance than anything else measured. *(Added in iteration 4: a third lead was already in the iteration-3 data, the landing composition per route arm. On connected components either route alone lands mostly on DFS, which is the generic landing of random pushes and the association answer of Qwen3-8B, and BFS is chosen only when both routes act; Section 4.2.2.)*

Three things follow for the next iteration. First, the contest needs events on which the default is unavailable and the families disagree, in numbers the paired tests can use: the modal bench bans give 5 gated events in Qwen3-8B, so pooling with Llama (11) and adding bench tasks where bans take is the arithmetic, with the template entered as a random effect rather than pooled over. Second, the first body token is now a measured locus in behaviour; a decoder or patch there, in states saved at that position for each task, would ask what is decided when the ban gives way. Third, the generic perturbation rival needs a behavioural test where its runner-up and the associate differ, which the Qwen3-8B bench rarely provides; Llama's present minor events are where the named ban gained the associate about 0.25 of attempts beyond the veto on two of six events, and that is the next place to look.

Request items still open: a same seed temperature arm with thinking on (dropped again), manifold placement of the walk landings (dropped; the walk stalled), and an SAE readout that keeps the ban displacement. *(Added in iteration 4: the same seed arm with thinking on ran in iteration 4, Section 4.5.)*

**The hypothesis update.** The update reframed the run around a result that had sat in the control arms of the iteration-3 locus experiment [ARTIFACT:art_pVlCZ272hDV7]. Isotropic random directions added to the task-specification states at blocks 12 to 23, at the size of the displacement a ban itself causes, had made Qwen3-8B [5] write two or three different correct algorithms for one prompt at no loss of correctness. On kth smallest, 7 of 15 directions moved at least 20% of programs off the default, and five reached a correct-only Hill-1 of 2 or more. The update read this as evidence that the algorithm is chosen in those states before any code is written. We call that state the *plan* below, with one caveat stated now: the word names a site in the network, and whether a plan representation sits there is what this iteration tested. Temperature never touches the plan, which would explain why it changes wording and not ideas, while a nudge to the plan changes ideas. The question that ran through iterations 1 to 3, substitution against subtraction, becomes a special case: a ban is one large displacement of the plan, plus generated tokens reading the ban. Three claims followed, each with a rule committed before its first decisive sample.

- *The price claim.* Plan noise moves the algorithm while temperature moves only the wording, and on tasks where the plan is movable it buys correct algorithmic diversity more cheaply than every token-level and prompt-level knob tested. Two sub-claims: the effect is specific to the task-specification states at blocks 12 to 23 (the site claim), and with the token seed held fixed, temperature changes the algorithm in at most 1 of 20 seeds while a change of plan noise draw changes it often (the same seed claim, which is question 1a-c of the request).
- *The subspace claim.* The choice is represented in a low-dimensional subspace of the task-specification states, spanned by the differences between per-algorithm centroids under forced prompts, and a push changes the algorithm to the extent that it moves the state along that subspace.
- *The movability claim.* Whether a ban on the default of a task is obeyed is predicted, without any ban sample, by whether random pushes can move that task, and the ban lands where the pushes land unless generated tokens read the ban. The claim was to be confirmed in a model family never run in this study. Two further tests rode along: a norm sweep to the point of breakage with a full audit for novel algorithms, and the top-five prohibition of the request applied as a push at the plan.

We define the instruments once. A *ban unit* is the norm of the ban minus neutral twin displacement per layer and per task-specification position at blocks 12 to 23, averaged over the five modal ban templates; for a model never banned it is estimated without ban text from the residual norm times the median ratio, in Qwen3-8B, of ban displacement to residual norm at the same relative depth. *Plan noise* at dose alpha is a fresh isotropic random direction per sample, added during prefill at every task-specification position of blocks 12 to 23, with the displacement along it set to alpha ban units at each block, so the edits do not compound. A fixed direction *escapes* when, over its first 10 samples, the share of attempts off the default exceeds that of the twin by at least 0.20 at a pass rate of at least 0.8 times that of the twin; two experiments added a confirmation at N = 30 by an exact binomial test. The *escape fraction* of a task is the share of its fixed directions that escape, and we call a task *movable* when its escape fraction is above zero at some dose of at most 2. The *plan subspace* of a task is the span of the differences between per-algorithm centroids of the task-specification states under 30 forced paraphrases per algorithm, with a name-masked twin built from descriptions. The *push-landing forecast* names the modal catalogue survivor among off-default attempts of escaping directions, and the *opening ladder* ranks survivors by the teacher-forced log probability of their modal forced-program body opening under the neutral twin. We price a knob by its *5-point Hill-1*, the highest correct-only rarefied Hill-1 (depth 25) it reaches at a cost of at most 5 pass points, and by its *price of 1.5* and *price of 2*, the smallest pass cost at which it reaches a Hill-1 of 1.5 and of 2. The plan noise and site experiments compute them on the *randomisation hull* of each knob, the set of mixtures of the reference arm with the settings of the knob, which turns the dial of a knob into a continuous price curve.

**The strategy.** Seven artifacts ran (Table 122). One evaluation repaired the record from rows on disk and froze the push screen by hash, so that every later analysis cites one screen. Four Qwen3-8B experiments tested the price, site, same seed and subspace claims, and one experiment ran the movability claim in a held-out family. A research artifact positioned the iteration-3 and iteration-4 claims against published work. Two departures from the plan shaped what could be claimed. The held-out family was planned as gemma-2-9b-it, but the only GPU available held 16 GB, so the experiment ran gemma-3-4b-it [76], another family never run in this study. Every Qwen3-8B GPU artifact ran on the same 16 GB card with 8-bit floating point weight and activation linear layers, the engine of the iteration-3 screen; each reproduced the rows of the screen byte for byte, so every plan noise result below is a result for that engine, with no measured gap to bf16. ## 4.3 Plan noise priced against every other knob (Qwen3-8B)

**Why.** The price claim was the primary claim of the iteration and the question of the request in its plainest form: which knob buys correct algorithmic diversity most cheaply. The iteration-3 evidence for random pushes came from fixed directions, three per task on most of the bench, chosen by nobody. This experiment [ARTIFACT:art_mWn-MQEnNelg] drew a fresh direction for every sample, which is the form a practitioner would use, and priced it on the six movable tasks of the frozen screen against every token-level and prompt-level knob the run had tried, all under one statistic and one price convention.

**Design.** Qwen3-8B ran with 8-bit linear layers on the 16 GB card, thinking off, and every arm of a task shared the same uniform stream per template and slot, so arms differ only by the knob. Plan noise ran at alpha 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 (and 8 in the dose sweep). The comparison knobs were temperature 1.3 and 1.6 without truncation, top-k 10, the nonce ban, the novelty instruction, the semantic seed on the path tasks and the iteration-3 signature vetoes (one-shot, persistent and iterated, reused rows); min-p 0.1 at temperature 1.6 and 2.0 and a verbalized sampling prompt [46] were preregistered sensitivities. Every cell had N = 50 (5 templates by 10 slots): 202 cells and 10,100 labelled programs, with no cell dropped. The 5-point Hill-1 and the prices of 1.5 and 2 were computed on the randomisation hull of each knob with 2,000 bootstrap replicates, and the choice of the best setting of a knob was made inside every replicate. The rule, committed by hash before the first sample beyond stage 10, confirmed the price claim if plan noise reached a 5-point Hill-1 of at least 1.5 on at least 3 of the 6 tasks, beat the 5-point Hill-1 of the best non-activation knob on at least 4 of 6, and had a pooled margin with a task-bootstrap 95% interval above 0.

**The rule returned PARTIAL.** Plan noise is not the uniformly cheapest knob (Table 137). It reaches a 5-point Hill-1 of at least 1.5 on only 2 of 6 tasks, against the 3 required, and beats the best non-activation knob on 4 of 6, but the pooled margin is -0.22 with an interval from -0.89 to 0.30 (one-sided p = 0.76; exact sign test over the six margins p = 0.34). Plan noise wins clearly on kth smallest (2.72 against 1.96 for the novelty instruction, ahead in every bootstrap replicate) and on connected components (2.09 against 1.96 for the iterated veto, ahead in 91%), and on both it reaches Hill-1 of 1.5 and of 2 at no pass cost. It edges two sum and the grid task by margins inside their intervals. It loses decisively on find duplicate, where it does not move the hash set at alpha 2 or less while the reused iterated veto reaches 2.73, and on the shortest path task, where the semantic seed reaches 1.93 against 1.35 for plan noise because pushed Bellman-Ford/SPFA programs cost 14 to 26 pass points.

## 4.4 Where the noise must enter (Qwen3-8B)

**Why.** If the plan lives in the task-specification states, the same random displacement should change the algorithm there and nowhere else. If any perturbation of matched size does as well, the effect is generic sensitivity, and the word plan names nothing. This experiment [ARTIFACT:art_Cx9JOh8soBw7] wrote one random displacement per common-random-number slot into six sites at matched per-position dose in ban units and priced each site on the randomisation hull.

**Design.** The six sites were the task-specification states at blocks 12 to 23 (the plan site of the hypothesis), the read position, the condition sentence, generated tokens 1 to 32 (through teacher-forced shadow rows), the task-specification states at blocks 0 to 11, and the same states at blocks 24 to 35. Each ran at alpha 1, 2 and 4 with N = 30 per cell (twin N = 50) on the six movable tasks, with energy-matched variants of the read position and condition sites and the plan site at alpha 8 for the boundary. One fresh direction and one stream of token uniforms per slot were shared by every arm, so every site contrast is an exact paired flip. In all 4,510 programs ran; 4,460 decisive rows followed the commitment, and none preceded it. The preregistered rule called the site claim confirmed if the plan site had the highest 5-point Hill-1 on at least 4 of 6 tasks.

**The rule returned PARTIAL, and three sites are inert.** The plan site has the best 5-point Hill-1 on 3 of 6 tasks (kth smallest, the grid task and the shortest path task; p = 0.062 against a binomial with chance 1/6), generated-token noise is best on two sum and find duplicate, and early-block noise on connected components (Table 143). Every per-task margin is a bootstrap close call except the shortest path task, where the plan site is ahead in 97% of replicates. The read position and the condition sentence never changed the algorithm at per-position doses of 1 to 4 ban units (corrected in iteration 5 from the phrase *at any dose*; the energy-matched read position below is weaker but not inert): 0 of 526 and 0 of 527 correct programs off the default at alpha 1 to 4. The late blocks are almost as inert (6 of 521). The outputs at these three sites are often byte-identical to those of the twin, 90% to 100% at alpha 1 on kth smallest, two sum and find duplicate for the read position and the late blocks.

**The effect is not generic transmission.** Noise at the read position produces as large a displacement at the last block as the plan site does (medians 141, 250 and 474 against 159, 272 and 461 at alpha 1, 2 and 4), yet it flips nothing. A logistic regression of a correct program being off the default on the log of the realised displacement at the read position, with template and task fixed effects, over 2,769 correct programs from the prefill sites, gives the plan site an indicator of +2.15 [1.79, 2.51] beside a displacement slope of +0.88 [0.62, 1.14]. In the matched-dose bins (the upper three quintiles of displacement) the plan site is off the default in 16% to 27% of programs, against 3% to 7% for the other prefill sites. A hand-coded Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio, which pools the odds of an off-default program at the plan site against the other prefill sites across task and displacement quintile strata, gives 5.72 [3.94, 8.30], and its placebo, with plan-site labels shuffled within task, has a median of 0.98. A Bayesian mixed logistic model with random task and template effects puts the site effects relative to the plan site at -3.0 (read position), -2.9 (condition sentence), -3.0 (late blocks), -0.8 (generated tokens) and -1.1 (early blocks), with the slope of the plan site on log2 alpha at +1.11. Concentrating the whole ban energy at the read position (median displacement there 1,002, six times that of the plan site at alpha 1) moved find duplicate by +0.23 and connected components by +0.18 at pass ratios of 0.87 to 0.93; spreading it over the condition span stayed inert. Generated-token noise produces the most phrasing clusters per idea (4.2 and 4.7 at alpha 1 and 2, against 2.8 and 3.4 for the plan site, AST-shingle components at Jaccard 0.8).

**The boundary.** At alpha 8 the task specification is effectively erased (Table 147): the model echoes the condition sentence, writes placeholder code or asks for clarification, and the pass rate is 0.00 on every task. Correct-only diversity peaks at alpha 2 (kth smallest, grid, shortest path) or alpha 4 (two sum, find duplicate, connected components), and alpha 4 already costs 33% to 97% of the passes. Across every arm 3,555 programs were correct, and exactly one was labelled other: a find duplicate program from generated-token noise at alpha 2 that calls a count of each element over the list. The judges called it degenerate and a labeller miss, and the manual read, beside its three nearest known solutions, called it the textbook quadratic brute force. No novel algorithm appeared (rule-of-three bound 3/3,555 = 0.08% per correct program [67]).

## 4.5 Same seed: temperature against plan noise (Qwen3-8B, question 1a-c of the request)

**Why.** The request asks three things about temperature: with a tight temperature and top-k 10, does the model produce one idea in many phrasings or many ideas; does loosening it multiply ideas or phrasings; and does the answer hold with the same seed. The run had answered the first two in iteration 1 and the third with thinking off in iteration 2, and had dropped the thinking-on arm twice. This experiment [ARTIFACT:art_Yu6GN6pLxW8f] ran the seed-coupled design on the grid task, the shortest path task and kth smallest, with the thinking-on arm made non-droppable, and added plan noise as the second factor so that the same seed could be varied in temperature or in plan.

**Design.** Each task had 20 token seeds, one per template and slot, and each seed kept one noise stream across every condition (inverse-CDF sampling with common random numbers). The temperature block ran each seed at 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 (top-p 1) and with top-k 10 at 0.7. The plan noise block ran 6 fixed isotropic directions at alpha 1 and 2 and temperature 0.7 and 1.0. The change count of a task is the number of seeds whose algorithm differs across the conditions of a block; for plan noise it is averaged over the 20 three-direction subsets of the 6 directions. Thinking on ran in vLLM with per-request seeds (an exponential race coupling, confirmed by recomputing the first token in 32 of 32 requests), a 16k cap and the completion rate reported. *(Correction, iteration 5: the top-k 10 answer to the request with thinking off is Table 76 of iteration 2: with seeds coupled, the label changed in 0 of 30 seeds in 10 of 12 cells. **Temperature never changed the algorithm; plan noise changed it in most seeds on the shortest path task.** With thinking off, the algorithm stayed the same across all four temperatures in 20 of 20 seeds on all three tasks, and with thinking on in 20 of 20 seeds on the shortest path task (Table 150); the exact 95% upper bound on the per-seed change rate is 0.168 for each count of 0 in 20. ## 4.6 The plan subspace: does the geometry of forced prompts explain which pushes move the algorithm? (Qwen3-8B)

**Why.** The site experiment located the choice in the task-specification states at early to middle blocks, but a site is not a representation. The subspace claim gave the internal account the request asks for a testable form: if the algorithm choice is represented along the directions that separate the per-algorithm centroids, a random push should change the algorithm to the extent that it moves the state along them. This experiment [ARTIFACT:art_SHaWv77P1XCI] built the subspace from forced prompts alone and asked whether it ranks 40 fresh random directions by their effect, whether removing the in-subspace component of a push removes the effect, and whether a push aimed at the runner-up centroid crosses at the predicted distance.

**Design.** For each of 15 tasks the plan subspace at blocks 12 to 35 was the span of the centroid differences of the task-specification states (mean over the specification positions) under 30 forced paraphrases per algorithm (10 forced templates by 3 names), and a masked twin used 30 leak-checked descriptions per algorithm. The projection share of a direction is its squared norm in the subspace over its total, averaged over blocks. Forty never-run directions at alpha 1 and 2, with N = 10 each and passers topped up to N = 30, ran on the six movable tasks; 8 directions at both doses ran on the other nine, including cycle detection on its ban-free unit. Every predictor was committed by hash before the first population sample. The run sampled 13,500 programs in 675 batches of 20 over 2.51 GPU hours, labelled by runtime tracer and AST rules with a blind judge on 752 disagreements; 4 disputed and 97 invalid rows were excluded from shares.

**The subspace is real and reliable.** At block 18 the split-half principal-angle cosine between two halves of the paraphrases is 0.89 to 0.97 on all 15 tasks, against 0.02 to 0.03 for random subspaces of equal dimension, and every centroid difference has a split-half cosine of at least 0.74. Named and masked differences agree only moderately (cosine 0.12 to 1.00 at block 18), so the subspace carries a lexical component. The iteration-3 ban displacement projects strongly onto it (projection share 0.02 to 0.77; 0.08 to 0.39 on the six movable tasks), while a random direction has a share near k/4096, about 0.001. The committed plausibility ratio, the expected in-subspace part of a random push over the distance from the default to the runner-up centroid, is 0.10 to 0.29 on 14 tasks and 0.51 on the grid task: a linear plan account predicted before sampling that random pushes would almost never cross to the runner-up through the subspace.

**The projection share does not predict which pushes move the algorithm.** The preregistered test, a within-task Spearman correlation of at least 0.4 with p below 0.01 on at least 4 of 6 tasks, failed on all six, and so did the masked variant (Table 153). The pooled within-task correlation is 0.03 [-0.03, 0.09], and the correlation of every task lies inside its random-subspace null. The null is not for want of movers: 34 to 37 of 40 directions moved the algorithm at least once on kth smallest, the shortest path task and connected components. Nor is it noise. Splitting the first 10 samples of each direction by template, the two halves rank the 40 directions alike (Spearman 0.80 on kth smallest, 0.81 on the shortest path task, 0.76 on two sum, 0.90 on connected components; projected to full length by the Spearman-Brown formula, 0.86 to 0.95), and alpha 1 and alpha 2 rank them alike (0.61 to 0.72). Which direction moves the algorithm is a stable property of the direction, with a ceiling near 0.9 for any predictor, and the subspace share explains none of it. The only signal came from the signed component toward the runner-up on connected components (0.32 to 0.33, unadjusted p near 0.02), and the within-class control did as well (0.37).

## 4.7 Movability and compliance in a held-out model family (gemma-3-4b-it)

**Why.** The movability claim was frozen on Qwen3-8B data that had also produced it: in the screen every movable task obeyed its ban and no immovable task did. Only a family never run in this study could test it. This experiment [ARTIFACT:art_k6nzFCDLOjQP] froze the screen rule, measured movability in gemma-3-4b-it [76] without any ban text, committed every per-task prediction by hash chain before any ban prompt was built (a grep audit of the 460 prompts fed in the ban-free stage found no ban frame), and then sampled 1,500 modal ban programs.

**Design.** For each of 15 tasks (the 12 bench tasks, the grid and shortest path tasks, and cycle detection), the model wrote 50 neutral twin programs, and 8 fixed isotropic directions at alpha 1 and 2 were added to the task-specification states of blocks 11 to 22, the middle third of its 34 blocks, during prefill. A direction escaped by the rule of Section 4.1, confirmed at N = 30 by an exact binomial test, and a task predicted to obey its modal ban when its escape fraction was above zero. The ban unit had to change before the commitment. In Gemma the five largest channels carry 99% of the squared residual norm at the specification positions, against 40% in Qwen3-8B, so the committed unit erased the task in a 24-row calibration probe; an outlier-excluded unit was adopted before the first commitment, and after the bans the measured ban displacement turned out to be 1.29 times it (0.92 to 2.1 by block). The rival predictors, the plan noise and temperature arms, the novelty instruction and four landing forecasts ran in the same engine under the same common random numbers.

**The movability claim is inconclusive in the held-out family.** Movability relates to compliance in the predicted direction but does not separate the tasks well enough (Table 159). The confusion matrix is 3, 3, 1, 8 (predicted obey or fail against observed): balanced accuracy 0.74 [0.40, 0.95], Fisher p = 0.24 (0.71 under the committed three-claim bound), Spearman 0.54 (one-sided permutation p = 0.025) and Kendall 0.47. The rule needed balanced accuracy of at least 0.8, Fisher p below 0.05 and Spearman of at least 0.5. Four tasks broke the prediction: kth smallest obeyed although no direction moved it, and substring search, connected components and longest increasing subsequence were movable but did not obey. A task-permutation placebo has mean balanced accuracy 0.50 (probability 0.13 of reaching the observed value), and leaving one task out gives 0.70 to 0.86.

## 4.11 What the next iteration takes from this one

The iteration answered the first question of the request in its strictest form and narrowed the second. Temperature, at any setting and with the seed fixed, changes how the code is written and not which algorithm it implements, with thinking off and on. The algorithm can be influenced, cheaply on some tasks, by a random displacement of the task-specification states at early to middle blocks, and the read position, the condition sentence and the late blocks are inert. *(Correction, iteration 5: the read position and the condition sentence are inert at per-position doses up to 4 ban units, weaker but not inert at matched energy, and the late blocks almost inert.)* What the iteration did not find is a representation of the choice: the forced-prompt subspace does not explain which displacements work, although which displacements work is reproducible. The open question is therefore what property of a direction makes it move the algorithm. The exploratory signed-progress correlations (up to 0.57) point at direction toward the runner-up rather than share, and the targeted push on connected components shows that one axis can be causally exact. A preregistered test of signed progress on fresh directions, with the reproducible ranking of the directions as the target, is the next step. *(Correction, iteration 5: that step was not taken, and signed progress is closed. Its positive cells concentrate on one task, it is negative on average on two, and on connected components the committed signed component was matched by a within-class control (0.33 against 0.37). Per task over 24 block cells: kth smallest 1 cell with p below 0.05 and a mean of -0.02 over the edited blocks (-0.29 at block 15); shortest path 3 and +0.20; two sum 7 and +0.31; connected components 22 and +0.37; find duplicate 0 and -0.12; grid 2 and +0.05 (Table 177; the record's count of 22 of 35 cells was 22 of 24). The next budget goes to more tasks, not to a further predictor at the level of directions on the same five: new tasks with the base model's repertoire committed before any push, so that which tasks move can be predicted from the base model and tested on units never seen.)*

The movability claim needs more than one held-out family at one size, a labeller re-gated on the style of each family, and a comparison with the novelty instruction, which predicted compliance better in Gemma. The landing claim needs events on which the push forecast and association disagree: Gemma gave 2 of 4, and the Qwen3-8B bench gave 3 defined events. The contrast set of the price claim lacks the text-level plan samplers that the positioning audit names [73, 74] and a decoding baseline matched to the departure of plan noise from greedy decoding; until both are run, the claim is that plan noise beats the token-level and prompt-seed knobs tested, on the tasks where it moves the model. The route-landing lead from Section 4.2.2 ties these threads together: where one route alone removes the default, the landing is the generic neighbour that pushes reach, and the ban departs from it only when both routes act. *(Correction, iteration 5: this lead rests on connected components alone; find duplicate is the counterexample and two sum has no agreed neighbour, Section 4.2.2. Movability as a forecast of ban compliance and the contest over where a ban lands are closed beyond descriptive reporting; the next test is the narrowed repertoire account, Section 5.1.)*

**The hypothesis update.** The update kept the plan noise lead of iteration 4 and asked what sets its boundary. Plan noise moved the algorithm on some tasks and on no others, and where it moved it, it landed on one runner-up per task. On the two path tasks those runner-up algorithms were exactly the algorithms the untuned base model writes next to its default: under the chat template Qwen3-8B-Base wrote BFS in 49 of 57 correct grid programs and Dijkstra in 63 of 90 correct shortest path programs, with DFS and Bellman-Ford/SPFA second (Section 1.9). The update therefore proposed what it called the *narrowed repertoire account*: post-training narrowed a choice that the base model makes more evenly, the narrowed choice is set while the model reads the task specification, and a nudge to those states undoes part of the narrowing, reopening the base model's alternatives and only those. A task that no nudge moves would then be one on which the base model itself writes almost one algorithm, and post-training [35, 57, 87] would have narrowed only what pretraining left open.

We use the following quantities throughout. The *base off-default share* of a task, beta, is the share of the base model's correct programs that use an algorithm other than the instruct model's default, with both models given identical token ids under the chat template; the *base runner-up* is the base model's most frequent correct algorithm other than that default. We call a task *diverse in the base* when beta is at least 0.2 and *collapsed in the base* when beta is below 0.05; between the two it is intermediate. The instruct default comes from a twin of at least 50 samples as the modal correct label with a share of at least 0.6; a task below that has *no default* and enters no movability or landing test. One *ban-free unit* is the residual norm of the task-specification states times the median ratio, in Qwen3-8B at the same relative depth, of a ban's displacement to the residual norm; it replaces the ban's own displacement as the dose unit everywhere, so that a task's dose no longer depends on how far its ban moved it. We call the edit h ← h + lambda (h_base − h_instruct), applied during the instruct prefill at every task-specification position of blocks 12 to 23 with the base states computed on the same prompt, a *transplant of base plan states*, in the spirit of cross-model activation patching [88].

Eight claims were preregistered, each with its rule committed by sha256 before its first decisive sample.

- *The movability half: the base repertoire predicts which tasks move* (primary): across new tasks, beta ranks the escape fraction of 8 fixed random directions at Spearman of at least 0.6 with a permutation p within parent clusters below 0.01, at least 80% of tasks collapsed in the base are immovable, and beta is ahead of each rival. Disconfirmed if Spearman is below 0.3 or most tasks diverse in the base are immovable.
- *The landing half: landings follow the base runner-up* (primary): on movable new tasks the push landing is the base runner-up in at least 70% of events (exact test against per-event chance, p below 0.05), and the base composition beats the association forecast by at least 0.10 nats in log score.
- *The transplant claim* (primary, causal): on at least two thirds of the tasks diverse in the base among the 15 existing ones, the transplant at its best lambda (with pass of at least 0.8 times the twin's) reaches a correct off-default share of at least half of beta, beats a matched-norm random displacement and what we call a *borrowed shift* (another task's base minus instruct direction at the same norm) on paired flips, and lands on the base runner-up; tasks collapsed in the base and a transplant at the read position stay within 0.05 of the twin.
- *The plan sampler comparison* (secondary): plan noise prices at least as well as the best of four text-level plan samplers on at least 3 of the 5 tasks movable on fresh draws: intent factored generation [73], plan search [74], a sampler we call *enumerate and pick* (the model lists algorithms and an external random draw picks one) and what we call *base intent* (the base model writes an intent of one sentence and the instruct model writes the code).
- *The push toward the base*: a push along the base minus instruct direction, which we call a push toward the base, escapes at no more than half the norm a random push needs (secondary).
- *The Gemma replication* (secondary): both halves in gemma-3-4b-pt against gemma-3-4b-it [76], a replication on fresh samples because Gemma's iteration-4 outcomes were seen.
- *The literal cell* of the request (descriptive) and *the novelty count* (secondary).

**The strategy.** Seven artifacts ran (Table 167). One evaluation on CPU only repaired the iteration-4 record from rows on disk and froze eight rival task predictors by hash before reading any outcome. The transplant experiment measured the base repertoire of all 15 existing tasks, committed it, and only then ran the transplant with its controls. Two panels built new coding tasks, committed each task's base repertoire, and only then pushed the instruct model; they split the new tasks between them so that the pooled confirmation would have more units than either could build alone. The knob experiment ran the text-level plan samplers and what we call *decoding at matched departure* (a decoding temperature set so that the output departs from the twin as much as under plan noise) on all 15 existing tasks, and the literal cell. The Gemma experiment repeated both halves and the transplant in a second family, and a research artifact searched the literature for each new claim. The 16 GB card of iteration 4 was replaced by cards of 23 to 24 GB, so every Qwen3-8B experiment of this iteration ran in bf16 rather than with 8-bit linears; this change of engine, together with the change from the ban unit to the ban-free unit, turns out to matter (Section 5.10).

**Rival task predictors, frozen before any target was read.** For the movability half to mean anything, beta had to beat simpler explanations of why a task moves. The audit computed eight ban-free predictors for the 15 existing tasks and catalogue size as a covariate, wrote them to a canonical file, and froze them by sha256 in a hash chain before opening any outcome file (frozen at 11:59:44 UTC, first scored at 11:59:50; two later freezes left the values identical). The predictors are the twin's opening margin (the margin in log probability, under teacher forcing, of the opening of the default over that of the runner-up), the forced can rate, association clarity, the off-default excess under the novelty instruction, the diversity of human solutions (Mercury solutions labelled by the frozen rules with a judge on unknowns; audit agreement 0.97, kappa 0.97, 121 programs), the runtime merit gap between the reference programs of the runner-up and of the default (76 references timed on their hidden tests), the twin modal share and the ratio of ban unit to residual norm. Five of them (the opening margin, the novelty excess, the merit gap, the twin modal share and catalogue size) can be computed on new tasks and were frozen for the confirmation panels. Scored against the pooled escape fraction of the screen, none is informative after Holm correction (every adjusted p is 1.0), and 10 of the 15 tasks are tied at an escape fraction of 0 (Tables 179 to 181). These scores are descriptive: the escape fractions generated the hypothesis, so the freeze protects only the confirmation on new tasks.

## 5.3 Transplanting the base model's plan states into the instruct model (Qwen3-8B)

**Why.** If post-training narrowed the choice at the plan site, the narrowing should be undone by giving the instruct model the base model's own task-specification states. No earlier iteration had tried this: iteration 1 subtracted an instruct minus base direction estimated at the read position only, which destroyed the output format (Section 1.9). This experiment [ARTIFACT:art_CcZLW-9NX00l] was the first causal test of the transplant claim, and it also measured the base repertoire that every other Qwen3-8B analysis of the iteration needed.

**Design.** Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-8B-Base (revision 49e3418f, the base revision of iteration 1) ran in bf16 on one RTX 4090 with thinking off, temperature 1.0, top-p 1 and no top-k. The base model sampled 100 programs per task under the instruct chat template on identical token ids (200 on the two path tasks, with top-ups to 200 on connected components, nonoverlapping intervals and cycle detection) and 100 in plain completion. Its labels used the iteration-4 labellers with a blind judge on disagreement, and a 15-program judge audit per task agreed at least 0.86 everywhere. The base repertoire (default, beta with a 95% interval, stratum, base runner-up) was committed by hash before any hooked sample. The transplant set the hooked states to h_instruct + lambda (h_base − h_instruct) at blocks 12 to 23 for lambda in {0.25, 0.5, 1}; the states were set, not added, so nothing compounded, and at lambda 1 the hooked blocks carried the base state exactly. The controls on the same common-random-number slots were a matched-norm random displacement (per block and position), the borrowed shift (another task's mean base minus instruct direction at the same norm), and, where the random control broke the model, a random push matched on pass rate. Site controls transplanted at the read position, at blocks 0 to 11 and at blocks 24 to 35. Lambda was selected on one set of slots and confirmed on fresh slots, both under commits made before the samples.

**The base model is more diverse than the instruct model on most tasks** (Table 182). Under the same prompt the instruct twin wrote its default in 96% to 100% of programs on all 15 tasks, while 5 tasks were diverse in the base (kth smallest, shortest path, connected components, grid and top-k frequent), 7 intermediate and 3 collapsed in the base (merge intervals, nonoverlapping intervals and topological order). The base model under the chat template is a poor programmer: it wrote 14 to 55 correct programs per 100 to 200 samples, and on the grid task only 14 of 200, so the grid beta rests on attempts. On connected components it writes DFS more often than union find (32 against 19 correct programs), so the instruct default is the base model's second choice there.

Control is asymmetric: instruct states pull the base model toward the instruct default and toward correct code, but base states do not pull the instruct model back.

## 5.4 Panel A: does the base repertoire predict which new tasks move? (Qwen3-8B)

*Three instruct twins of new units are mixed: trapped rain water (default share 0.64), minimum spanning tree weight (default share 0.66) and valid anagram (default share 0.76); on two units the instruct model is more diverse than the base: trapped rain water (twin off-default 0.36 against beta 0.23) and minimum spanning tree weight (twin off-default 0.34 against beta 0.11) (iteration-6 note).*

**Why.** The screen correlation of 0.78 was measured on the tasks that generated the hypothesis. The movability and landing halves could only be confirmed on tasks never seen, with every forecast committed from base samples before the first push. Panel A [ARTIFACT:art_8WbrpoEFslk9] built one half of those tasks.

**Design.** Nine new units derived from LeetCode problems [12] were frozen up front in new wording (a grep audit found no algorithm word or catalogue name), each with hidden tests from the dataset's input and output pairs plus seeded edge, random and stress cases, one reference per algorithm, mutants that must fail, quadratic baselines and runtime and AST labellers. A labeller passed its gate at a kappa of at least 0.8 between runtime and AST labels, an agreement of at least 0.9 between runtime and adjudicated labels and 100% of references, with one revision round on a holdout. Six of the seven planned units passed; number of islands failed after its revision (holdout kappa 0.74), and the two reserves, jump game and median of two sorted lists, ran as a logged extension. Per unit, the instruct twin drew 50 programs and the base model 100 on identical ids plus 50 in plain completion, the rivals were computed, and the forecast (default, beta with its interval, base runner-up, rivals) was committed by hash; a guard in the GPU worker refused push jobs until then. Only then did 8 isotropic directions at alpha 1 and 2 (N = 10, confirmed at N = 30 by an exact binomial test), plan noise at alpha 1 and 2 (N = 50) and temperature 1.3 (N = 50) run. The 15 existing tasks were remeasured in the same engine on the ban-free unit; we call this the remeasurement arm.

**The movability half is not supported in panel A** (Table 191). Over the six preregistered units, Spearman between beta and the escape fraction is -0.03 (exact one-sided p 0.56; Kendall 0). The one unit collapsed in the base, maximum block sum (beta 0), is immovable, as the movability half predicts, but 2 of the 5 units diverse in the base are also immovable, among them the most diverse: count primes (beta 0.81) never escapes. A bootstrap over measurement error gives a median of -0.09 (90% interval -0.37 to 0.21). With the two extension units, both diverse in the base (0.47 and 0.71) and both immovable, Spearman falls to -0.33 (p 0.80). Simple rivals tracked movability better than beta (Tables 192 and 193), and so did beta's own variants: Spearman with the escape fraction is -0.09 for beta from plain completion, -0.03 for beta that also counts correct programs labelled other as off-default (identical to beta on these units) and 0.40 for the base Hill-1 (0.16, -0.33 and 0.22 with the extension units). The three units that moved have an alternative at least twice as fast as the default (minimum runtime merit ratio 0.10 to 0.51), the three that did not have ratios of 0.86 to 4.35, and the runtime merit rival reaches -0.88; the extension unit median of two sorted lists breaks this (ratio 0.11, never escapes), and with it the rival falls to -0.66. The twin's own modal share reaches -0.70, ahead of beta by a task-bootstrap interval that excludes zero (-1.90 to -0.09).

## 5.5 Panel B: seven more new tasks and disguised variants (Qwen3-8B)

*Three instruct twins of new units are mixed: trapped rain water (default share 0.64), minimum spanning tree weight (default share 0.66) and valid anagram (default share 0.76); on two units the instruct model is more diverse than the base: trapped rain water (twin off-default 0.36 against beta 0.23) and minimum spanning tree weight (twin off-default 0.34 against beta 0.11) (iteration-6 note).*

**Why.** Panel B [ARTIFACT:art_9a8LrIv2lHbV] built the other half of the confirmation units under the same protocol, and added what we call *disguised variants*, eight bench tasks rewritten as narratives, each with a paired remeasurement of its parent, to separate a task's wording from its algorithmic affordances.

**Design.** Seven units (missing number, single number, minimum spanning tree weight, integer square root, all subsets, valid anagram and count inversions) were built with wording free of algorithm words, hidden tests checked by two independent oracles, three to six references, mutants and excluded brute force methods, and gated labellers; all seven gated, four after one revision round, and the 15-program blind audits of base labels agreed at 0.93 to 1.0. Because the base model was 46% to 61% off task under the chat template, its repertoire was raised to N = 200 per unit before any commit. Each unit's beta, base runner-up, base composition and rivals were hash-chained before its first push; then came 8 directions at alpha 1 and 2, plan noise and temperature 1.3.

## 5.7 Plan noise against text-level plan samplers, decoding at matched departure, and the literal cell (Qwen3-8B)

**Why.** The positioning audit of iteration 4 found that the price comparison lacked its strongest competitors: text-level plan samplers, which diversify code by sampling a plan before the program [73, 74], and a decoding baseline matched to plan noise's own departure from the twin, the baseline under which an ICLR 2027 submission (OpenReview oag3wgNLRh) found activation steering no better than ordinary decoding. The review also asked for the literal cell of the request. This experiment [ARTIFACT:art_jR6Pyy3W9xum] ran both.

**The literal cell never changes the algorithm** (Table 206). On the shortest path task with thinking on, top-k 10 and the same 20 token seeds as the iteration-4 thinking arm, moving the temperature over 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 changed the final program's algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds (one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound 0.14), and the first approach named in the thinking changed in 0 of 20. All 100 traces completed, every final program was heap-based Dijkstra, and every trace named Dijkstra first. Temperature changed the tokens: a repeat at temperature 0.7 was byte-identical on only 4 of 20 traces while the labels agreed on 20 of 20 (median common prefix 309.5 tokens), and paired with the top-p 1 traces of iteration 4 at the same seed and temperature the labels agreed on 100 of 100 pairs although the traces shared a median of only 34 tokens. A judge agreed with the first-approach lexicon on 19 of 19 audited traces. With this cell, question 1a-c of the request is answered under every sampler the run used: with thinking off at top-k 10 (Table 76), with thinking off and on at top-p 1 (Section 4.5), and with thinking on at top-k 10 here.

**Design of the knob comparison.** Every knob ran in one HF bf16 engine with exact inverse-CDF common random numbers, so all arms of a slot shared the uniform stream of the code stage, on all 15 existing tasks (N = 50 per cell on the five decisive tasks, 30 on the other ten). Plan noise drew a fresh isotropic direction per sample at the task-specification positions of blocks 12 to 23, prefill only, at alpha 1 and 2 ban-free units, under the twin frame and on the plain prompt. The text-level plan samplers used the twin's frame, with the twin's neutral sentence first: intent factored generation at the direction's (1.3, 0.7) and the paper's tuned (0.73, 0.60) temperatures [73]; a lite plan search (five observations, a random pair of them combined into a plan, then code) [74]; enumerate and pick, in which the model lists up to eight algorithms and an external random number picks one; and base intent, in which Qwen3-8B-Base writes the intent sentence and the instruct model the code. Decoding at matched departure applied a temperature to generated tokens 1 to 32, bisected per task so that its mean per-token KL from the twin equalled plan noise's own at each alpha, measured on prefixes used only for calibration. Prices came from a randomisation hull over the full simplex with 2,000 slot bootstraps that select the best mixture again inside every replicate. The committed rule calls the plan sampler comparison supported if the 5-point Hill-1 of plan noise is at least that of the best text sampler on at least 3 of the 5 decisive tasks.

**The plan sampler comparison is DISCONFIRMED** (Table 207) (ban-free unit and iteration-5 seeds; pending the 2x2 of Step K). In Table 207 the margin is the 5-point Hill-1 of plan noise minus that of the best text sampler. Plan noise matched or beat the best text sampler on 1 of the 5 decisive tasks, kth smallest (1.98 against 1.83 for enumerate and pick, P(plan noise at least best) 0.58, unresolved). On connected components, the shortest path task and two sum, base intent won (2.53, 1.45 and 1.61 against 1.09, 1.18 and 1.17), and on the grid task nothing moved much. The mean margin is -0.40 (95% interval -0.70 to -0.24), and only 1.8% of bootstrap replicates reach three wins. Every sensitivity keeps the verdict except one (Table 209): with the multistage samplers dropped (they were padded on the left), intent factored generation is the only text sampler left and plan noise beats it on 4 of 5 tasks, so the disconfirmation rests on base intent and on enumerate and pick. On the ten other tasks (Table 208) plan noise moved only cycle detection and first and last position, while text samplers moved substring search, find duplicate, Fibonacci, longest increasing subsequence, top-k frequent and first and last position. Two prompt knobs outside the text-sampler set also beat plan noise where it was strongest: the novelty instruction on kth smallest (2.03) and the semantic seed on the shortest path task (2.12). The plan's one allowed wording revision was used after the first format pilot failed (the model wrote code at once), the committed drop order fired after stage 100 and the dropped cells were restored when the queue finished early, and cells with fewer than 30 (decisive) or 15 (other) programs were excluded from hulls, a rule decided after a dry run that favours plan noise on kth smallest. ## 5.8 The second family: gemma-3-4b-pt against gemma-3-4b-it

**Why.** The Gemma replication asked whether the account replicates in a second family, with the base repertoire of gemma-3-4b-pt committed before a fresh, never-run push population was applied to gemma-3-4b-it [76]. Gemma's iteration-4 push outcomes were seen, so this experiment [ARTIFACT:art_hG0QPiaIPNhP] is a replication on fresh directions and samples, not a held-out confirmation.

**Design.** Both models ran in bf16 on one 23 GB NVIDIA GPU, one at a time. A fresh it twin (N = 50 per task) fixed each task's default under the iteration-5 rule; the grid twin now gave DFS on 30 of 40 correct programs, so every one of the 15 tasks had a default. The pt model wrote 100 programs under the it chat template on the same token ids and 50 in plain completion of a `def solve(...)` stub. Under the chat template 91% of its programs had no usable code and only 10 of 1,500 passed, so the preregistered chat validity gate failed, both formats were pooled, and every unit fell under the low-correct rule: beta, the runner-up and the landing forecast come from valid attempts, not correct programs. These were committed by hash before 16 never-run isotropic directions (seeds 52001 to 52016) were applied at alpha 1 and 2 to the task-specification positions of blocks 11 to 22 on the outlier-excluded ban-free unit. A transplant from pt into it at lambda 1 then ran on the seven tasks diverse in the base with a matched random control, a borrowed shift and a transplant at the read position on the same slots, and on three controls collapsed in the base.

**In Gemma the movability half is inconclusive and the landing half passes** (Table 214). Spearman between beta and the escape fraction is 0.42 (one-sided permutation p 0.060, n = 15), against a bar of 0.5 at p below 0.01; 2 of 3 tasks collapsed in the base are immovable against a bar of 80%; and beta is ahead of no rival, with the twin modal share (0.67) and the novelty instruction (0.64) tracking movability better (Table 215). The direction is the predicted one: 6 of 7 tasks diverse in the base are movable against 2 of 8 others (one-sided Fisher p 0.032, not registered). The partial Spearman given catalogue size and the forced can count is 0.41 (0.45 given catalogue size alone), and the fresh population agrees with iteration 4's movability on 13 of 15 tasks (8 movable now, 6 then). No sensitivity meets the preregistered bar (Table 216); beta from the chat template alone reaches 0.62 (p 0.0095), but that arm is 91% unusable output, and beta from correct programs only reaches 0.27. The pt runner-up equals the modal landing of confirmed escapes in 5 of 7 events (hit rate 0.71 against a mean chance of 0.30; exact Poisson-binomial p 0.025), and the pt composition beats iteration 4's association forecast by 1.50 nats per event (exact Wilcoxon p 0.023) and AST proximity by 0.51 (Table 217). The two misses are kth smallest (landing size-k heap, runner-up quickselect) and connected components (landing union find, pooled runner-up BFS; union find is the runner-up under the chat template alone).

**The transplant moves two of seven tasks diverse in the base** (Table 218). Every transplanted program stayed valid (pass ratio 0.98 to 1.00). Substring search moved from the naive scan to the built-in find in 40 of 50 programs (twin 6 of 50), and first and last position from the linear scan to binary search in 39 of 50 (twin 4 of 50); both land on the pt runner-up. The other five tasks diverse in the base stayed at their default. The two that moved are exactly the tasks diverse in the base whose it twin already writes the pt runner-up 8% to 12% of the time, so the transplant amplified an existing minority mode and did not install an absent one. The pt-minus-it difference at the task-specification positions is large (median 5.2 ban-free units, 4.7 to 5.8 across blocks), above the dose at which random noise broke programs in iteration 4, and five massive channels carry 86% of its squared norm at block 11, falling to 31% to 36% by blocks 21 and 22. Random controls and borrowed shifts that copy the massive-channel move and match the remaining norm broke most programs (pass ratio 0.16 to 0.50 and 0 to 0.22), so the random comparison is confounded by norm and the borrowed shift is itself broken: what the controls show is that the coherent pt content is benign where an equally large random displacement or borrowed shift is destructive. The transplant at the read position and the three controls collapsed in the base stayed within 0.05 of the twin (Table 219); on nonoverlapping intervals the transplant halved the pass rate without moving the algorithm.

Three flags summarise the search. The transplant flag, a paper that writes base-model hidden states into its tuned descendant and reports a change in output diversity, did not fire, narrowly: cross-patching writes base upstream states into a descendant's late stack but measures a next-token margin [91], and earlier patching work measured backdoor removal [89], factual recall [90] or entity tracking [88]; the goal of restoring diversity is published at the weight level, by restoring layer intervals to pretrained weights [92] or merging aligned lower layers with base upper layers [93], and at the token level [94]. The transplant may not be called first. The forecast flag, a forecast from the base model of where post-training narrows, partly fired: forecasts per prompt at training time exist, and one finds that base pass rate and likelihood explain only 0.30 and 0.24 of the explainable variance in post-training gains [99]; inference-time movability and the identity of the landing remain open. The audit recommends further baselines for any later report: weight interpolation between Qwen3-8B-Base and Qwen3-8B [102], layer restoration and splicing at the transplant's block ranges [92, 93], token routing between base and aligned models [94], arithmetic on the logits of base and tuned models, and template control for every base minus instruct contrast [103].
