## 5.10 Comparisons across this iteration's experiments

**The base repertoire against movability: screen, confirmation and second family.** The same quantity, beta against the escape fraction, was measured five ways in this iteration, and the answer depends on which tasks enter. On the 15 existing tasks, with the beta of Step 1 and the escape fractions of iteration 4, Spearman is 0.78 to 0.79; with this iteration's own bf16 escape fractions it is 0.59; on the new tasks it is -0.03 in panel A, 0.21 in panel B and 0.15 pooled; in Gemma it is 0.42. The screen correlation is carried by many tasks with low beta that never move, while on new tasks those diverse in the base that never move are common: count primes and valid anagram (beta 0.81 each), median of two sorted lists (0.71), jump game (0.47), all subsets (0.37) and longest common prefix (0.30). The figure, corrected in iteration 6, plots both sets like for like under bf16: the existing tasks at their bf16 escape fraction under the ban-free unit (filled; the 8-bit screen value as an open ghost marker joined by a segment) and the new units, both at iteration 5's ban-free unit. Existing tasks (n 15): Spearman 0.59, one-sided permutation p 0.010, Bonett-Wright 95% [0.06, 0.86]; with the 8-bit screen E instead 0.79. New units (n 13): 0.15, p 0.315, [-0.44, 0.65]; with the two reserve units 0.01. Pooled bf16 (n 28): 0.48, p 0.005. The existing-task correlation is carried by many tasks with low beta that never move; open markers show the 8-bit screen value of each existing task. Per set, the base runner-up named the push landing 5 of 5 on the 8-bit screen, 1 of 2 on the bf16 remeasurement of existing tasks, 3 of 3 in panel A, 3 of 4 in panel B and 5 of 7 in Gemma (17 of 21, Poisson-binomial p 5.8e-07); the bf16 remeasurement's kth smallest and connected components events were missing from the earlier count of 16 of 19 (kth smallest a miss: landing size-k heap against runner-up quickselect; connected components a hit). On the 8 held-out events where the instruct twin wrote no correct program off the default the base runner-up named 5 (p 0.053; Qwen3-8B 3 of 4, p 0.052; Gemma 2 of 4, p 0.422) (iteration-6 correction).

**Movability depends on the engine and the unit.** Table 222 sets the existing tasks' movability side by side across the measurements of iterations 4 and 5. Under iteration 4's 8-bit engine and the ban unit, six tasks were movable; under this iteration's bf16 engine and the ban-free unit, only kth smallest and connected components escape with 8 fixed directions, and per-sample plan noise moves more than 10% of programs off the default only on kth smallest (0.28 at alpha 2). On the shortest path task, per-sample plan noise moved 26% of all samples at alpha 1 in iteration 4 (13 of 50 valid attempts off the default; 9 of 43 correct programs) and 0 of 50 correct programs at alpha 1 here (2 of 47 at alpha 2, 1.67 8-bit ban units by the ratio of mean norms and 1.78 by the mean ratio). A dose-bracketed comparison (iteration 6) sets the bf16 alpha-2 cell, which delivers more than the 1.00 ban unit of the 8-bit alpha-1 cell under either dose definition, against the 8-bit alpha-1 cell: a lower bf16 share there cannot be a dose shortfall. By the rule fixed before computing, connected components and shortest path did not replicate in bf16 at the population level (correct-only bracket one-sided Fisher p kth smallest 0.588, connected components 0.056, shortest path 0.017, two sum 1.000, grid 0.732); kth smallest: not established; two sum: not established (no 8-bit effect of at least 10% at alpha of 2 or less to replicate); grid: not established; find duplicate: not established (no 8-bit effect of at least 10% at alpha of 2 or less to replicate). This rules out the dose unit, not the CRN slots, the labels or the kernels (iteration-6 correction; record audit, Table 228). The engine control of Section 6.3 then tested the numerics directly: at iteration 4's own absolute displacement, direction seeds and slots, the bf16 engine reproduces the 8-bit rows (per-sample plan noise at alpha 2: connected components 25 of 50 valid attempts off the default under bf16 against 30 of 50 under the 8-bit engine; shortest path 22 of 50 under both), so the non-replication tagged here belongs to iteration 5's ban-free unit and direction seeds, not to the bf16 numerics. The engine checks pushed two fixed escaping directions at the ban unit in both engines and agreed within or near the resampling null (shortest path: Dijkstra 31 and Bellman-Ford/SPFA 19 in bf16 against 26 and 24 in the 8-bit engine). Those two directions therefore do not explain the difference, and its cause is not established here. *(Correction, iteration 6: the engine control of Section 6.3 establishes that the cause is not the bf16 numerics. At the absolute unit, direction seeds and slots of iteration 4 itself, bf16 escapes on almost the same directions as the 8-bit engine (connected components 26 of 40 against 29 of 40; shortest path 6 of 40 against 8 of 40). The shrinkage belongs to the ban-free unit of iteration 5 or its direction seeds, and the heading should read that movability depends on the unit and the direction draw.)* Movability is therefore a property of a task under a given engine, unit and direction population, and the confirmation panels measured it under bf16 and the ban-free unit only.

## 5.12 What the next iteration takes from this one

The narrowed repertoire account split in two. Its landing half held descriptively in both families and on unseen tasks (5 of 5 on the 8-bit screen, 1 of 2 on the bf16 remeasurement of existing tasks, 3 of 3 in panel A, 3 of 4 in panel B and 5 of 7 in Gemma (17 of 21, Poisson-binomial p 5.8e-07)), but it is not yet separated from the instruct twin's own minority (on the 8 held-out events where the instruct twin wrote no correct program off the default the base runner-up named 5 (p 0.053; Qwen3-8B 3 of 4, p 0.052; Gemma 2 of 4, p 0.422); iteration-6 correction): when a nudge moves the instruct model, it moves it to the algorithm the base model writes next, and a forecast built from base samples, before any push, names that landing better than the model's stated alternative. Its movability half failed on unseen tasks: a base model that writes many algorithms does not mark a task the instruct model can be nudged off, and its states, written into the instruct prefill, reopen the choice on one task in five. The base repertoire marks where a nudge can lead, not whether it can lead anywhere.

The open question is therefore what makes a task diverse in the base immovable. Count primes and valid anagram (beta 0.81 each) never moved, while trapped rain water (0.23) did. Two leads came out of this iteration's data. In panel A the three units that moved had an alternative at least twice as fast as the default and the three that did not had none, although median of two sorted lists broke the pattern. And in the transplant experiment early blocks 0 to 11 moved kth smallest and connected components more than the main band, which suggests the narrowing sits at least partly upstream of blocks 12 to 23. The positioning audit names the baselines a further test needs: weight interpolation between the base and instruct models, layer restoration at the transplant's block ranges, and token-level base and aligned collaboration [92, 93, 94, 102]. Base intent, which beat plan noise on three of five tasks, is the strongest practical knob the run has priced, and it is itself a form of that collaboration at the level of sentences. Finally, movability has to be measured under the engine and unit at which it will be used: the six screen-movable tasks of iteration 4 shrank to two under bf16 and the ban-free unit, for reasons this iteration did not establish. *(Iteration-6 correction: a dose-bracketed contrast rules out a scalar dose shortfall on connected components and shortest path, and the engine control rules out the bf16 numerics, since at iteration 4's absolute unit and seeds bf16 reproduces the 8-bit escapes (Section 6.3). What remains is the per-position and per-block profile of the ban-free unit, or the direction seeds; every verdict that rests on bf16 plan noise or escape fractions at the ban-free unit is conditional on that design.)*

**The hypothesis update.** The update turned from the outside of the model to its inside. Five iterations had mapped what moves the algorithm from outside: a ban, a meaningful hint, a plan sentence written by the base model, a list-then-pick step. None had located where the model holds its choice. The update proposed one concrete answer, which it called the plan-variable account. While the model reads the task, it computes a small hidden variable that says which algorithm to write. We call this variable the *plan*. On tasks where a ban acts through the prompt states (shortest path, kth smallest, connected components) the plan sits in the residual stream at the task-specification positions; on tasks where generated tokens read the ban directly (two sum, find duplicate) it sits at the first generated tokens. Exchanging a few of its dimensions between two prompts should switch the algorithm the model writes, with correct code. Random noise should change the algorithm only through the part of it that falls inside the plan, which would explain why most random directions do nothing; temperature should never touch it.

The update tested the account with the instruments the request names and the run had not yet used. An *interchange intervention* replaces a component's activations under one input with those under another and measures the change in output. *Distributed alignment search* (DAS) fits an orthonormal low-rank subspace in which such an exchange reproduces a counterfactual behaviour [110, 111]. A *natural language autoencoder* (NLA) pairs an activation verbalizer, which writes a text explanation of a residual-stream state, with an activation reconstructor, which maps text back to a state; released checkpoints exist for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [124] at layer 20, not for Qwen3-8B. Gemma Scope 2, released in December 2025, provides JumpReLU sparse autoencoders [114] and transcoders trained on gemma-3-4b-it itself, the successor of the Gemma Scope release for Gemma 2 [113], so no transfer test from a base model is needed.

Eleven claims were preregistered, each with a rule committed by sha256 before its first decisive sample. We call them by their content rather than by their codes: the engine claim, the localization claim, the mediation claim, the discreteness claim, the token claim, the resampling claim, the verbal readout claim, the feature claim, the site rerun, the landing contest and the novelty count.

- *The engine claim* (primary): on connected components and shortest path, the same 40 directions and common-random-number slots at the same absolute displacement under four numerics. Activation rounding is the cause if the escape fraction under bf16 weights with 8-bit floating-point activations (W16A8) exceeds bf16 by at least 0.2, the full 8-bit engine (W8A8) matches W16A8 within 0.1 and 8-bit floating-point weights with bf16 activations (W8A16) match bf16 within 0.1, on both tasks. The result is called not reproduced if W8A8 minus bf16 is below 0.1.
- *The localization claim* (primary). Stage A, with no training: exchanging the full residual states of the ban prompt into the neutral twin transfers the ban's substitute at a transfer share of at least 0.5 on at least two of shortest path, kth smallest and connected components, at a pass rate of at least 0.8 times the twin's, and at most 0.2 on two sum and find duplicate. Stage B: DAS at one layer recovers at least 0.8 of the full-state transfer at a rank of 16 or less on held-out templates.
- *The mediation claim* (primary): the energy that a random direction puts into the fitted plan subspace predicts which directions switch the algorithm (Spearman at least 0.5).
- *The discreteness claim*, *the token claim* (temperature leaves the plan coordinate flat while state noise at generated tokens beats temperature at matched per-token KL) and *the resampling claim* (resampling the plan as a diversity knob) (secondary).
- *The verbal readout claim* (secondary): the NLA names the substitute of a ban before any code is written at a rate at least 0.3 above a judge reading the visible text; editing the explanation's algorithm phrase and reconstructing transfers the algorithm by at least 0.2.
- *The feature claim* (secondary): in Gemma's natural BFS against DFS split on the grid task, Gemma Scope 2 features decode the upcoming algorithm at least 0.10 balanced accuracy above a classifier on the visible text, and steer at least as well as a difference-in-means direction at matched pass.
- *The site rerun* (secondary): the iteration-4 noise-site comparison in bf16; the prefill-site claim survives if the task-specification site beats the read position and the condition sentence at matched downstream displacement on at least one task, and is withdrawn otherwise.
- *The landing contest* (secondary): the base runner-up against the instruct twin's own teacher-forced ranking of algorithm openings, on every recorded push-landing event.
- *The novelty count* (secondary).

**The strategy.** Seven artifacts were planned (Table 225). One evaluation on CPU, which we call the record audit, repaired the record from rows on disk and ran the second novelty adjudication. An experiment we call the engine control ran the four numerics on a 16 GB RTX 2000 Ada, an Ada-generation card with the 8-bit floating-point tensor cores that the 8-bit engine needs. A bf16 experiment, which we call the exchange and site experiment, ran the Stage A exchanges, the site rerun, state noise against matched temperature, the top-five push and the landing contest. Gemma and the NLA each received their own experiment, which we call the Gemma feature experiment and the NLA experiment, and a research artifact, which we call the positioning audit, searched the literature for each claim. ### 6.2.2 Engine and dose

## 6.3 The engine control: are the random-push escapes a property of the model or of 8-bit rounding?

**Why.** The engine claim was the primary test of the iteration, because its answer decides which internal results of iteration 4 belong to Qwen3-8B. The review had pointed at a plausible mechanism without establishing it: a displacement changes the per-token absmax of each linear input, so under dynamic per-token 8-bit floating-point scaling it changes the rounding of every downstream activation, and the engine adds its own perturbation to the push. The 8-bit floating-point format in question is e4m3, with a maximum of 448 [115]. The engine control [ARTIFACT:art_lpQalcAXMGr1] separated weight rounding from activation rounding by running iteration 4's own design under four numerics, all built from one bf16 snapshot of Qwen3-8B (Table 235).

**Table 235.** The four numerics of the engine control.

| Engine | Weights | Activations | Role |
|-|-|-|-|
| W8A8 | e4m3, per-output-channel absmax / 448 | e4m3, per-token absmax / 448 | iteration 4's engine (native 8-bit floating-point matrix multiply) |
| W8A16 | e4m3, the same codes | bf16 | weight rounding only |
| W16A8 | bf16 | e4m3, fake-quantised per token | activation rounding only |
| bf16 | bf16 | bf16 | full-precision reference |

**Design.** Everything except the numerics was held fixed: the 40 direction files of iteration 4 (seeds 9101 to 9140, checked bitwise), the absolute displacement per block and position at blocks 12 to 23 and the task-specification positions (the bench unit of iteration 4), the twin prompts, the common-random-number slots and uniforms, the stop rule, a 1,024-token cap, one labeller version (that of iteration 4 plus the iteration-5 re-gate that reads array-based Dijkstra correctly) applied to every row, and the two-stage escape rule of iteration 4, with each engine scored against its own twin. ## 6.4 Where a ban and an instruction are carried, and where noise acts, in bf16 (Qwen3-8B)

**Why.** The localization claim predicted, from the route classes of iterations 2 and 3, where the substitute of a ban is carried: in the task-specification states on the prompt-route tasks, at the condition span on the direct-route tasks. Stage A tests that prediction without any training, by moving the states themselves. The same experiment [ARTIFACT:art_rMlbrjVB1c__] reran the iteration-4 noise-site comparison in bf16, set state noise at generated tokens against a temperature matched on per-token KL, applied the top-five plan push, and ran the landing contest. Everything ran in one bf16 engine with exact common random numbers on a 16 GB card, with the input embedding table kept in CPU memory; per-slot twin labels agreed with iteration 5's bf16 engine on 0.975 of slots for kth smallest and shortest path and 1.00 for the other tasks. Seven commitments formed an unbroken sha256 chain, and a standard-library script re-derived every headline from raw rows (295 checks, 0 mismatches) while a placebo version of each test failed.

### 6.4.1 Stage A: full-state exchange of the ban

We call a *full-state exchange* the replacement, in the forward pass of the neutral twin, of the residual states at a set of positions and blocks by the states the full ban prompt produces at the same positions; because the twin and the ban have identical token ids from the task text on, every task-specification position aligns. The exchanges covered four block bands at the task-specification positions (0 to 11, 12 to 23, 24 to 35, 0 to 35), a splice of the key-value cache of the condition span (the direct route), and the read position at all 36 blocks. The controls were the twin, a matched-norm random exchange (the state of the twin plus a fresh random direction scaled to the displacement that the ban itself causes per slot, block and position), a placebo that takes a second neutral twin as the source, and an identity exchange. The outcome, as committed before sampling (commit0: "share(label == Y | cell) - share(label == Y | TWIN), all samples (invalid rows count as not-Y)"), is the *Y share*: the share of all attempted programs labelled Y, invalid rows counting as not-Y; the *transfer* of a cell is that share minus the twin's; a cell counts only if its pass rate is at least 0.8 times the twin's (commit0: "pass_X / pass_TWIN (validity gate >= 0.8)"); and its *recovery* is the transfer divided by that of the full ban. The *correct Y* column added to Tables 244 to 250 counts programs labelled Y that pass every hidden test, because an attempted share counts broken programs as Y: on the grid task the exchange at blocks 0-35 has 14 attempts labelled DFS but 3 correct DFS programs. Each cell has N = 30 on paired slots. Tables 244 to 249 give every cell on the six tasks. (iteration-7 correction)

The prediction held where the route data said it should, and failed at one task where they said it should not. On shortest path, exchanging the full ban's task-specification states at all blocks into the twin turns 24 of 30 slots from Dijkstra to Bellman-Ford/SPFA (24 of 30 attempts, 21 of 30 correct programs; transfer 0.80, McNemar 24:0, Holm p 7e-7, pass ratio 0.90), while the condition-span splice and the read-position exchange transfer nothing. Blocks 12 to 23 alone carry 0.60 (18 of 30 attempts, 11 of 30 correct programs, at a pass ratio of 0.73, below the 0.8 gate) and blocks 24 to 35 alone 0.37 (11 of 30 attempts, 11 of 30 correct programs); blocks 0 to 11 carry none. On kth smallest the same exchange transfers 0.57 to quickselect (17 of 30 attempts, 16 of 30 correct programs) with every slot leaving the full sort, blocks 0 to 11 alone already transfer 0.40 (12 of 30 attempts, 12 of 30 correct programs), and here the condition span also carries the ban (0.93; 28 of 30 attempts, 25 of 30 correct programs). On connected components every slot leaves union find under the exchange at blocks 12 to 23 or 0 to 35 (off-default transfer 1.00), but only 0.37 to 0.47 land on the ban's BFS (11 and 14 of 30 attempts, 11 and 14 of 30 correct programs) and the rest on DFS. On the grid task, whose route was carried by the prompt states in likelihood and mixed in behaviour, the exchange at all blocks transfers 0.47 toward DFS (14 of 30 attempts, 3 of 30 correct programs, pass ratio 0.59, below the 0.8 gate) and the condition-span splice 0.33 (10 of 30 attempts, 7 of 30 correct programs, pass ratio 0.89), so each carries part of the ban in attempts and only the splice passes the committed validity gate. On the direct-route tasks the condition-span splice alone reproduces the ban (two sum 1.00, 30 of 30 attempts, 30 of 30 correct programs; find duplicate 0.90, 27 of 30 attempts, 26 of 30 correct programs), as predicted, but on two sum the task-specification states also transfer brute force at 0.43 (13 of 30 attempts, 13 of 30 correct programs), above the predicted ceiling of 0.2. The committed verdict is therefore not supported. The secondary predictions hold: the condition span carries at least 0.5 on the direct-route tasks and at most 0.2 on shortest path, the read position carries at most 0.2 everywhere (it carries 0.00 on all six tasks), the placebo moves at most 0.03, and the exchange beats the matched-norm random exchange where it transfers (shortest path 23:0, kth smallest 16:2, connected components 11:0, on attempted Y as preregistered); counted on correct Y instead, a post-hoc contrast added in iteration 7, the same pairs give 21:0 (exact p 9.5e-07), 15:2 (p 2.3e-03) and 11:0 (p 9.8e-04). The ban's information, not the size of the perturbation, is what moves the algorithm. (iteration-7 correction)

### 6.4.2 Where noise acts, in bf16

The site rerun repeated iteration 4's grid on kth smallest and connected components in bf16, at the ban-free unit, with a fresh direction per sample, N = 30 per cell and alpha 1, 2, 4 and 8 (Tables 251 and 252). Noise at the task-specification positions moves the algorithm in bf16: on kth smallest blocks 12 to 23 reach a correct off-default share of 0.37 at alpha 2, and on connected components blocks 0 to 11 reach 0.33 at alpha 4. The read position, the condition span and the late blocks barely move it below alpha 8. On kth smallest the plan site (the task-specification states at blocks 12 to 23, as in iteration 4) beats the read position in paired slots 24:5 (exact p 5.5e-4) and the condition span 22:0, and a Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio [129] within quintiles of the downstream displacement is 4.6 [1.9, 11.3]. Connected components shows a weaker picture: its plan site moves only 0.07 at alpha 2 and 0.17 at alpha 4, the early blocks beat it (4:18, p 0.004), and the read position starts moving at alpha 8 (0.30).

The committed rule fitted a Firth logistic regression [125] of a correct off-default program on site indicators and the log displacements, so that sites are compared at matched downstream displacement (Tables 253 and 254). It returned the verdict withdrawn, for two reasons. The raw condition-span arm never reaches the plan site's downstream displacement, so it has no common support and its energy-matched arm stood in; and at alpha 8 every plan-site program failed (pass 0.00) while the read position began to move, which erases the read-position contrast in the preregistered model. A post-hoc sensitivity restricted to alpha of 4 or less (before breakage) puts the read position clearly below the plan site on both tasks: beta -3.76 (profile interval [-7.29, -0.47], cluster bootstrap [-8.18, -1.40]) on kth smallest and -4.98 ([-9.77, -0.89]; [-11.48, -1.53]) on connected components. The prefill-site claim is therefore withdrawn as preregistered. Post hoc (alpha of at most 4) the read position is below the task-specification site on both tasks; the condition-span clause fails post hoc as well (beta -1.70 [-3.96, 0.42] on kth smallest; -0.56 [-4.93, 2.91] on connected components, cluster bootstrap; profile intervals [-6.82, 1.16] and [-6.15, 3.41]), so the site of the choice remains open, as the artifact concludes; its rule label reads 'WITHDRAWN as FP8-specific: the site of the choice is open'. The 'FP8-specific' half of that label cannot apply: Section 6.3 shows that bf16 reproduces the escapes direction by direction (Spearman 0.96 and 0.87) and that activation rounding adds nothing, so the withdrawal comes from the missing common support and the breakage at alpha 8 in bf16, not from the engine. Noise sites and Stage A agree on the band on kth smallest and disagree on connected components (Table 254b): there noise moves the algorithm most at blocks 0 to 11 (mean 0.19 over alpha 1 to 4 against 0.08 at blocks 12 to 23; 0.33 correct off-default at alpha 4; coefficient +2.51 [1.39, 3.80] against the plan site; paired flips 4:18, p 0.004, between the plan site and blocks 0-11), while the exchange transfers BFS at blocks 12 to 23. The removal of the default there is depth-redundant: the exchange at blocks 0-11 alone takes 0.87 of attempts off union find and at blocks 24-35 alone 0.63. (iteration-7 correction)

### 6.4.4 The top-five push in bf16

On the grid task, iteration 4's top-five direction (from the mean of the five banned centroids toward the mean of the survivors) was applied at the plan site at alpha 1, 2, 4 and 8 (Table 256). At doses of 1 to 8 ban units, which overshoot the forced-prompt manifold, the push breaks programs before it moves the algorithm; an in-manifold dose was not tried: the pass rate falls from 0.67 at alpha 1 to 0.30, 0.03 and 0.00, with at most one correct program other than BFS per cell, so the landing test could not be computed. Projected onto the plane of the first two principal components of the ten forced-prompt centroids (36% and 25% of their variance), the push leaves the forced-prompt manifold: already at alpha 1 it moves farther along the first component than the whole spread of the ten centroids (the four alpha-1 points move from a twin mean of +0.09 to -0.44 on PC1, against centroids spread from -0.098 to +0.144). The prompt version of the top-five ban moves the task-specification states from below the centroid cloud into it, between the banned DFS and greedy best-first centroids and the three surviving centroids (bidirectional BFS and two variants of A*), and its behaviour stays inside the banned set (BFS 25, DFS 23 of 50; avoidance 0.00). ### 6.4.5 Who forecasts the landing

The landing contest scored, on the 21 recorded push-landing events, three forecasts: the base runner-up, the most frequent algorithm other than the default in the instruct twin itself (defined on 7 events), and a teacher-forced ranking of the openings of the catalogue algorithms by the instruct twin, the log-mean-exp likelihood of the first 48 tokens of each algorithm over its reference and forced programs, which we call the opening ranking (Table 257). The base runner-up named 17 of 21 landings and the opening ranking 10. On the 9 events where they disagree the base runner-up wins 8:1 (exact one-sided sign test p 0.020), and its mean log score is higher by 1.62 nats (Wilcoxon p 0.032). Where the twin wrote an alternative, its own minority does as well as the base runner-up (6 of 7; log-score difference 0.02, p 0.69). The comparison is retrospective, because the landings were known when the rule was frozen, and the opening ranking rests on 1 to 6 programs per algorithm. The base model adds information beyond the ranking of openings by the instruct model itself; it does not add information beyond the minority algorithm of the twin where one exists.

## 6.5 Gemma: a one-token fork, and Gemma Scope 2 features against difference in means

**Why Gemma.** Asked one and the same grid-path prompt, gemma-3-4b-it [76] writes DFS about 70% of the time and BFS about 30%, so it offers what Qwen3-8B never does: the request's BFS-against-DFS contrast inside one prompt, with no ban or instruction to confound it. Gemma Scope 2 provides sparse autoencoders on the residual stream after each block, trained on this instruct model, so the feature claim needs no transfer test. Qwen-3 transcoders for circuit tracing exist as well [123], but they would have to study a choice Qwen3-8B does not make naturally. The experiment [ARTIFACT:art_zNyBP6zieI5u] asked where the choice forks, whether it can be read from the internals beyond what the visible text already says, and whether the SAE features steer it better than plain baselines: a difference-in-means direction, the raw residual, random features, isotropic directions, DAS and prompting. It used the residual-stream SAEs at layers 9, 17, 22 and 29 (16k latents, at the release's medium sparsity), one 16 GB card and exact common random numbers, under two hash-chained commitments.

**Natural splits.** Over 200 samples per task, the grid prompt gave DFS 139 and BFS 61 (Wilson interval for DFS 0.63 to 0.75), with DFS on 134 of 172 correct programs (Table 258). The choice depends on the template: BFS takes 6 to 18 of 40 attempts per template. Substring search (naive 173, built-in find 27) and first and last position (linear scan 170, binary search 29) split as well. Labels agreed with iteration 5's Gemma rows on 0.94 of the grid slots and 1.00 of the substring slots.

**The plan is a single-token fork.** Prefix resampling with change-point detection, the method of forking-path analyses [30, 31], located the fork: 24 base paths, 16 prefix lengths, 8 continuations each and a refinement, 3,712 continuations in all, scored by a partial-code labeller that agreed with the full labeller on 200 of 200 programs. Every one of 12 BFS base paths had a significant change point with a rise of at least 0.4, at prefix lengths 16 to 36. In 177 of 200 programs the first 32 tokens are identical (the code fence, `def solve(grid, start, goal):`, `rows = len(grid)`, `cols = len(grid[0])` and an indent), and the next token decides (Table 260): ` visited` leads to DFS (BFS probability 0.011 over 1,409 continuations), while a blank line, `if`, `queue` or `q` lead to BFS (0.95 to 1.00). The first token that identifies the algorithm in code comes a median of 138 tokens after the fork (10th to 90th percentile 80 to 181). The fork index was chosen by the token class with the most mutual information with the outcome (0.62 bits at index 32), after the first median rule landed on a deterministic indentation token; the change was made before the second commitment.

*Executed but not reported until iteration 7.* The fork's unit test U6 failed mildly: continuations from the empty prefix give BFS 0.38 (73 of 192) against the natural 0.305 [0.245, 0.372] (outside the interval; exact binomial p 0.028 against 0.305), so the resampled continuations are slightly richer in BFS than the natural samples. The deviation log records what did not run (D12, verbatim): "Not run: U4 (clamp readback) and U5 (matched-norm realisation) as separate unit tests (the matched norm is imposed by construction in src/clamp.py and each edit's realised norm is logged per row); the clamp-cell overlay on the S11 generated-position panel; the T04 fork and the T04/R6 cross-prompt readouts (drop order); per-sample displacement at generated tokens 1-32 (prefill displacement at blocks 11-33 is logged)." **Readable beyond the text, at the fork, but not specifically through the SAE.** Within one prompt, decodability before the first identifying token is at ceiling for every method, the visible-text control included (balanced accuracy 1.00 at all four layers), so the SAE has no advantage there; at the fork itself the test is undefined, because 185 of 200 samples share their prefix with a sample of the other class. Across prompts, the experiment built 120 neutral prompt variants by changing nouns and measured each variant's fork log-odds of BFS, which we write y (mean -0.92 nats, SD 0.67; the sampled BFS share tracks it at Spearman 0.65 over 60 variants of 10 samples). A Lasso on layer-29 SAE codes at the fork position predicts held-out y with R-squared 0.66, against 0.18 for a text-only model (difference 0.49, 95% interval 0.26 to 0.65, permutation p 0.003), above the difference-in-means readout (0.34) and a 16-component PCA of the raw residual (0.56) (Table 261). That meets the preregistered bar. Two checks outside the preregistration qualify it: a tuned ridge on the raw layer-29 residual reaches 0.72, and ridge on the same SAE codes reaches at most 0.09. Beside the Lasso, the standardised ridge on the same layer-29 SAE codes reaches R-squared 0.15 against 0.086 for a template-plus-noun-norm control (delta 0.064, below the preregistered 0.10 bar); the unstandardised SAE ridge ranges from -0.76 to 0.06 across penalties while the raw ridge stays at 0.70 to 0.72, which is why the SAE advantage depends on the estimator. Moreover, a linear readout of the fork log-odds from the residual at the fork position is close to a next-token readout, so the raw-residual 0.72 shows that the next-token distribution is linearly encoded there, not that a plan is; no logit-lens control of matched capacity was run. At the task-specification positions, before any response token, the SAE codes do no better than the text (0.18). (iteration-7 correction)

**Steering: the features move the fork, difference in means moves it more, and edits toward BFS cost correctness.** We call an *SAE clamp* setting the k latents that best separate forced-BFS from forced-DFS prompts (input-selected) to their BFS-class mean at the fork position; output-scored latents are chosen instead by their attribution to the fork's logit difference, and the two sets of 20 share 2 latents. At the fork position of layer 22, edits at matched norm moved y by +4.04 nats for the difference-in-means direction, +1.78 for the SAE clamp of the top 20 input-selected latents, +0.51 for 20 random latents and +0.12 for an isotropic direction. Table 261b gives the whole dose-response sweep over the 120 prompt variants (11,280 measurements), at the fork and at the task-specification positions. In generation (N = 50 paired slots), the twin wrote BFS in 13 programs; the SAE clamp raised this to 30 (top 20 latents) and 36 (top 50), the difference-in-means edit at the same norm to 46 and 49, and random latents to 21 (Table 262). Edits toward BFS at the fork lowered the pass rate from 0.84 for the twin to 0.58 and 0.48 for the top-20 and top-50 SAE clamps and 0.32 and 0.16 for difference in means (0.60 to 0.78 for the other BFS-ward fork edits, 0.00 for the DAS interchange), except the SAE top-5 clamp (18 BFS of 50, pass 0.84), so the preregistered outcome, correct BFS programs, shows no significant effect anywhere after Holm correction, and no feature claim is made. The preregistered feature rule (SAE target-correct count at least the difference-in-means count, at a pass rate of at least 0.8 times the twin's) is also met by random latents at k = 50 (9 against 7, pass 0.76), so it cannot discriminate here. The informative comparisons are on attempted BFS, and they are descriptive: the SAE clamp beats the twin (17:0 and 23:0 discordant slots, p 1.5e-5 and 2.4e-7) and random latents (15:0, p 6.1e-5), and difference in means beats the SAE clamp at matched norm (16:0, p 3.1e-5). At matched effect on y rather than matched norm, difference in means and the SAE clamp shift the plan equally (32 against 30 BFS, p 0.50; 34 against 36, p 0.63) and difference in means keeps slightly more programs correct (13 against 9, 14 against 10). Edits at the task-specification positions do nothing (12 to 19 BFS against 13). Steering toward DFS works cleanly for both (SAE 47 of 50, difference in means 50 of 50, against 37 for the twin; pass 0.98 to 1.00). Difference-in-means steering of a code model's choice of language and library has shown the same trade-off, with overly strong interventions reducing output quality [130]. AxBench found simple baselines ahead of SAE steering [34], and a 2026 reanalysis puts SAEs close to AxBench's reference when latents are selected and labelled by a supervised pipeline [131]; here, at comparable norms, neither the input-selected nor the output-scored clamp reached the difference-in-means edit (Table 261b). **DAS moves the fork log-odds within the controls it had, and forcing it breaks the program.** DAS at the fork position of layer 22, with forced-BFS prompts as sources, moved held-out y by +8.8, +9.5 and +9.8 nats at ranks 1, 2 and 4, against -0.08 to +0.05 for random subspaces of the same rank (Table 263). The shuffled-source control was uninformative as built, because every source was a forced-BFS prompt. In generation the rank-4 interchange made 50 of 50 programs BFS and 0 of 50 passed. Stated within its controls, a rank-1 DAS subspace fitted on forced-BFS sources moves the held-out fork log-odds by 8.8 nats (random subspaces of the same rank -0.08 to +0.05); because every source was forced-BFS, the shuffled-source control is uninformative by construction (10.1 nats); no random-initialisation or target-shuffled control was run; and the rank-4 interchange gives BFS in 50 of 50 attempts with 0 of 50 programs passing, so this does not show that the choice is one-dimensional. With unrestricted alignment maps interchange accuracy reaches 100% even on randomly initialised language models (Sutter et al., Table 277 row 14), so the fit stays uninterpretable until those controls run; pushing hard costs correctness, as subspace interventions can when they leave the model's natural range [122]. The prohibition lands inside the banned region, not at its edge or on the opposite side. ## 6.6 The plan in words: a natural language autoencoder on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

**Why.** The request names NLA as an instrument, and the release of NLA checkpoints for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [124] made it possible to ask, in words, whether the residual stream states before the first code token say which algorithm will be written. The experiment [ARTIFACT:art_dbUtqBjT0tPf] read layer-20 states with the released verbalizer and reconstructor pair, judged the explanations blind, and tested an edit of the explanation as a steering vector. Published verbalizers of the same kind include LatentQA [117] and SelfIE [118], and a 2026 analysis of a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer found that only a small share of an explanation's specific claims are ones the reconstruction depends on [119]. Pre-registration was a sha256 chain of four commitments, each preceding its samples; the parts added after the committed nulls are marked exploratory.

**Behaviour.** Over eight tasks, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct defaults to BFS, Dijkstra (0.88), a hash map (0.98), a hash set (0.71), DFS for connected components (0.62, where Qwen3-8B writes union find), the naive scan and binary search; kth smallest has no default (quickselect 0.40, size-k heap 0.34) and failed the style re-gate. The model mostly ignores bans (Table 267). Only two sum gave a substitute (brute force in 32 of 46 correct programs). On connected components a ban of DFS raised DFS from 29 to 43 correct programs, with 15 paired slots flipping from union find to DFS, the rebound that naming a forbidden concept can cause [7, 53]. Every one of the 70 programs written under the fourth template attempted the banned default. The shortest path semantic seed barely moved the model (Dijkstra 28, Bellman-Ford 6, against 38 and 5 for the twin). The labellers recognised 51 of 51 references, and the style re-gate passed on 7 of 8 tasks against two blind code judges.

**The NLA never names the planned algorithm before the code.** Two blind judges from different families (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite and Mistral Small 3.2, both scoring 1.00 on calibration; a third model resolved 1,064 disagreements) mapped each of 6,180 explanations to a catalogue algorithm or to none named (Table 269). Every preregistered readout at the end-of-prompt positions is exactly zero (Table 270). On ban prompts, explanations named the substitute in 0 of 16 states (only two sum had a substitute, so this test is underpowered); on twin prompts they named the default in 0 of 112, as did the text-only reader; on ban failures they named the default the model still writes in 0 of 96. The positive control failed too: on forced `Implement Y` prompts the explanations called Y planned in 0 of 7 tasks, while the text-only reader did so on all of them, and they mentioned the algorithm named in the prompt in 0.7% of cases. The explanations describe the local format line, such as a request for no explanation or a Python code block to follow, and confabulate the task (Fibonacci, medians, prime numbers); 4,733 of 5,700 judged explanations name no algorithm at all. At generated tokens the NLA sometimes names the realised algorithm before the visible text identifies it (up to 0.28 at token 8 under the ban), but an outside reader who sees only the prompt and prefix predicts the realised algorithm better, per sample (0.25 against 0.07; exact McNemar 20:88, p 2e-11 when the 364 units are treated as independent). The units are nested in 104 samples and 5 task clusters: the task-cluster bootstrap interval of the difference is [-0.35, 0.02], with one unit per sample (the first in position order, 104 samples) the contrast is 0:25 (exact p 6.0e-08), a median over 2,000 draws of one random unit per sample of 4:29 (p 1.9e-05; 1.00 of draws below 0.05), a sign test on the per-sample differences 12:38 (p 3.1e-04) and a Durkalski-adjusted McNemar with samples as clusters p 6.5e-05. The samples share 5 task clusters, and with 5 clusters no cluster-level test can reach a two-sided p below 0.0625, so the evidence at the task level is inconclusive whatever the sample-level p. **The information is local and fades within a sentence (exploratory).** To tell an instrument limit from information that fades along the prompt, the same NLA and judges read states at the token that names the algorithm inside the condition sentence and at the final period of that sentence (220 states, 660 explanations; Table 271). At the name token the explanations mention the algorithm in 80% of forced and 89% of ban states, and they respect the negation: they call it planned in 48% of forced states and in 6% of ban states. Two to eight tokens later, at the end of the sentence, the mention rates fall to 27% and 6%, and about 170 tokens later, at the end of the prompt, to 0.7%. The null therefore says that the pre-code positions do not carry the algorithm choice in a form this NLA puts into words, not that the instrument is blind.

**At the generated-token site and large doses, the verbal edit steers two of four tasks (exploratory).** After the committed nulls, the experiment extended the doses and moved the edit to the read position plus generated tokens 1 to 64 (Tables 274 and 275). On find duplicate the edit at dose 8 (about 0.3 of the state norm at each position) raised Floyd cycle detection from 0.28 to 0.76 (25:1 over 50 paired slots), replicated on fresh slots (15 of 20, 13:0, p 2e-4), and beat a matched random push (28:1), an unrelated-word edit built the same way (12:1, p 0.003) and a norm-matched round trip (13:1, p 0.002); at dose 16 the programs broke (pass 0.37). On two sum brute force rose from 0 to 10 of 50 at dose 8 and to 23 of 30 at dose 16 with a pass rate of 0.90, while the random push never moved it. On connected components only the forced-state difference in means steered (union find 0.80 at dose 16, 15:1); on substring search nothing steered short of breaking the program. The prefill site stayed inert even at dose 16 or at the natural norm of the difference in means. Asking for the algorithm in the prompt remained the ceiling (forced adherence 0.90 to 1.00 on all four tasks), as the AxBench comparison of prompting and steering predicts [34]. The NLA paper itself reports that editing a plan explanation and steering at one token succeeds roughly half the time; this run's success on two of four tasks is of the same kind and is not a reliable control knob.

Three of the audit's flags bear on what this run may claim. No source localizes which algorithm a code model will write by interchange or DAS and validates it by scoring the generated programs, so that combination is open; the method itself is DAS. Editing an NLA explanation of a plan and steering with the reconstruction is published, so the NLA arm is a replication on a new object. Steering under quantization has been compared with full precision only for weight-only 8-bit integer and 4-bit NormalFloat quantization, with activations kept in 16-bit floating point [116]; no source found measures how dynamic per-token activation rounding changes the effect of random perturbations, which is the question the engine control answered, in the negative. The audit also recorded that community NLAs exist for Qwen3-8B at layer 24, that circuit-tracer ships Qwen-3 transcoders including 8B [123] (so the choice of Gemma for the feature claim needs its reason, which is the natural within-prompt split), and that Gemma Scope 2 dates from 22 December 2025 with instruct SAEs initialised from the pretrained ones.

## 6.8 Planned but not run

The seventh artifact of the strategy never existed. It was to fit DAS subspaces of rank 1 to 16 at one layer of the task-specification positions in bf16 Qwen3-8B on three training templates and confirm them on two held-out templates (Stage B of the localization claim), test whether a fresh random direction's energy in that subspace predicts its effect (the mediation claim), interpolate and extrapolate the plan coordinate between algorithms (the discreteness claim), measure the plan coordinate's variance across temperatures (the first half of the token claim), resample the plan per generation as a diversity knob (the resampling claim), and draw the request's manifold of algorithms in the fitted plan subspace, with the top-five prohibition placed on it. ## 6.10 What iteration 6 established, what it ruled out, and what it abandoned

Everything below is one model per claim except where a second family is named, at 4B to 8B parameters, on memorised tasks in the style of LeetCode.

**Established.**

1. *Iteration 4's random-push escapes are a property of Qwen3-8B, not of 8-bit floating-point rounding.* At the same absolute displacement, the same 40 directions and the same slots, bf16 escapes on connected components at 0.65 against 0.725 under W8A8 and on shortest path at 0.15 against 0.20, with per-direction shares ranked alike (Spearman 0.96 and 0.87), and per-sample plan noise reproduces (25 and 22 of 50 against 30 and 22). Activation rounding alone adds nothing; a 5-point per-slot boost on connected components comes from the 8-bit floating-point weights or the native kernel. Iteration 5's bf16 null belongs to its ban-free unit or its direction seeds.
2. *In Qwen3-8B the substitute of a ban and the algorithm of an instruction are carried by the residual states at the task-specification positions on the prompt-route tasks.* Exchanging those states alone transfers the ban on shortest path (24 of 30 attempts, 21 of 30 correct programs) and kth smallest (17 of 30 attempts, 16 of 30 correct), and a forced instruction on shortest path (30 of 30 attempts, 30 of 30 correct) and connected components (28 of 30 attempts, 24 of 30 correct); matched-norm random exchanges and a placebo twin transfer at most 0.13. The condition span carries the ban on the direct-route tasks (two sum 1.00, find duplicate 0.90). The read position carries nothing. (iteration-7 correction)
3. *Gemma's BFS-or-DFS choice is made at one generated token,* ` visited` against a blank line, `if` or `queue` at response index 32, about 138 tokens before any algorithm-identifying code, and its fork log-odds is linearly decodable from the residual stream at that position across prompts (Lasso on SAE codes R-squared 0.66 against 0.18 for text, preregistered; ridge on the raw state 0.72, post hoc); at the fork position that is close to a next-token readout, so it shows that the next-token distribution is linearly encoded there, not that a plan is, and the standardised ridge on the same layer-29 SAE codes reaches R-squared 0.15 against 0.086 for a template-plus-noun-norm control (delta 0.064, below the preregistered 0.10 bar). (iteration-7 correction)
4. *Steering the fork works and costs correctness.* Difference in means moves the fork 2.3 times as far as the SAE clamp at matched norm, both move the plan equally at matched effect, and edits toward the minority algorithm lowered the pass rate from 0.84 to 0.16-0.58, except the SAE top-5 clamp (18 BFS, pass 0.84); edits toward the default are clean. (iteration-7 correction)
5. *The NLA does not verbalise the planned algorithm at pre-code positions in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct,* although it names an algorithm at the token where the prompt names it; an outside reader of the text predicts the realised algorithm better than the NLA per sample (0:25 at one unit per sample, p 6.0e-08), and at the task level the evidence is inconclusive (5 task clusters; bootstrap interval [-0.35, 0.02]). (iteration-7 correction)
6. *Record repairs.* The landing half is descriptive (17 of 21 per set, 5 of 8 where the twin wrote no alternative, p 0.053); the movability half is not a strong predictor with a moderate relation not excluded (0.15, interval -0.44 to 0.65); the 14 disputed programs are not novel.

**Ruled out, or not supported.**

- *Activation rounding as the cause of the escapes* (the engine claim's preregistered account): W16A8 escapes like bf16 or slightly less, on both tasks.
- *The Stage A rule of the localization claim* as preregistered: the task-specification states of two sum also transfer brute force at 0.43, above the predicted 0.2.
- *A feature claim for Gemma Scope 2:* the SAE clamp never beats difference in means, and the preregistered feature rule is met by random latents.
- *The verbal readout claim:* 0 of 16, 0 of 112 and 0 of 96 at the end of the prompt; the preregistered verbal edit moves nothing at the prefill site.
- *State noise against token temperature at matched KL* in bf16: 12:6 and 7:3 at alpha 2, not significant.

**Withdrawn.**

- *The prefill-site claim in its preregistered form* in bf16: no common support for the condition span, and breakage at alpha 8. Post hoc (alpha 4 or less) the read position is below the task-specification site on both tasks, but the condition-span clause fails (-1.70 [-3.96, 0.42] and -0.56 [-4.93, 2.91]), so the site of the choice is open, as the artifact's rule label says ('WITHDRAWN as FP8-specific: the site of the choice is open'); its engine half is refuted by Section 6.3. (iteration-7 correction)

**Dead ends, with the evidence that closed them.**

- *8-bit floating-point numerics as an explanation of anything in this run's internal results:* closed by Table 237 and Table 239.
- *The read position as a carrier of the choice:* zero transfer in six Qwen3-8B tasks (Tables 244 to 249) and only the format line in the NLA explanations. Gemma's read position was never read or edited (its SPEC site is a mean over the task-specification positions, from the first token of 'Task:' to the last token of the user message, `src/cfg.py` line 7), so Gemma does not bear on this dead end. (iteration-7 correction)
- *The released layer-20 NLA as a readout of algorithm plans in code:* code is out of distribution for it (fraction of variance explained 0.39 to 0.45), and its pre-code explanations name no algorithm.

**Planned but not run.** DAS in Qwen3-8B (Stage B), the mediation, discreteness and resampling claims, the temperature half of the token claim, and the causal manifold (Section 6.8).

## 6.11 What the next iteration takes from this one

The plan-variable account was tested in part, and its two halves came out differently. Three different quantities were measured, one per model (Table 279): where a ban or instruction is carried in Qwen3-8B (the task-specification states on the prompt-route tasks), where Gemma's natural choice is made (one generated token), and whether Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's plan is verbalisable before the code (not to this NLA); Qwen3-8B's natural choice and Gemma's read position were never measured. Whether the choice is a low-rank variable in Qwen3-8B, and whether random pushes act through it, is untested, because the DAS experiment was lost at planning. The engine control has removed the obstacle that made such a test look premature: random pushes at iteration 4's absolute unit move the algorithm in bf16 as they did in 8-bit floating point, so the escapes are a stable target that a fitted plan subspace can be asked to explain. The next measurements are DAS at the task-specification positions of shortest path and kth smallest, with the Stage A exchanges as the full-state ceiling, and the projection of iteration 4's 40 directions onto the fitted subspace. (iteration-7 correction)

Three leads come with it. The ban-free unit moves fewer programs than the ban unit at a larger scalar dose, so its per-position and per-block profile, or the direction seeds, decide movability; a controlled comparison of the two units on the same seeds would say which. Gemma's one-token fork offers a clean site where a rank-1 DAS subspace moves the fork log-odds by 8.8 nats, a fit that needs the Sutter controls (random initialisation, shuffled targets, forced-DFS sources) before it says anything about dimensionality; whether a smaller push there switches the algorithm without breaking the program is the question for a usable knob. And two sum's task-specification states carry part of a ban that iteration 3 had classed as direct, so the route classes are not all-or-none. (iteration-7 correction)

# What we have learned so far

After six iterations the run has a firm picture of the collapse, a complete answer on temperature, a confirmed internal handle on the algorithm in Qwen3-8B, a measured map of where three models hold the choice, a measured but incomplete account of what a prohibition does, and no correct novel algorithm. Qwen3-8B [5] writes BFS and Dijkstra almost without exception on the two path search tasks and one algorithm on each of 13 further coding tasks (modal share 1.00 on 12, 0.98 on one). The collapse is not universal: three of 15 new tasks are already mixed in the instruct twin (trapped rain water, default share 0.64; minimum spanning tree weight, 0.66; valid anagram, 0.76), and on two of them the instruct model is more diverse than its base model (twin off-default 0.36 against a base off-default share of 0.23, and 0.34 against 0.11). Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [22] attempts more algorithms but its correct grid programs are BFS 20 of 20; gemma-3-4b-it [76] writes DFS in 70% and BFS in 30% of programs for one grid prompt; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [124] shares most of Qwen3-8B's defaults.

Sampling temperature, top-k, top-p, min-p, thinking mode and random context seeds change how the code is worded, not which algorithm it implements. With the token seed coupled across temperatures from 0.3 to 1.3, the algorithm changed in 0 of 20 seeds on three tasks with thinking off, and in 0 of 20 on the shortest path task with thinking on, under top-p 1 and under top-k 10. Phrasings per idea rose from 3 to 13 clusters on the grid task with thinking off; in the literal cell with thinking on, the clusters rise only at temperature 1.3 (5/7/12 at Jaccard thresholds 0.7/0.8/0.9, against 3/6/10 for a repeat at 0.7). State noise on generated tokens against a temperature matched on per-token KL was not established in bf16 (12:6 and 7:3 discordant flips). On other problems temperature above 1 has been reported to raise algorithmic diversity at a correctness cost [72], so the null belongs to these tasks.

A random displacement of the task-specification states at early to middle blocks, sized to the displacement a ban itself causes, changes the algorithm, and this is a property of Qwen3-8B, not of the 8-bit engine on which it was found. At iteration 4's own absolute displacement, directions and slots, bf16 escapes on 26 of 40 directions on connected components and 6 of 40 on shortest path, against 29 and 8 under the 8-bit W8A8 engine, with the same directions escaping (Spearman of per-direction shares 0.96 and 0.87), and per-sample plan noise moves 25 and 22 of 50 attempts against 30 and 22. Rounding the activations to e4m3 per token adds nothing; a 5-point per-slot boost on connected components comes from the 8-bit floating-point weights or the native kernel. The smaller effects that iteration 5 measured in bf16 belong to its ban-free dose unit or its direction seeds: its alpha-2 push was larger at the first edited block than the control's alpha-1 push, which still moved 7 of 50. In bf16 at the ban-free unit, noise at the task-specification positions moves the algorithm (kth smallest 0.37 correct off-default at alpha 2 through blocks 12 to 23; connected components 0.33 at alpha 4 through blocks 0 to 11), while the read position and the condition span barely do; the preregistered site rule was withdrawn for lack of common support and breakage at alpha 8, and a post-hoc model at alpha 4 or less puts the read position below the task-specification site on both tasks but not the condition span (beta -1.70 [-3.96, 0.42] and -0.56 [-4.93, 2.91]), so the site of the choice remains open; on connected components noise acts most at blocks 0 to 11 while the exchange transfers at blocks 12 to 23. Noise in generated tokens 1 to 32 also redirects the choice. The 8-bit site odds ratio (5.72) and the same-seed contrast (17.25 of 20 seeds) were not rerun in bf16. (iteration-7 correction)

Priced as a knob, plan noise is not the practical answer on the evidence so far. Under the 8-bit engine at the ban unit it was the cheapest route to a second correct algorithm on kth smallest (Hill-1 2.72 within 5 pass points) and connected components (2.09); fixed random directions reached above 2 at no cost on kth smallest and two sum, but as maxima over 21 and 9 directions. Against text-level plan samplers, measured in bf16 at the ban-free unit where plan noise was weak, plan noise matched the best sampler on 1 of 5 decisive tasks (ban-free unit and iteration-5 seeds; pending the 2x2 of Step K): an intent sentence written by the base model, with the code written by the instruct model, won on connected components, the shortest path task and two sum (2.53, 1.45 and 1.61), and enumerate and pick reached the most raw diversity at 16 to 62 pass points. That comparison has not been repeated at the absolute unit at which plan noise is strong. Plan noise beat decoding at matched departure on kth smallest at alpha 2 (13:0) and not elsewhere (6:3). Generate then select [43] and enumerate and pick, which hand the choice to an external random draw, remain ceilings with large pass costs. (iteration-7 correction)

Three quantities have now been measured, one per model and each at its own site (Table 279). In Qwen3-8B the residual states at the task-specification positions carry the substitute of a ban and the algorithm of an instruction on the prompt-route tasks: exchanging those states alone into a neutral twin transfers the ban on shortest path (24 of 30 attempts, 21 of 30 correct programs) and kth smallest (17 of 30 attempts, 16 of 30 correct) and a forced instruction on shortest path (30 of 30 attempts, 30 of 30 correct) and connected components (28 of 30 attempts, 24 of 30 correct), while matched-norm random exchanges and a placebo transfer at most 4 of 30; on the direct-route tasks the condition span carries the ban. Qwen3-8B's natural choice was not measured. In gemma-3-4b-it the natural choice between BFS and DFS is made at one generated token after a shared 32-token opening (` visited` leads to DFS with BFS probability 0.011; a blank line, `if` or `queue` lead to BFS at 0.95 to 1.00), about 138 tokens before the code identifies the algorithm. Its fork log-odds is linearly decodable across prompts from the residual stream at that position (a preregistered Lasso on Gemma Scope 2 SAE codes R-squared 0.66 against 0.18 for the text; a post-hoc ridge on the raw state 0.72), but a linear readout of the fork log-odds from the residual at the fork position is close to a next-token readout, so the raw-residual 0.72 shows that the next-token distribution is linearly encoded there, not that a plan is, and the standardised ridge on the same layer-29 SAE codes reaches R-squared 0.15 against 0.086 for a template-plus-noun-norm control (delta 0.064, below the preregistered 0.10 bar). Within the controls it had, a rank-1 DAS subspace fitted on forced-BFS sources moves the held-out fork log-odds by 8.8 nats (random subspaces of the same rank -0.08 to +0.05); because every source was forced-BFS, the shuffled-source control is uninformative by construction (10.1 nats); no random-initialisation or target-shuffled control was run; and the rank-4 interchange gives BFS in 50 of 50 attempts with 0 of 50 programs passing, so this does not show that the choice is one-dimensional; a difference-in-means edit moves the fork log-odds 2.3 times as far as the SAE clamp at matched norm, and edits toward the minority algorithm lowered the pass rate from 0.84 to 0.16-0.58, except the SAE top-5 clamp (18 BFS, pass 0.84), so no feature claim is made. Gemma's read position was never read or edited. In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct a natural language autoencoder names the algorithm at the token where the prompt names it and not 170 tokens later, and its pre-code explanations name no algorithm; an outside reader of the text predicts the realised algorithm better per unit (20:88), and with one unit per sample (the first in position order, 104 samples) the contrast is 0:25 (exact p 6.0e-08), with a task-cluster interval of [-0.35, 0.02] that is inconclusive at the task level; a verbal edit steered two of four tasks only at the generated-token site and large doses, in an exploratory follow-up. The read position is inert as a carrier in Qwen3-8B and in the NLA's reading. Whether the choice in Qwen3-8B is a low-rank variable, and whether random pushes act through it, is untested: the DAS experiment was lost at planning. The forced-prompt subspace of iteration 4 did not predict which directions move the algorithm (within-task Spearman 0.03), although which directions move is reproducible. (iteration-7 correction)

The internal results that hold under bf16 are therefore: the route of a ban (iterations 2 and 3), the band patching on kth smallest and connected components, the exchange of Stage A, the escape fractions and per-sample plan-noise rates of iteration 4 at their absolute unit, the transplant results of iteration 5, and the read-position transplant that breaks the output without moving the algorithm; the post-hoc site ordering is not among them, because its condition-span clause fails post hoc. The 8-bit site odds ratio, the same-seed contrast and the forced-prompt subspace tests are 8-bit results not rerun. (iteration-7 correction)

A single prompt ban, where the model obeys it, removes the default and the output collapses on one replacement: Bellman-Ford/SPFA on the shortest path task (272 of 272 compliant iteration-1 programs; 255 of 260 iteration-2 attempts not banned), DFS on the grid task (116 of 128; 257 of 257), and quickselect and size-k heap, brute force, index marking and BFS on the bench tasks where Qwen3-8B obeys (4 of 12 once avoidance counts only catalogue algorithms). Shown a correct program of another algorithm and told not to use it, the model goes home to its default (0.05 of attempts under the copy prompt, 0.72 under the ban), and Llama does the same on five of six present minor bans. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct mostly ignores bans, and its ban of DFS on connected components raised DFS from 29 to 43 correct programs. How often a ban is obeyed depends on its wording more than on anything else measured; the fourth template, which states only that X is not allowed here, is the weakest in every artifact, in Gemma and in Qwen2.5, where all 70 of its programs used the banned default. Bans of five names fail by reimplementation in both families tested: Qwen3-8B and Gemma write no algorithm outside the banned set (avoidance 0.00), Gemma moving from its default DFS to its minority BFS (10 to 41 of 50) at half the pass rate, with its prompt states beside a banned centroid in activation space; at doses of 1 to 8 ban units, which overshoot the forced-prompt manifold, a push along the top-five direction breaks programs before it moves the algorithm; an in-manifold dose was not tried. (iteration-7 correction)

What decides the replacement under a modal ban has measured leads and no confirmed rule. The likelihood instrument of iteration 2 cannot decide it, and substitution by the alternative the model states is not supported in Qwen3-8B. The runner-up of the base model names where a push lands in 17 of 21 recorded events across Qwen3-8B and Gemma (5 of 5 on the 8-bit screen, 1 of 2 on the bf16 remeasurement, 3 of 3 and 3 of 4 on new tasks, 5 of 7 in Gemma), and it beats the instruct twin's teacher-forced ranking of algorithm openings 8:1 where the two disagree (p 0.020, retrospective). But where the instruct twin already writes an alternative, that alternative names the landing as often (6 of 7), and on the 8 held-out events where the twin wrote none the base runner-up named 5 (p 0.053): the landing half is descriptive. The base model's own variety does not say whether a task can be moved: over 13 new units its off-default share ranks movability at Spearman 0.15 (95% interval -0.44 to 0.65; power 0.63 at a true 0.6; 0.035 if count inversions' share is taken from its correct programs), so a strong relation is excluded and a moderate one is not; only the runtime merit of the fastest alternative tracks movability after Holm correction (0.71). Both verdicts are conditional on the ban-free unit and seeds of iteration 5 (ban-free unit and iteration-5 seeds; pending the 2x2 of Step K). Writing the task-specification states of the base model into the instruct prefill reopened the base runner-up on 1 of 5 Qwen3-8B tasks and 2 of 7 Gemma tasks, the latter where the instruct twin already wrote it 8% to 12% of the time. (iteration-7 correction)

Where a ban acts depends on the task. On the path tasks it is carried mostly by the prompt states (likelihood readout 0.85; behaviour 0.98 on the shortest path task, mixed on the grid task), and Stage A now shows the same for shortest path and kth smallest in behaviour. On the bench, pooled over five gated tasks, the direct route carries 0.744 [0.38, 1.11] of the behavioural effect and the prompt states 0.611 [0.06, 1.17], with overlapping intervals; two sum, classed as direct, also carries 0.43 of its ban in the task-specification states. The ban is enforced at the opening of the program body, to a single token on kth smallest; Gemma's natural choice falls at the same point, the first algorithm-specific statement after an opening shared by every algorithm. The read position predicts how strongly a wording will be obeyed (-0.41 across 110 wordings) but carries none of the effect when exchanged or spliced. Push movability as a forecast of which bans a model obeys is closed: inconclusive in the held-out family under its primary rule and disconfirmed under its drop sensitivity.

No instruction, knob, push, transplant, feature clamp or verbal edit produced a correct novel algorithm. Iterations 1 to 3 produced 116 correct programs outside the catalogue and none was new; iteration 4, none of 14,206 correct programs of the site and subspace experiments; iteration 5, none of 130 correct programs outside the catalogue. In iteration 6 a second blind adjudication of the 14 transplant programs that two of three judges had called novel, by two model families the run had not used and with ten controls of known class, found 1 novel call by one judge (a linear search, overturned on a full read) and 0 by the other, a final count of 0; the exchange experiment, the Gemma experiment (1 of 1,450 correct programs outside the catalogue) and the NLA experiment (10 correct programs labelled other) found none either. The long-form instruction of the request makes most outputs claim novelty while their code is a catalogue algorithm or absent. Within single-sample generation the reachable ideas are the model's known catalogue; search with an evaluator, which this run did not test, is the documented route to new programs [81, 82].

What remains open follows from this. First, the plan-and-fork account: whether Qwen3-8B's choice is a low-rank plan variable at the task-specification positions that is realised at a fork token in generation, tested by DAS fitted against the Stage A exchanges (whose correct-Y counts are the full-state denominator) and by the projection of iteration 4's 40 directions onto the fitted subspace. Second, DAS with the Sutter controls (a fit on a randomly initialised model, shuffled targets and forced-DFS sources), without which neither Gemma's fork subspace nor a Qwen3-8B one says anything about dimensionality. Third, the fork-margin test of temperature: whether temperature changes the algorithm only where the margin at a fork token is small, which would reconcile the temperature nulls with forking-path accounts. Fourth, the circuit at Gemma's fork, the transcoder attribution graph that the first-order fallback replaced. Fifth, evaluator-guided search, the documented route to new programs [81, 82], which this run has not tried. The question of what makes the ban-free unit weaker than the ban unit (its per-position and per-block profile or its direction seeds) and whether base intent holds on more tasks remain as before. Of the items of the request, the following have been run: the geometry plots in activation coordinates (at a label-dependent position in iteration 2, at the plan site in iteration 4, and for the top-five prohibition in Qwen3-8B and Gemma in iteration 6), the top-five prohibition by prompt, token veto and plan push, natural BFS against DFS internals (within a ban in Qwen3-8B, within one prompt in Gemma), thought anchors, the logit and tuned lenses, the same seed test with thinking on and off and with top-k 10, natural language autoencoders (on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), sparse autoencoders (Qwen-Scope on Qwen3-8B, Gemma Scope 2 on Gemma) and a first-order attribution in place of a circuit graph. The manifold of algorithms in a causally fitted plan subspace was planned and not run. (iteration-7 correction)
